Yet you hold fast my name, and you did not deny my faith even in the days of Antipas my faithful witness, who was killed among you, where Satan dwells.<sup>14</sup>But I have a few things against you: you have some there who hold the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to put a stumbling block before the sons of Israel, so that they might eat food sacrificed to idols and practice sexual immorality.<sup>15</sup>So also you have some who hold the teaching of the Nicolaitans.<sup>16</sup>Therefore repent. If not, I will come to you soon and war against them with the sword of my mouth.<sup>17</sup>He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. To the one who conquers I will give some of the hidden manna, and I will give him a white stone, with a new name written on the stone that no one knows except the one who receives it.’<sup>18</sup>“And to the angel of the church in Thyatira write: ‘The words of the Son of God, who has eyes like a flame of fire, and whose feet are like burnished bronze.<sup>19</sup>”‘I know your works, your love and faith and service and patient endurance, and that your latter works exceed the first.<sup>20</sup>But I have this against you, that you tolerate that woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess and is teaching and seducing my servants to practice sexual immorality and to eat food sacrificed to idols.<sup>21</sup>I gave her time to repent, but she refuses to repent of her sexual immorality.<sup>22</sup>Behold, I will throw her onto a sickbed, and those who commit adultery with her I will throw into great tribulation, unless they repent of her works,<sup>23</sup>and I will strike her children dead. And all the churches will know that I am he who searches mind and heart, and I will give to each of you according to your works.<sup>24</sup>But to the rest of you in Thyatira, who do not hold this teaching, who have not learned what some call the deep things of Satan, to you I say, I do not lay on you any other burden.<sup>25</sup>Only hold fast what you have until I come.<sup>26</sup>The one who conquers and who keeps my works until the end, to him I will give authority over the nations,<sup>27</sup>and he will rule them with a rod of iron, as when earthen pots are broken in pieces, even as I myself have received authority from my Father.<sup>28</sup>And I will give him the morning star.<sup>29</sup>He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.’

3.title: Letters to Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea
3.overview:
The final three letters of the seven complete the range of pastoral diagnosis the risen Christ brings to his churches. Sardis has a reputation for life but is spiritually dead. Philadelphia is small and weak but receives no rebuke and the most lavish promises. Laodicea is wealthy and self-satisfied and receives the most devastating rebuke of all.

Together the seven letters form a kind of mirror in which every church and every believer can find themselves. There is no congregation in history that does not exist somewhere on the spectrum these letters describe. The genius of John’s use of seven churches is that seven is the number of completeness: these seven letters are the full portrait of the church in every age, not just the church of Asia Minor in the first century.

The chapter ends with Christ standing at the door and knocking. The cosmic drama of the throne room is inseparable from the intimate pastoral reality of the local congregation. The one who will come with the clouds of heaven (1:7) is the same one who stands at the door of Laodicea and knocks (3:20). The book does not let us choose between the cosmic and the personal, the eschatological and the pastoral. Both are always in play.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — To the Church in Sardis
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Sardis had been the capital of Lydia and the seat of Croesus, and the first coins ever struck were minted there. By John’s day it was a comfortable provincial town with a magnificent past and no importance. Verse 1 introduces Christ as the one who has the seven spirits of God and the seven stars — the Spirit and the messengers both in his hand — and then delivers the shortest, harshest assessment in the seven letters: you have the reputation of being alive, but you are dead. The word for reputation is onoma, a name. No heresy is named here and no persecution; Sardis is one of only two churches with no enemies mentioned at all.

Verse 2 issues the remedy: wake up, and strengthen what remains and is about to die, for I have not found your works complete in the sight of my God. The works are not wrong but unfinished — finished enough for the province, not for God. Verse 3 adds three more commands, remember what you received and heard, keep it, repent, and then the threat: I will come like a thief, and you will not know at what hour I will come against you. Sardis stood on a spur thought impregnable and fell twice, in 546 and 214 BC, both times to a night climber up the cliff while the garrison slept.

Verse 4 turns: you have still a few names in Sardis, people who have not soiled their garments. The word is names again — the church has a name and is dead; these have no name and are alive. Verse 5 gives them three promises: white garments, a name never blotted out of the book of life (a city kept a citizen register and struck names from it at death or conviction), and confession of that name before the Father and the angels (cf. Matt. 10:32). Verse 6 sounds the refrain.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Name for Being Alive

Sardis had a reputation for life and was dead. Christ calls it to wake up, strengthen what remains, remember and repent, and he counts the few who have not soiled their garments.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The city had twice fallen to a night climb while the guards slept.

Now: Ask whether the reasons you would give for your church’s health are reasons Sardis could have given.

verseByVerse.quote: "And to the angel of the church in Sardis write: 'The words of him who has the seven spirits of God and the seven stars. "I know your works. You have the reputation of being alive, but you are dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ tells Sardis that it has a reputation for being alive but is in fact dead.

Sardis. Once a great and wealthy capital, by John’s day living on its past.

The seven spirits and the seven stars. The Spirit who gives life, and Christ who holds the churches.

Reputation. Busy, admired and well spoken of. Activity can disguise death.

On a Tuesday. What would Christ say if he looked past your church’s reputation, or your own?
verseByVerse.note: Sardis had been a great royal city. Its seemingly impregnable citadel was taken by surprise more than once in its history.

verseByVerse.quote: Wake up, and strengthen what remains and is about to die, for I have not found your works complete in the sight of my God. Remember, then, what you received and heard. Keep it, and repent. If you will not wake up, I will come like a thief, and you will not know at what hour I will come against you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ commands Sardis to wake up and strengthen what is left, remember what they received, keep it and repent, or he will come like a thief.

Wake up. Sardis had twice been captured because its watchmen slept. The church was repeating its city’s history.

Not complete. Started well, never finished.

Remember, keep, repent. The gospel they first heard is the cure.

Like a thief. Unexpected and unwelcome to the unprepared (Matthew 24:43).

On a Tuesday. What have you neglected that is about to die? Strengthen it today.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet you have still a few names in Sardis, people who have not soiled their garments, and they will walk with me in white, for they are worthy. The one who conquers will be clothed thus in white garments, and I will never blot his name out of the book of life. I will confess his name before my Father and before his angels. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
A few in Sardis have not soiled their garments and will walk with Christ in white; the conqueror will be clothed in white, never blotted out of the book of life, and confessed by name before the Father.

A few names. Christ knows the faithful remnant by name.

White. Purity and victory, given, not earned (7:14).

Worthy. Not by merit, but fit for what they have been given.

Where Christians differ: can a name be blotted out? Arminians read this as warning that a true believer may lose salvation. Verdict: the verse is a promise that the conqueror’s name will never be blotted out. Those whose names are written before the foundation of the world (13:8; 17:8) persevere. The promise is the means by which Christ keeps them.

I will confess his name. Matthew 10:32.

Textual note. One letter separates “in this way” (houtōs) from “this one” (houtos) at the start of v. 5. The earliest read “in this way”; either way, the conqueror is clothed in white.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–13 — To the Church in Philadelphia
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Philadelphia was the youngest of the seven cities, founded as a missionary outpost of Greek culture on the edge of the uplands, and it sat on a fault line. The earthquake of AD 17 destroyed it, aftershocks went on for years, and people camped outside the walls rather than sleep under a roof. Twice the city took a new name to thank an emperor who paid for its rebuilding.

Verse 7 introduces Christ with four descriptions, none of them drawn from the vision of chapter 1: the holy one, the true one (alēthinos, the genuine article as against the counterfeit), and the holder of the key of David who opens and no one shuts — quoted from Isaiah 22:22, where the key of the royal house is laid on the shoulder of a new steward. Verse 8 sets before them an open door no one can shut, and gives the most encouraging assessment in the seven letters: I know that you have but little power, and yet you have kept my word and have not denied my name.

Verse 9 promises that the accusers who deny them a share in the promises will come and bow before them — and the sentence ends not with humiliation but with they will learn that I have loved you. Verse 10 is the disputed one: I will keep you from the hour of trial that is coming on the whole world, where both the hour of trial and keep from are argued over, and the readings are set out at the verse. Verse 11 gives the instruction: I am coming soon. Hold fast what you have, so that no one may seize your crown.

Verse 12 answers the city’s history point by point: a pillar in the temple of God, never to go out of it, for people who had lived in tents outside their own walls; and three names written on him — God’s name, the name of the new Jerusalem, and Christ’s own new name (cf. 19:12) — for a town that had twice taken a new name and twice seen it fade. Verse 13 closes with the refrain.
verseByVerse.theology:
Little Power, No Rebuke

Christ holds the key of David and sets an open door before a weak church that has kept his word. Its accusers will learn that he has loved it; the faithful will be pillars in the temple of God and bear his names.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A small congregation in an earthquake town had been told it had no share in the promises.

Now: Christ measures a church by faithfulness, not size.

verseByVerse.quote: "And to the angel of the church in Philadelphia write: 'The words of the holy one, the true one, who has the key of David, who opens and no one will shut, who shuts and no one opens. "I know your works. Behold, I have set before you an open door, which no one is able to shut. I know that you have but little power, and yet you have kept my word and have not denied my name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The holy and true one, who holds the key of David, has set an open door before Philadelphia that no one can shut, because with little strength they kept his word and did not deny his name.

The key of David. Isaiah 22:22. Christ alone controls access to God’s kingdom.

An open door. Where Christians differ. An opportunity for the gospel (1 Corinthians 16:9), or entry into the kingdom. Verdict: probably both: assurance of their welcome into the kingdom, and opportunity to bring others in.

Little power. A small, weak church, yet no rebuke from Christ.

On a Tuesday. Small strength is no barrier to faithfulness or to God’s opened doors.
verseByVerse.note: Philadelphia was a small city often shaken by earthquakes.

parallels.desc: he shall open, and none shall shut

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I will make those of the synagogue of Satan who say that they are Jews and are not, but lie—behold, I will make them come and bow down before your feet, and they will learn that I have loved you. Because you have kept my word about patient endurance, I will keep you from the hour of trial that is coming on the whole world, to try those who dwell on the earth. I am coming soon. Hold fast what you have, so that no one may seize your crown.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ will make their opponents acknowledge his love for them, keep them from the hour of trial coming on the whole world, and he is coming soon, so they must hold fast.

Bow before your feet. Isaiah 60:14 is turned around: the persecutors will know who God loves.

Where Christians differ: kept from the hour of trial. Pre-tribulationists read this as a promise that the church will be removed from the earth before a future great tribulation. Verdict: the same phrase in John 17:15 means protection within trouble, not removal from the world. Christ promises to keep his people through trial, not to rapture them secretly beforehand.

Your crown. Hold on, so that no one takes away your reward.

On a Tuesday. Christ keeps you in trouble, not always from it.

verseByVerse.quote: The one who conquers, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God. Never shall he go out of it, and I will write on him the name of my God, and the name of the city of my God, the new Jerusalem, which comes down from my God out of heaven, and my own new name. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The conqueror will be a pillar in God’s temple, never to leave, and Christ will write on him the name of God, the new Jerusalem, and his own new name.

A pillar. Philadelphia was shaken by earthquakes; people often fled the city. Here is permanence.

Names written. Ownership and belonging. You will be marked as God’s, as Jerusalem’s citizen, and as Christ’s.

The new Jerusalem. Described in chapter 21.

For worship. Thank God that his people will never again have to leave his presence.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–22 — To the Church in Laodicea
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Laodicea sat at the junction of three trade roads and made its money three ways: banking, a glossy black wool exported across the empire, and a medical school producing a famous eye ointment. When an earthquake levelled it in AD 60 it refused imperial relief and rebuilt at its own expense — Tacitus records it, and the city was proud of it. Every line of this letter is written against that fact.

Verse 14 gives three titles, each a rebuke before any criticism: the Amen (the God of Amen, Isa. 65:16; cf. 2 Cor. 1:20), the faithful and true witness, and the beginning of God’s creation — archē, origin and source, not first creature.

Verses 15–16 turn on local geography. Hierapolis six miles north had hot healing springs; Colossae ten miles east had cold mountain water; Laodicea had to pipe water in and it arrived tepid and unpleasant. So cold is not indifference on a scale. Cold water is good and hot water is good; the charge is uselessness. I will spit you out of my mouth renders emeō, to vomit — the involuntary reaction to a cup of Laodicean tap water.

Verse 17 quotes the church’s own words, the only congregation permitted to speak in these letters: I am rich, I have prospered, and I need nothing — not realizing that you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked. The last three answer the three industries exactly. Verse 18 responds with an offer rather than a command — I counsel you to buy from me — gold refined by fire for the bank, white garments for the wool town, eye salve for the medical school (cf. Isa. 55:1).

Verse 19 reframes everything: Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline (Prov. 3:12; Heb. 12:5–11), using phileō, the warmer word. Verse 20 has Christ knocking outside his own church, offering the evening meal to whoever opens — and the invitation narrows to the singular, if anyone. Verse 21 gives the last and largest promise of the seven, a seat on his own throne, grounded on a conquest already finished. Verse 22 closes the letters with the refrain for the seventh time.
verseByVerse.theology:
Useless, Not Merely Lukewarm

Laodicea’s water was neither hot nor cold and good for nothing, and so was its church. Rich and self-sufficient, it did not know it was poor, blind and naked. Christ counsels it to buy from him, disciplines because he loves, and knocks at the door.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A city that refused imperial relief produced a church that said, “I need nothing.”

Now: Ask who in your town is helped because your church exists — and open the door to him.

verseByVerse.quote: "And to the angel of the church in Laodicea write: 'The words of the Amen, the faithful and true witness, the beginning of God's creation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ addresses Laodicea as the Amen, the faithful and true witness, and the beginning of God’s creation.

Laodicea. A wealthy banking city, with a medical school famed for eye-salve and a textile trade in black wool.

The Amen. Isaiah 65:16, “the God of truth” (literally “of Amen”). Christ is God’s final “yes” (2 Corinthians 1:20).

The beginning of God’s creation. Where Christians differ. Arians, and today Jehovah’s Witnesses, read this as saying Christ was the first thing God created. Verdict: archē means origin or ruler here, as in Colossians 1:15–18, written to the neighbouring church. Christ is the source and ruler of creation, not a creature (John 1:3).
verseByVerse.note: Laodicea, about ten miles from Colossae, was a wealthy banking and textile city. Rebuilt without imperial aid after an earthquake in AD 60, it prided itself on needing nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: "I know your works: you are neither cold nor hot. Would that you were either cold or hot! So, because you are lukewarm, and neither hot nor cold, I will spit you out of my mouth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Laodicea is neither cold nor hot but lukewarm, and Christ will spit it out.

Laodicea’s water. Hierapolis had hot springs; Colossae had cold water; Laodicea’s water arrived tepid by aqueduct and full of minerals.

Cold is good too. The point is not enthusiasm against apathy. Hot water heals; cold refreshes. Laodicea did neither: it was useless.

What it does not mean. Christ is not preferring open rejection (“cold”) to lukewarm faith.

On a Tuesday. Is your faith doing anyone any good?
verseByVerse.note: Often explained from local water: hot springs at nearby Hierapolis and cold water at Colossae, while Laodicea’s piped-in water arrived tepid. Both hot and cold are useful; lukewarm is not.

verseByVerse.quote: For you say, "I am rich, I have prospered, and I need nothing," not realizing that you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked. I counsel you to buy from me gold refined by fire, so that you may be rich, and white garments so that you may clothe yourself and the shame of your nakedness may not be seen, and salve to anoint your eyes, so that you may see.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Laodicea thinks it is rich and needs nothing, but is wretched, poor, blind and naked; Christ counsels it to buy from him gold, white garments and eye-salve.

I need nothing. The most dangerous words a church can say.

Three gifts. Gold for a banking city, white garments for a city of black wool, eye-salve for a city of medicine. Christ offers what they think they have.

Buy from me. Buying without money (Isaiah 55:1): coming to Christ empty-handed.

On a Tuesday. Where is comfort hiding your need of Christ?

verseByVerse.quote: Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline, so be zealous and repent. Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and eat with him, and he with me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ disciplines those he loves, so they must repent; he stands at the door and knocks, and whoever opens will have fellowship with him.

Discipline is love. Proverbs 3:12; Hebrews 12:5–11.

At the door of a church. Christ stands outside a church that has left him out.

Where Christians differ: an evangelistic invitation? The verse is often used to invite unbelievers to “open the door” to Christ. Some Arminians use it to show that salvation depends on the human will. Verdict: its first meaning is a call to a lukewarm church to restore fellowship. It may be applied to unbelievers, since Christ freely invites all, but opening comes by his grace, not by our unaided will (John 6:44).

Eat with him. The intimacy of a shared meal, and a foretaste of the marriage supper (19:9).

On a Tuesday. Has Christ been left outside some part of your life? Open the door.

verseByVerse.quote: The one who conquers, I will grant him to sit with me on my throne, as I also conquered and sat down with my Father on his throne. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The conqueror will sit with Christ on his throne, as Christ conquered and sat with the Father on his.

From the door to the throne. The church Christ nearly spat out is offered the highest promise in the letters.

As I conquered. By the cross (5:5–6).

He who has an ear. Seven times. Every church must listen to every letter.

For worship. Thank Christ, who shares his victory and his throne with weak, lukewarm people who repent.

4.title: Holy, Holy, Holy: The Throne Room of Heaven
4.overview:
After the letters to the seven churches, the scene shifts dramatically. John is drawn up through an open door in heaven and finds himself standing before the throne of God. Everything changes. The pastoral specificity of the seven letters gives way to cosmic, overwhelming, dazzling vision. Before any seal is opened, before any trumpet sounds, before any judgment falls, John must see — and the church must see with him — what actually governs history. The answer is: this throne. This worship. This God.

Chapters 4 and 5 together form the interpretive center of the entire book. Chapter 4 answers the question: Who is God? Chapter 5 answers the question: How has God chosen to rule? The answer to the first is: the Creator of all things, infinitely holy, eternally worshipped, Almighty. The answer to the second is: through the slaughtered Lamb who has conquered. Everything that follows in Revelation — every seal, every trumpet, every bowl, every beast, every judgment, every promise — flows from these two chapters as from a spring.

Interpretive flag — “Come up here” (v. 1): Dispensational premillennialists have often read “Come up here” as a prophetic picture of the Rapture — the moment at which the church is caught up to heaven before the tribulation begins. The supporting observation is that the word “church” (ekklēsia) does not appear again in Revelation after chapter 3 until 22:16, suggesting the church has been removed from the scene. The amillennial/idealist reading understands “Come up here” as the commission given specifically to John for his visionary experience — John, not the church, is called up to receive the vision. The church’s absence from the term ekklēsia in chapters 4–22 is explained by the fact that the church is addressed throughout these chapters under other designations: the 144,000, the two witnesses, the great multitude, the bride, the new Jerusalem. The amillennial reading is followed here, with genuine respect for the dispensational position.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Throne Room of Heaven
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2 open the vision: a door standing open in heaven, the trumpet voice of 1:10 calling come up here, John at once in the Spirit, and then the sentence the whole book turns on — a throne stood in heaven, with one seated on the throne. The word throne occurs some forty-seven times in Revelation and about fifteen times in the whole of the rest of the New Testament. Nothing else in the room is described first.

Verse 3 describes the one seated with three colours and nothing else: jasper (clear as crystal, 21:11), carnelian (blood-red), and around the throne a rainbow like an emerald. Carnelian was the first stone of the high priest’s breastpiece and jasper the last (Ex. 28:17–20). The rainbow is the sign given after the flood, a warrior’s bow hung up and pointed away (Gen. 9:13–16). No face is described, and the restraint is the point.

Verse 4 sets twenty-four elders on twenty-four thrones around it, in white garments with golden crowns — every reward promised to the seven churches, already being worn. Verse 5 fills the room with Sinai: lightning, rumblings and peals of thunder out of the throne itself (Ex. 19:16–19), and seven burning torches which John identifies as the seven spirits of God.

Verse 6 gives the floor — a sea of glass, like crystal, chaos frozen solid in front of the throne (cf. Ex. 24:10; 21:1) — and introduces four living creatures, nearer than the elders, covered in eyes. Verse 7 names them: lion, ox, the face of a man, and an eagle in flight, drawn from Ezekiel’s cherubim (Ezek. 1:5–11).

Verse 8 gives them Isaiah’s six wings and Isaiah’s song — Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come (Isa. 6:2–3) — sung without ceasing, day and night. Verses 9–11 close the chapter with a repeated movement: whenever the creatures give glory, the twenty-four elders fall down, cast their crowns before the throne, and say Worthy are you, our Lord and God… for you created all things, and by your will they existed and were created.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Throne Comes First

Before any seal is opened, John is shown an occupied throne, ringed by a rainbow and surrounded by unceasing worship: holy, holy, holy. The Creator of all things is worthy.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Domitian liked to be called “our Lord and God”; the elders give those words to the true throne.

Now: Lay down every crown you were given before the one who gave it.

verseByVerse.quote: After this I looked, and behold, a door standing open in heaven! And the first voice, which I had heard speaking to me like a trumpet, said, "Come up here, and I will show you what must take place after this." At once I was in the Spirit, and behold, a throne stood in heaven, with one seated on the throne.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John is called up through an open door in heaven and, in the Spirit, sees a throne with someone seated on it.

The throne. The word appears more than forty times in Revelation, and seventeen in chapters 4–5. Before any judgment falls, John sees who rules.

Seated. God is not pacing, anxious or reacting. The throne is occupied.

Where Christians differ: is this the rapture? Dispensationalists read “Come up here” as a picture of the church caught up before the tribulation, noting that “church” is not named again until chapter 22. Verdict: the summons is to John, as to the prophets before him (Ezekiel 1). The church is present on earth throughout, under other names: saints, servants, the bride (13:7; 19:7). There is no secret rapture here.

On a Tuesday. Before reading the news, look up. The throne is not empty.

verseByVerse.quote: And he who sat there had the appearance of jasper and carnelian, and around the throne was a rainbow that had the appearance of an emerald.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one on the throne shone like precious stones, and a rainbow like emerald encircled the throne.

No description of God. John describes light and colour, not a form (Ezekiel 1:26–28). God is beyond depiction.

The rainbow. God’s covenant promise to Noah (Genesis 9:13). Mercy surrounds the throne before judgment is unleashed.

For worship. Thank God that his throne is circled by promise.

verseByVerse.quote: Around the throne were twenty-four thrones, and seated on the thrones were twenty-four elders, clothed in white garments, with golden crowns on their heads. From the throne came flashes of lightning, and rumblings and peals of thunder, and before the throne were burning seven torches of fire, which are the seven spirits of God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Around the throne sat twenty-four elders in white with golden crowns, and from the throne came lightning and thunder, with seven torches, the seven spirits of God.

Where Christians differ: who are the elders? Some see an order of angels. Others see the people of God, represented by the twelve tribes and twelve apostles (21:12–14). Verdict: probably the whole people of God, Old and New Testament, represented in heaven, since they wear white and crowns as believers are promised (3:5; 2:10).

Lightning and thunder. As at Sinai (Exodus 19:16). God’s holy presence.

Seven torches. The Holy Spirit in his fullness (1:4; Zechariah 4:2–6).
verseByVerse.note: Twenty-four may combine the twelve tribes and the twelve apostles — the whole people of God.

verseByVerse.quote: and before the throne there was as it were a sea of glass, like crystal. And around the throne, on each side of the throne, are four living creatures, full of eyes in front and behind: the first living creature like a lion, the second living creature like an ox, the third living creature with the face of a man, and the fourth living creature like an eagle in flight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the throne was a sea of glass like crystal, and around it four living creatures full of eyes, like a lion, an ox, a man and an eagle.

The sea of glass. In the Bible the sea often means chaos and evil (13:1; 21:1). Here it lies still before God’s throne.

The living creatures. Like Ezekiel’s cherubim (Ezekiel 1:10) and Isaiah’s seraphim (Isaiah 6:2): the highest of created beings.

Lion, ox, man, eagle. The noblest, strongest, wisest and swiftest of creatures. All creation is represented in worship.

Full of eyes. Ceaseless watchfulness.

What it does not mean. The church later linked the four with the four Gospels. That is a pious application, not the meaning of the text.

verseByVerse.quote: And the four living creatures, each of them with six wings, are full of eyes all around and within, and day and night they never cease to say, "Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The living creatures cry day and night without ceasing, “Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come!”

Isaiah 6:3. Holiness is the attribute repeated three times: God’s utter otherness and purity.

Never cease. The highest creatures never tire of God.

Textual note. One major manuscript repeats “holy” eight times and a few others nine. The threefold reading, as in Isaiah, is surely original.

For worship. Sing “Holy, holy, holy” this Sunday as heaven does.

verseByVerse.quote: And whenever the living creatures give glory and honor and thanks to him who is seated on the throne, who lives forever and ever, the twenty-four elders fall down before him who is seated on the throne and worship him who lives forever and ever. They cast their crowns before the throne, saying, "Worthy are you, our Lord and God, to receive glory and honor and power, for you created all things, and by your will they existed and were created."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whenever the creatures give glory, the elders fall down, cast their crowns before the throne, and declare God worthy of glory because he created all things.

Our Lord and God. The emperor Domitian liked to be called this. The churches heard whose title it really was.

Casting crowns. Every reward goes back to the giver.

Worthy because Creator. All things exist by his will. Creation is the first reason for worship.

Textual note. Later manuscripts read “O Lord” for “our Lord and God”, and “they are” for “they existed”. The earliest support the ESV.

On a Tuesday. Lay down before God the things you are proudest of.

For worship. Praise God as Creator: everything you see exists because he wills it.

4.text: <sup>1</sup>After this I looked, and behold, a door standing open in heaven! And the first voice, which I had heard speaking to me like a trumpet, said, “Come up here, and I will show you what must take place after this.”<sup>2</sup>At once I was in the Spirit, and behold, a throne stood in heaven, with one seated on the throne.<sup>3</sup>And he who sat there had the appearance of jasper and carnelian, and around the throne was a rainbow that had the appearance of an emerald.<sup>4</sup>Around the throne were twenty-four thrones, and seated on the thrones were twenty-four elders, clothed in white garments, with golden crowns on their heads.<sup>5</sup>From the throne came flashes of lightning, and rumblings and peals of thunder, and before the throne were burning seven torches of fire, which are the seven spirits of God,<sup>6</sup>and before the throne there was as it were a sea of glass, like crystal. And around the throne, on each side of the throne, are four living creatures, full of eyes in front and behind:<sup>7</sup>the first living creature like a lion, the second living creature like an ox, the third living creature with the face of a man, and the fourth living creature like an eagle in flight.<sup>8</sup>And the four living creatures, each of them with six wings, are full of eyes all around and within, and day and night they never cease to say, “Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come!”<sup>9</sup>And whenever the living creatures give glory and honor and thanks to him who is seated on the throne, who lives forever and ever,<sup>10</sup>the twenty-four elders fall down before him who is seated on the throne and worship him who lives forever and ever. They cast their crowns before the throne, saying,<sup>11</sup>“Worthy are you, our Lord and God, to receive glory and honor and power, for you created all things, and by your will they existed and were created.”

5.title: The Scroll and the Lamb
5.overview:
Chapter 5 is perhaps the most emotionally dramatic chapter in the entire Bible. It begins with a crisis — a sealed scroll that no one can open — passes through grief — John weeps uncontrollably — and arrives at an explosion of worship that fills all of heaven and earth. The transition from weeping to worship is accomplished by a single announcement: the Lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered, and he can open the scroll. And when John looks for the conquering Lion, he sees — a Lamb, standing as though slaughtered.

The scroll sealed with seven seals is the interpretive key to the chapter. A scroll sealed with seven seals in the ancient world was typically a legal document of great importance: a will, a deed of purchase, or a covenant document. Most scholars understand it as the scroll of history — God’s redemptive plan for the world, the title deed to creation, the covenant document of the new age. Seven seals indicates absolute sealing: only the one who is truly worthy can break them and open what they guard. The entire drama of Revelation — the seals, the trumpets, the bowls — is the Lamb opening this scroll.

The Lion who is the Lamb — the great reversal at the heart of chapter 5 — is the christological center of Revelation and, in a sense, of the entire New Testament. John is told to look for a conquering Lion. He looks and sees a slaughtered Lamb. The conquest was accomplished through the cross. The power that governs history is the power of self-giving love. The one who has the authority to open the seals of history is the one who was willing to be the sacrifice that history required. This is the theological answer to every form of worldly power: the crucified one reigns.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — The Scroll and the Lamb
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2 put a scroll in the right hand of the one on the throne, written within and on the back, sealed with seven seals. Writing on both sides meant the contents were complete; seven seals was the number required for a Roman will, openable only by the rightful heir. A mighty angel heralds one question across creation — not who is strong enough but who is worthy?

Verses 3–4 answer it: nobody, in heaven or on earth or under the earth. Not the elders, not the living creatures, not Abraham or Moses or David. And John breaks down — I began to weep loudly — the only tears anyone sheds in the throne room of this book, and they are not rebuked. An unopened scroll means a world with no resolution: the martyrs never answered, Rome for ever, history running down like a clock nobody winds.

Verse 5 stops the weeping with an announcement rather than an argument: the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered (Gen. 49:9–10; Isa. 11:1–10). The verb is the past tense of the word that ends every one of the seven letters. Whatever the churches are being asked to do, he has already done.

Verses 6–7 are the hinge of the book. John is told a Lion and sees a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain — arnion, the diminutive, a lambkin, which becomes John’s main name for Christ twenty-eight times over. The participle is perfect: a past slaughter whose marks are still present. Seven horns are complete power, seven eyes complete knowledge (Zech. 4:10). Then, without ceremony, he went and took the scroll.

Verses 8–10: the creatures and elders fall before the Lamb — worship no creature in this book may receive (19:10; 22:8–9) — holding harps and golden bowls of incense which are the prayers of the saints (cf. Ps. 141:2). The new song grounds his worthiness in his death: you were slain, and by your blood you ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation, made them a kingdom and priests, and they shall reign on the earth.

Verses 11–12 widen the circle to myriads of myriads of angels (cf. Dan. 7:10) with a sevenfold ascription: Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honor and glory and blessing. Verses 13–14 widen it to every creature in heaven, on earth, under the earth and in the sea, addressing one doxology to the throne and the Lamb together; the living creatures say Amen, and the elders fall down and worship in silence.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lion Is the Lamb

No one is worthy to open the sealed scroll of God’s purpose until the Lion of Judah is announced — and John sees a Lamb standing, as though slain. He takes the scroll, and heaven and earth worship him who ransomed a people by his blood.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: John wept at a world with no resolution; his tears were answered by a person, not an argument.

Now: No prayer offered in faith is lost; the prayers of the saints are held in golden bowls before the throne.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw in the right hand of him who was seated on the throne a scroll written within and on the back, sealed with seven seals. And I saw a mighty angel proclaiming with a loud voice, "Who is worthy to open the scroll and break its seals?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
John sees a scroll sealed with seven seals in God’s right hand, and a mighty angel asks who is worthy to open it.

A scroll written on both sides. Full and complete, like Ezekiel’s (Ezekiel 2:9–10).

Seven seals. Fully sealed. Only the right person may open it.

Where Christians differ: what is the scroll? The title deed of creation, God’s plan for history, or the covenant inheritance of the saints. Verdict: it is God’s purpose of judgment and redemption for history; opening it sets that purpose in motion (chapter 6 onwards).

Who is worthy? The question is about worthiness, not strength.

verseByVerse.quote: And no one in heaven or on earth or under the earth was able to open the scroll or to look into it, and I began to weep loudly because no one was found worthy to open the scroll or to look into it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one anywhere was found worthy to open the scroll, and John wept loudly.

No one. In heaven, on earth, or under the earth. No angel, saint or ruler.

Weeping. If the scroll stays sealed, history has no resolution and evil no end.

On a Tuesday. Bring your grief at the world’s injustice to God. John’s tears were not rebuked.

verseByVerse.quote: And one of the elders said to me, "Weep no more; behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered, so that he can open the scroll and its seven seals."
verseByVerse.commentary:
An elder tells John to stop weeping: the Lion of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered and can open the scroll.

Lion of Judah. Genesis 49:9–10, the promised king.

Root of David. Isaiah 11:1, 10. Both David’s source and his descendant (22:16).

Has conquered. Past tense. The victory is already won.

For worship. Weep no more. Christ has won.

verseByVerse.quote: And between the throne and the four living creatures and among the elders I saw a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain, with seven horns and with seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent out into all the earth. And he went and took the scroll from the right hand of him who was seated on the throne.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John turns to see the Lion and sees a Lamb, standing as though slain, with seven horns and seven eyes, the seven spirits of God, and he takes the scroll.

He heard a Lion, he saw a Lamb. The centre of the book. Christ conquers by being slain.

Standing. Slain, but alive.

Seven horns, seven eyes. Complete power and complete knowledge, through the Spirit sent into all the earth.

Between the throne. The Lamb is at the centre of heaven’s worship.

On a Tuesday. Christ’s way of winning is the cross. Do not expect yours to be different.
verseByVerse.note: The Lion of v. 5 turns out to be a slain Lamb. Horns stand for power and eyes for knowledge.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had taken the scroll, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell down before the Lamb, each holding a harp, and golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints. And they sang a new song, saying, "Worthy are you to take the scroll and to open its seals, for you were slain, and by your blood you ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation, and you have made them a kingdom and priests to our God, and they shall reign on the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the Lamb takes the scroll, the creatures and elders fall before him with harps and incense, the prayers of the saints, and sing a new song: he is worthy because by his blood he ransomed people from every nation, and made them a kingdom and priests who will reign on the earth.

The prayers of the saints. Your prayers are kept before God, and they move history (8:3–5).

Worship of the Lamb. What was given to God in chapter 4 is given to the Lamb. He is God.

From every tribe. The church is multinational by design.

Where Christians differ: ransomed whom? Many hold that Christ’s death made salvation possible for all. Verdict: his blood actually ransomed a people for God, drawn from every nation. This supports definite atonement, as well as a worldwide mission.

Reign on the earth. Where Christians differ. Premillennialists see a future earthly millennium. Verdict: believers reign with Christ now (1:6) and fully in the new earth (22:5).

Textual note. Later manuscripts read “ransomed us” and “made us”, making the elders the redeemed. The earliest read “people” and “them”. Manuscripts also differ between “they shall reign” and “they reign”.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I looked, and I heard around the throne and the living creatures and the elders the voice of many angels, numbering myriads of myriads and thousands of thousands, saying with a loud voice, "Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honor and glory and blessing!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Countless angels around the throne cry loudly that the slain Lamb is worthy to receive power, wealth, wisdom, might, honour, glory and blessing.

Myriads of myriads. Daniel 7:10. Beyond counting.

Seven ascriptions. Complete praise.

Worthy because slain. Heaven’s worship centres on the cross.

For worship. Add your voice: worthy is the Lamb who was slain.

verseByVerse.quote: And I heard every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea, and all that is in them, saying, "To him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honor and glory and might forever and ever!" And the four living creatures said, "Amen!" and the elders fell down and worshiped.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every creature everywhere joins in, giving blessing, honour, glory and might to God and to the Lamb for ever, and the elders fall down and worship.

Every creature. Worship spreads from the throne to the whole creation (Philippians 2:10–11).

To him and to the Lamb. The Father and the Son, worshipped together. Revelation will not let an angel be worshipped (19:10; 22:8–9), yet the Lamb is.

Amen. The creatures seal the worship.

Textual note. Later manuscripts add “him who lives for ever and ever” at the end of v. 14.

For worship. Worship the Father and the Son together this Sunday.

5.text: <sup>1</sup>Then I saw in the right hand of him who was seated on the throne a scroll written within and on the back, sealed with seven seals.<sup>2</sup>And I saw a mighty angel proclaiming with a loud voice, “Who is worthy to open the scroll and break its seals?”<sup>3</sup>And no one in heaven or on earth or under the earth was able to open the scroll or to look into it,<sup>4</sup>and I began to weep loudly because no one was found worthy to open the scroll or to look into it.<sup>5</sup>And one of the elders said to me, “Weep no more; behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered, so that he can open the scroll and its seven seals.”<sup>6</sup>And between the throne and the four living creatures and among the elders I saw a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain, with seven horns and with seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent out into all the earth.<sup>7</sup>And he went and took the scroll from the right hand of him who was seated on the throne.<sup>8</sup>And when he had taken the scroll, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell down before the Lamb, each holding a harp, and golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints.<sup>9</sup>And they sang a new song, saying, “Worthy are you to take the scroll and to open its seals, for you were slain, and by your blood you ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation,<sup>10</sup>and you have made them a kingdom and priests to our God, and they shall reign on the earth.”<sup>11</sup>Then I looked, and I heard around the throne and the living creatures and the elders the voice of many angels, numbering myriads of myriads and thousands of thousands,<sup>12</sup>saying with a loud voice, “Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honor and glory and blessing!”<sup>13</sup>And I heard every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea, and all that is in them, saying, “To him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honor and glory and might forever and ever!”<sup>14</sup>And the four living creatures said, “Amen!” and the elders fell down and worshiped.

6.title: The Opening of the Seals
6.overview:
The Lamb begins to open the seven seals, and with each seal a new dimension of history is revealed. The first four seals release the famous Four Horsemen — one of the most powerful images in Western literature. The fifth seal lifts the veil on the souls of the martyrs beneath the heavenly altar and their agonizing cry: “How long, O Lord?” The sixth seal unleashes cosmic convulsion on a terrified earth. The seventh seal — which will bring complete silence in heaven — is withheld until chapter 8.

Interpretive flag — Sequential or Recapitulatory? This is the second major structural decision point of Revelation. The sequential reading (predominant in dispensational premillennialism) understands the seals, trumpets, and bowls as three successive series of events: the seals run their course, then the trumpets begin, then the bowls pour out — covering the seven-year tribulation in ascending severity. The recapitulatory reading (predominant in amillennial/idealist interpretation) understands the three series as parallel sweeps, each covering the same period (the church age and/or the final tribulation) from different vantage points and with increasing intensity. Several features of the text favor recapitulation: (1) the sixth seal already appears to describe the final judgment (vv. 12–17), yet the narrative continues; (2) the sixth trumpet and sixth bowl also appear to describe the same climactic events; (3) the interludes (chapters 7, 10–11) break the sequential pattern; (4) the phrase “the great day of their wrath has come” (v. 17) sounds like a finale, yet much remains. The seals are read here as the first of three parallel sweeps, with the sequential reading noted respectfully.

The Four Horsemen are among the most theologically misread images in Revelation. They are not four distinct events in a future tribulation timeline. They are the recurring instruments of divine governance that have marked history since the fall: war, internecine conflict, famine, and death. They describe the ongoing reality of a fallen world under the Lord’s providential judgment — not unprecedented novelties but the intensified concentration of what the church has always known. The question the martyrs ask — “How long?” — is the question the church has been asking since Abel’s blood first cried from the ground.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2: the Lamb opens the first seal, a living creature calls Come! with a voice like thunder, and a white horse rides out whose rider has a bow and a crown that was given to him. Whether that rider is Christ, the gospel’s advance, or conquest itself is genuinely disputed and is set out at the verse. Verses 3–4: a bright red horse, whose rider is permitted to take peace from the earth so that people should slay one another — mutual killing, the neighbour with the knife — and is given a great sword.

Verses 5–6: a black horse, its rider holding scales, and a voice from the midst of the living creatures quoting the price list. A denarius was a day’s wage; a quart of wheat was one man’s daily ration. A labourer in full work can feed himself and nobody else. Do not harm the oil and wine sets a limit on the famine and also describes its injustice: bread is rationed while the luxury trade goes on undisturbed.

Verses 7–8: a pale horse — chlōros, the green of a corpse — and the only rider who is named. Death rides, and Hades follows to collect. They are given authority over a fourth of the earth, with the four instruments of Ezekiel 14:21. The fraction matters: the trumpets will touch a third, and only at the end does anything become total.

Verses 9–11 break the pattern: no horse, no rider. Under the altar, where the blood of every sacrifice was poured out (Lev. 4:7), are the souls of those slain — esphagmenōn, the word used of the Lamb at 5:6. They cry how long? like a third of the psalter. Verse 11 answers with a white robe each, permission to rest, and a reason for the delay that is very hard: until the number of their brothers who are to die in the same way is complete.

Verses 12–14: the sixth seal removes every fixed point in the universe — earthquake, sun black as sackcloth (goat hair, so the comparison is exact), moon like blood (Joel 2:31), stars falling like the winter figs a gale brings down, the sky rolled up (Isa. 34:4), every mountain and island moved. Verses 15–17: seven classes of people, from kings down to slaves, hide in caves and beg the mountains to fall on them — choosing burial over being looked at — and the chapter ends on an unanswered question: who can stand?
verseByVerse.theology:
The Seals in the Lamb’s Hand

Conquest, war, famine and death ride out only when the Lamb opens the seals, and every one of them is given or permitted within a limit. The martyrs cry “How long?” and are robed and told to rest; the sixth seal removes every fixed point but the throne.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The churches met the red horse and the pale one without being told why.

Now: Crying out for justice is not unbelief; handing vengeance to God is obedience. And who can stand? Those washed in the Lamb’s blood.

verseByVerse.quote: Now I watched when the Lamb opened one of the seven seals, and I heard one of the four living creatures say with a voice like thunder, "Come!" And I looked, and behold, a white horse! And its rider had a bow, and a crown was given to him, and he came out conquering, and to conquer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lamb opens the first seal, a living creature cries “Come!”, and a rider on a white horse goes out conquering.

The Lamb opens. Everything that follows is released by Christ. Nothing in history escapes his hand.

Zechariah 1 and 6. Horses of different colours sent out through the earth.

Where Christians differ: who is the white rider? Some see Christ or the gospel advancing (19:11; Mark 13:10). Others see conquest and false messiahs, since the four riders belong together and Jesus’ warnings begin with deceivers (Matthew 24:4–5). Verdict: more likely the spirit of conquest, perhaps counterfeiting Christ: the four riders form a set of sorrows, and Christ is the one opening the seals, not riding out of them.

Where Christians differ: seals, trumpets and bowls. Futurists read them in sequence, at the end. Many Reformed readers (Augustine, Hendriksen, Beale) see them as parallel cycles, each covering the age between Christ’s comings and ending at the final judgment. Verdict: the recapitulation reading fits best, since each series ends at the end (6:12–17; 11:15–18; 16:17–21).

Textual note. Later manuscripts read “Come and see” in vv. 1, 3, 5, 7. The earliest read simply “Come!”, addressed to the rider.
verseByVerse.note: The four horsemen draw on Zechariah’s visions. Some take the white rider to be Christ (compare 19:11); many see him as conquest, the first of four judgments.

verseByVerse.quote: When he opened the second seal, I heard the second living creature say, "Come!" And out came another horse, bright red. Its rider was permitted to take peace from the earth, so that people should slay one another, and he was given a great sword.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second seal releases a red horse whose rider takes peace from the earth, so that people kill one another.

Permitted. War does not escape God’s permission and limits.

A great sword. Bloodshed, civil and international.

On a Tuesday. When you watch news of war, remember that the rider does not ride beyond the Lamb’s permission, and pray.

verseByVerse.quote: When he opened the third seal, I heard the third living creature say, "Come!" And I looked, and behold, a black horse! And its rider had a pair of scales in his hand. And I heard what seemed to be a voice in the midst of the four living creatures, saying, "A quart of wheat for a denarius, and three quarts of barley for a denarius, and do not harm the oil and wine!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third seal brings a black horse with a rider holding scales, and a voice announces famine prices, but forbids harm to the oil and wine.

A day’s wage for a quart of wheat. Prices many times normal: scarcity, not total famine.

Do not harm the oil and wine. A limit. Judgment is restrained, and mercy is mixed with it.

On a Tuesday. Economic hardship is under God’s hand too. Share what you have.
verseByVerse.note: A denarius was a day’s wage; a quart of wheat was about one person’s daily ration — famine prices.

verseByVerse.quote: When he opened the fourth seal, I heard the voice of the fourth living creature say, "Come!" And I looked, and behold, a pale horse! And its rider's name was Death, and Hades followed him. And they were given authority over a fourth of the earth, to kill with sword and with famine and with pestilence and by wild beasts of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fourth seal releases a pale horse ridden by Death, followed by Hades, with authority over a quarter of the earth to kill by sword, famine, plague and beasts.

Pale. The greenish colour of a corpse.

A fourth. Limited again. These judgments are partial warnings, not the end.

Ezekiel 14:21. God’s four sore judgments.

The whole age. The horsemen follow Jesus’ warnings: wars, famines and plagues, the beginning of the birth pains (Matthew 24:6–8; Luke 21:10–11).

verseByVerse.quote: When he opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of those who had been slain for the word of God and for the witness they had borne. They cried out with a loud voice, "O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long before you will judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fifth seal shows the souls of the martyrs under the altar, crying to the Sovereign Lord, asking how long until he judges and avenges their blood.

Under the altar. Their deaths are seen as sacrifices offered to God (2 Timothy 4:6).

Souls. Believers who die are alive and conscious with God before the resurrection (Philippians 1:23).

How long? The cry of the psalms (Psalm 79:5, 10). It is not wrong to long for justice.

What it does not mean. This is not personal revenge, but an appeal to God to put the world right (Romans 12:19).

verseByVerse.quote: Then they were each given a white robe and told to rest a little longer, until the number of their fellow servants and their brothers should be complete, who were to be killed as they themselves had been.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Each martyr receives a white robe and is told to rest a little longer, until the number of their fellow servants to be killed is complete.

White robes. Vindication given now, before the final judgment.

Rest. Not anxiety, but peace (14:13).

The number complete. God has fixed the end. Suffering is not random.

On a Tuesday. Pray for the persecuted church, and trust God with the timing of justice.

verseByVerse.quote: When he opened the sixth seal, I looked, and behold, there was a great earthquake, and the sun became black as sackcloth, the full moon became like blood, and the stars of the sky fell to the earth as the fig tree sheds its winter fruit when shaken by a gale. The sky vanished like a scroll that is being rolled up, and every mountain and island was removed from its place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sixth seal brings a great earthquake, a black sun, a blood-red moon, falling stars, a sky rolled up and every mountain and island moved.

Prophetic language. The prophets used such pictures for the fall of nations (Isaiah 13:10; 34:4; Joel 2:31).

Where Christians differ: literal or symbolic? Some read these as literal events in the cosmos; others as pictures of political collapse. Verdict: the sixth seal brings us to the end itself, the day of the Lamb’s wrath (v. 17). The language describes the shaking of all things at Christ’s return (Hebrews 12:26–27), whose details we cannot chart.

For worship. The created order, so fixed to us, is held in God’s hand.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the kings of the earth and the great ones and the generals and the rich and the powerful, and everyone, slave and free, hid themselves in the caves and among the rocks of the mountains, calling to the mountains and rocks, "Fall on us and hide us from the face of him who is seated on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb, for the great day of their wrath has come, and who can stand?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
All people, from kings to slaves, hide in caves and beg the mountains to fall on them and hide them from the face of God and the wrath of the Lamb, for the great day of their wrath has come.

All people. Rank and wealth give no shelter.

The wrath of the Lamb. A startling phrase. The Lamb who was slain is also the judge (John 5:22).

Who can stand? The answer comes in chapter 7: those sealed by God.

Textual note. Some manuscripts read “his wrath” in v. 17; the ESV follows the reading “their wrath”, the wrath of God and the Lamb.

On a Tuesday. There are two places to stand: hiding from the throne, or standing before it, washed by the Lamb.

6.text: <sup>1</sup>Now I watched when the Lamb opened one of the seven seals, and I heard one of the four living creatures say with a voice like thunder, “Come!”<sup>2</sup>And I looked, and behold, a white horse! And its rider had a bow, and a crown was given to him, and he came out conquering, and to conquer.<sup>3</sup>When he opened the second seal, I heard the second living creature say, “Come!”<sup>4</sup>And out came another horse, bright red. Its rider was permitted to take peace from the earth, so that people should slay one another, and he was given a great sword.<sup>5</sup>When he opened the third seal, I heard the third living creature say, “Come!” And I looked, and behold, a black horse! And its rider had a pair of scales in his hand.<sup>6</sup>And I heard what seemed to be a voice in the midst of the four living creatures, saying, “A quart of wheat for a denarius, and three quarts of barley for a denarius, and do not harm the oil and wine!”<sup>7</sup>When he opened the fourth seal, I heard the voice of the fourth living creature say, “Come!”<sup>8</sup>And I looked, and behold, a pale horse! And its rider’s name was Death, and Hades followed him. And they were given authority over a fourth of the earth, to kill with sword and with famine and with pestilence and by wild beasts of the earth.<sup>9</sup>When he opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of those who had been slain for the word of God and for the witness they had borne.<sup>10</sup>They cried out with a loud voice, “O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long before you will judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?”<sup>11</sup>Then they were each given a white robe and told to rest a little longer, until the number of their fellow servants and their brothers should be complete, who were to be killed as they themselves had been.<sup>12</sup>When he opened the sixth seal, I looked, and behold, there was a great earthquake, and the sun became black as sackcloth, the full moon became like blood,<sup>13</sup>and the stars of the sky fell to the earth as the fig tree sheds its winter fruit when shaken by a gale.<sup>14</sup>The sky vanished like a scroll that is being rolled up, and every mountain and island was removed from its place.<sup>15</sup>Then the kings of the earth and the great ones and the generals and the rich and the powerful, and everyone, slave and free, hid themselves in the caves and among the rocks of the mountains,<sup>16</sup>calling to the mountains and rocks, “Fall on us and hide us from the face of him who is seated on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb,<sup>17</sup>for the great day of their wrath has come, and who can stand?”

7.title: The Sealed and the Standing: God's People in the Storm
7.overview:
Chapter 7 is the first great interlude of Revelation — a pause between the sixth and seventh seals that answers the question that ended chapter 6: “Who can stand?” The answer comes in two scenes that together present the whole people of God from two perspectives. The 144,000 sealed from the twelve tribes of Israel (vv. 1–8): the church as it endures on earth, the complete and protected people of God in the midst of judgment. The great multitude from every nation (vv. 9–17): the church as it will appear before the throne, the redeemed in their innumerable fullness, already standing where the kings of the earth could not.

The 144,000 has generated more interpretive controversy than almost any other passage in Revelation. A strictly literal reading — exactly 144,000 ethnic Jewish males from the twelve tribes of Israel — faces several difficulties: (1) Dan is missing from the list and Manasseh (Joseph’s son) substituted, while Levi (not a territorial tribe) is included, making this no straightforward census; (2) the twelve tribes as distinct ethnic communities had not existed since the Assyrian deportation of the northern tribes in 722 BC; (3) the number 12 × 12 × 1,000 is conspicuously mathematical — in a book where seven means completeness, twelve means the people of God, and 1,000 means an immense completeness, 144,000 is the fullness of the fullness of God’s people. The majority Reformed/amillennial reading understands the 144,000 as the complete church of both testaments, the spiritual Israel (Romans 2:28–29; Galatians 3:29; 6:16; Philippians 3:3), sealed for protection through the tribulation. The dispensational reading understands them as 144,000 literal Jewish evangelists who will be saved and minister during the tribulation.

The great multitude of verses 9–17 is most likely the same group seen from a different vantage point — not a second group that supplements the 144,000 but the 144,000 as they appear before the throne, their number now seen to be “a great multitude that no one could number.” The innumerable quality is not a contradiction of the 144,000 but its complement: both “complete” and “uncountable” describe the fullness of the redeemed. The scene before the throne anticipates the final state, giving the church a vision of its own destiny as it endures the trials of the present.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Chapter 6 ended with the sky rolled up and a question hanging: who can stand? The seventh seal is not opened until 8:1, and everything here sits in that gap, answering the question before the last seal breaks.

Verse 1: four angels at the four corners of the earth hold back the four winds, so that no wind blows on earth or sea or against any tree. The stillness before a storm — destruction under restraint. Verse 2: a fifth angel ascends from the rising of the sun with the seal of the living God, and outranks the four. Verse 3 gives his order: Do not harm the earth or the sea or the trees, until we have sealed the servants of our God on their foreheads. Judgment is not cancelled; it is delayed until God’s people are marked (cf. 2 Pet. 3:9).

The picture behind it is Ezekiel 9:4, where a man with a writing case marks the foreheads of those who sigh and groan over what is being done in Jerusalem, and the executioners are told to touch nobody who carries the mark. A seal marked ownership, gave protection, and guaranteed authenticity; all three apply.

Verse 4 gives the number: 144,000, sealed from every tribe of the sons of Israel. Verses 5–8 list the twelve, twelve thousand each — Judah, Reuben, Gad, Asher, Naphtali, Manasseh, Simeon, Levi, Issachar, Zebulun, Joseph, Benjamin. The list matches no tribal register in the Old Testament: Judah heads it rather than Reuben the firstborn; Dan is missing; Levi, which had no territorial allotment, is counted; and Manasseh is listed alongside Joseph, his own father. Who the 144,000 are is set out at the verse, with the evidence on both sides.
verseByVerse.theology:
Sealed Before the Storm

The winds of judgement are held back until God’s servants are sealed on their foreheads, as in Ezekiel 9. Whether the 144,000 are ethnic Israel or the whole people of God, God knows the number exactly.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The seal did not exempt them from the tribulation; it marked them as God’s within it.

Now: The text caps nobody’s hope: the next scene is a multitude no one could number.

verseByVerse.quote: After this I saw four angels standing at the four corners of the earth, holding back the four winds of the earth, that no wind might blow on earth or sea or against any tree. Then I saw another angel ascending from the rising of the sun, with the seal of the living God, and he called with a loud voice to the four angels who had been given power to harm earth and sea, saying, "Do not harm the earth or the sea or the trees, until we have sealed the servants of our God on their foreheads."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Angels hold back the four winds of judgment until God’s servants have been sealed on their foreheads.

An interlude. Between the sixth and seventh seals, the question “who can stand?” (6:17) is answered.

The seal. A mark of ownership and protection (Ezekiel 9:4). Paul says believers are sealed with the Holy Spirit (Ephesians 1:13; 4:30).

What it does not mean. The seal does not protect from suffering or death (6:9–11), but from God’s wrath and from final falling away.

On a Tuesday. You are marked as God’s. Nothing can remove the seal.

verseByVerse.quote: And I heard the number of the sealed, 144,000, sealed from every tribe of the sons of Israel: 12,000 from the tribe of Judah were sealed, 12,000 from the tribe of Reuben, 12,000 from the tribe of Gad, 12,000 from the tribe of Asher, 12,000 from the tribe of Naphtali, 12,000 from the tribe of Manasseh, 12,000 from the tribe of Simeon, 12,000 from the tribe of Levi, 12,000 from the tribe of Issachar, 12,000 from the tribe of Zebulun, 12,000 from the tribe of Joseph, 12,000 from the tribe of Benjamin were sealed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John hears the number of the sealed: 144,000, twelve thousand from each tribe of Israel.

Twelve times twelve times a thousand. A number of completeness.

An unusual list. Judah comes first (the Messiah’s tribe); Dan is missing; Joseph and Manasseh are both included.

Where Christians differ: who are the 144,000? Dispensationalists see a literal remnant of ethnic Israel in a future tribulation. Jehovah’s Witnesses apply it to a heavenly elite. Many Reformed interpreters see the whole people of God, the true Israel, pictured as an army ready for battle (Numbers 1). Verdict: the 144,000 John hears are the same as the countless multitude he sees (vv. 9–10), just as he heard of a Lion and saw a Lamb (5:5–6). It is the whole church, complete, counted and protected.

For worship. Not one of God’s people is missing from his count.
verseByVerse.note: The tribe list is unusual: Judah comes first, Dan is missing, and both Joseph and his son Manasseh appear.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–17 — A Great Multitude from Every Nation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 9–10: John looks and sees a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages — the fourfold phrase of 5:9, so that this chapter is the receipt for that purchase. They are standing, which answers 6:17 directly, in white robes and holding palm branches (Lev. 23:40–43; John 12:13), and they cry Salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb! Not a syllable of the song is about what they did.

Verses 11–12: all the angels stand in the outer ring — the redeemed are nearer the throne than the angelic host — and fall on their faces with a sevenfold doxology bracketed by Amen. It matches the ascription to the Lamb in 5:12, with thanksgiving replacing wealth. Heaven falls down because a crowd of forgiven human beings has just sung.

Verses 13–14: an elder asks who they are and where they have come from, and John answers Sir, you know (cf. Ezek. 37:3). The answer has two halves: these are the ones coming out of the great tribulation — a present, continuous participle, a stream still emerging — and they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb. Blood does not whiten cloth; the image is deliberately impossible.

Verse 15: therefore they are before the throne, serving him day and night in his temple in priestly service (latreuō), and he who sits on the throne will shelter them with his presence — literally, will spread his tent over them (cf. Ex. 40:34; John 1:14; Rev. 21:3). Verses 16–17 close with five promises quoted from Isaiah 49:10: no hunger, no thirst, no sun, no scorching heat; the Lamb in the midst of the throne as their shepherd, guiding them to springs of living water; and God wiping away every tear from their eyes.
verseByVerse.theology:
Washed in the Blood of the Lamb

A multitude from every nation stands before the throne and sings that salvation belongs to God and to the Lamb. They came out of the great tribulation, washed their robes in the Lamb’s blood, and are sheltered by God’s presence.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Hunger, thirst and scorching heat were the daily lot of many first hearers.

Now: God himself will wipe away every tear — every one, by name.

verseByVerse.quote: After this I looked, and behold, a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, clothed in white robes, with palm branches in their hands, and crying out with a loud voice, "Salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
John sees a great multitude, too many to count, from every nation, standing before the throne and the Lamb in white robes with palm branches, crying that salvation belongs to God and the Lamb.

No one could number. The promise to Abraham fulfilled (Genesis 15:5).

Every nation. The church is from every people and language.

Palm branches. The Feast of Tabernacles, and the welcome of the King (John 12:13).

Salvation belongs to our God. Salvation is God’s work from start to finish.

For worship. Join the multitude: salvation belongs to our God and to the Lamb.
verseByVerse.note: John hears a number (v. 4) but sees a multitude no one can count — likely the same people seen from two angles.

verseByVerse.quote: And all the angels were standing around the throne and around the elders and the four living creatures, and they fell on their faces before the throne and worshiped God, saying, "Amen! Blessing and glory and wisdom and thanksgiving and honor and power and might be to our God forever and ever! Amen."
verseByVerse.commentary:
All the angels fall on their faces and worship God with sevenfold praise.

Amen. The angels affirm the multitude’s song.

Seven ascriptions. Blessing, glory, wisdom, thanksgiving, honour, power, might.

Angels and saints. Angels worship over sinners saved (Luke 15:10).

verseByVerse.quote: Then one of the elders addressed me, saying, "Who are these, clothed in white robes, and from where have they come?" I said to him, "Sir, you know." And he said to me, "These are the ones coming out of the great tribulation. They have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An elder asks who the white-robed multitude are, and explains that they have come out of the great tribulation and washed their robes in the Lamb’s blood.

Coming out. Present tense: an ongoing stream.

Where Christians differ: the great tribulation. Dispensationalists see a seven-year future period. Others see the whole age of suffering between Christ’s comings, which comes to a climax at the end. Verdict: the tribulation John already shared (1:9), intensifying before the end (Matthew 24:21). The multitude are all the redeemed who have come through it.

Washed white in blood. A paradox. Only Christ’s blood cleanses (1 John 1:7).

On a Tuesday. Your suffering is not the end of your story.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore they are before the throne of God, and serve him day and night in his temple; and he who sits on the throne will shelter them with his presence.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore they serve God day and night in his temple, and he will shelter them with his presence.

Serve. The word for priestly worship.

Shelter. Literally “spread his tent over them”: God’s dwelling among his people (John 1:14; 21:3).

The same face. The face the kings tried to hide from (6:16) is now their shelter.

verseByVerse.quote: They shall hunger no more, neither thirst anymore; the sun shall not strike them, nor any scorching heat.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They will never again hunger, thirst or be scorched by the sun.

Isaiah 49:10. The return from exile, fulfilled.

Negatives. Heaven is described by what is gone, because we cannot imagine it otherwise.

On a Tuesday. Whatever you lack now will not be lacking then.

verseByVerse.quote: For the Lamb in the midst of the throne will be their shepherd, and he will guide them to springs of living water, and God will wipe away every tear from their eyes."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lamb at the centre of the throne will shepherd them to springs of living water, and God will wipe every tear from their eyes.

The Lamb as Shepherd. Psalm 23, fulfilled by the one who was himself a lamb.

Living water. Life with God (John 4:14).

Every tear. Isaiah 25:8. God himself does it, personally (21:4).

For worship. Thank God that he will wipe away your tears, every one.

7.text: <sup>1</sup>After this I saw four angels standing at the four corners of the earth, holding back the four winds of the earth, that no wind might blow on earth or sea or against any tree.<sup>2</sup>Then I saw another angel ascending from the rising of the sun, with the seal of the living God, and he called with a loud voice to the four angels who had been given power to harm earth and sea,<sup>3</sup>saying, “Do not harm the earth or the sea or the trees, until we have sealed the servants of our God on their foreheads.”<sup>4</sup>And I heard the number of the sealed, 144,000, sealed from every tribe of the sons of Israel:<sup>5</sup>12,000 from the tribe of Judah were sealed, 12,000 from the tribe of Reuben, 12,000 from the tribe of Gad,<sup>6</sup>12,000 from the tribe of Asher, 12,000 from the tribe of Naphtali, 12,000 from the tribe of Manasseh,<sup>7</sup>12,000 from the tribe of Simeon, 12,000 from the tribe of Levi, 12,000 from the tribe of Issachar,<sup>8</sup>12,000 from the tribe of Zebulun, 12,000 from the tribe of Joseph, 12,000 from the tribe of Benjamin were sealed.<sup>9</sup>After this I looked, and behold, a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, clothed in white robes, with palm branches in their hands,<sup>10</sup>and crying out with a loud voice, “Salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!”<sup>11</sup>And all the angels were standing around the throne and around the elders and the four living creatures, and they fell on their faces before the throne and worshiped God,<sup>12</sup>saying, “Amen! Blessing and glory and wisdom and thanksgiving and honor and power and might be to our God forever and ever! Amen.”<sup>13</sup>Then one of the elders addressed me, saying, “Who are these, clothed in white robes, and from where have they come?”<sup>14</sup>I said to him, “Sir, you know.” And he said to me, “These are the ones coming out of the great tribulation.
