They have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.<sup>15</sup>Therefore they are before the throne of God, and serve him day and night in his temple; and he who sits on the throne will shelter them with his presence.<sup>16</sup>They shall hunger no more, neither thirst anymore; the sun shall not strike them, nor any scorching heat.<sup>17</sup>For the Lamb in the midst of the throne will be their shepherd, and he will guide them to springs of living water, and God will wipe away every tear from their eyes.”

8.title: The Seventh Seal and the First Four Trumpets
8.overview:
The seventh seal does not release a horseman or a cosmic catastrophe. It releases silence. “When the Lamb opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour.” After the unceasing worship of chapters 4–7, after the thunder and lightning of the throne room, after the cries of the martyrs and the acclamation of the great multitude — silence. Heaven holds its breath. The silence of the seventh seal is more terrifying than any of the sounds that preceded it, because it signals that something of ultimate gravity is about to happen.

Out of the silence, seven trumpets are given to seven angels. Before the trumpets sound, another angel offers incense before the altar — and the prayers of the saints rise with the incense before God. This is the answer to the martyrs’ prayer of 6:10 (“How long, O Lord?”): the prayers of God’s people are not lost. They have been gathered. They are being presented before the throne. And now fire from the altar is thrown to the earth — the prayers of the saints become the fire of divine judgment.

The trumpets follow the pattern of the Exodus plagues, but escalated. Hail, fire, blood — the first trumpet echoes the seventh plague of Egypt. The sea turning to blood — the second trumpet echoes the first plague. Darkness — the fourth trumpet echoes the ninth plague. The Exodus pattern is deliberate: the God who judged Egypt to liberate his people is now judging the new Egypt (Rome, Babylon) to liberate the new Israel (the church). The judgments of Revelation are not arbitrary cruelties; they are the exodus of the new covenant people on a cosmic scale.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The Seventh Seal and the Golden Censer
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 1: the last seal is opened and nothing happens. There was silence in heaven for about half an hour. Everything the reader has heard for four chapters — the ceaseless holy, holy, holy of the living creatures (4:8), the myriads crying Worthy is the Lamb (5:12), a multitude nobody could number (7:10) — stops. Scripture repeatedly commands exactly this silence before God acts in judgment (Hab. 2:20; Zeph. 1:7; Zech. 2:13), and the crowd outside the temple prayed in silence while the incense was offered (Luke 1:10). Both are probably in view.

Verse 2: seven angels who stand before God are given seven trumpets — the second of the book’s three sevens. A trumpet in Israel sounded at Sinai (Ex. 19:16), brought down Jericho (Josh. 6:16–20), raised the alarm (Joel 2:1), announced Jubilee (Lev. 25:9) and will sound at the resurrection (1 Cor. 15:52).

Verses 3–4: before a trumpet sounds, another angel stands at the altar with a golden censer and is given much incense to offer with the prayers of all the saints, and the smoke rises before God. This is the payoff of 5:8, where the elders held golden bowls which John identified as those prayers. Three details matter: all the saints; the incense is added from the other side, so the prayers do not go up on their own account; and they arrive.

Verse 5 turns everything over. Then the angel took the censer and filled it with fire from the altar and threw it on the earth, followed by thunder, rumblings, lightning and an earthquake — the Sinai signs of 4:5 with an earthquake added. The same censer that carried the prayers up now carries fire down. The trumpets are the answer to the church’s praying.
verseByVerse.theology:
Prayer and the Censer

Heaven falls silent, and the prayers of all the saints rise with much incense given at the altar. Then the same censer is filled with fire and thrown to the earth: the trumpets are God’s answer to his people’s prayers.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The martyrs’ “How long?” is being answered.

Now: Prayers that seem to do nothing are gathered, perfected, and answered in God’s time.

verseByVerse.quote: When the Lamb opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the Lamb opens the seventh seal, heaven falls silent for about half an hour.

Silence. After ceaseless praise (4:8), a hush: awe before judgment (Habakkuk 2:20; Zephaniah 1:7).

Half an hour. A short, solemn pause.

The seventh seal. It unfolds into the seven trumpets. The end is reached again, from a different angle.

On a Tuesday. God’s silence is not absence. Heaven is listening to prayer (vv. 3–4).

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw the seven angels who stand before God, and seven trumpets were given to them. And another angel came and stood at the altar with a golden censer, and he was given much incense to offer with the prayers of all the saints on the golden altar before the throne, and the smoke of the incense, with the prayers of the saints, rose before God from the hand of the angel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seven angels receive trumpets, and another angel offers incense with the prayers of all the saints on the golden altar, and the smoke rises before God.

Trumpets. Warning and battle (Joshua 6; Joel 2:1).

The prayers of the saints. Including the martyrs’ cry (6:10). Prayer comes before judgment.

Where Christians differ: who is the angel? Some see Christ, our high priest. Verdict: Revelation never calls Christ an angel; this is an angelic servant. It does not teach that we pray through angels. Our only mediator is Christ (1 Timothy 2:5).

On a Tuesday. Your prayers are not lost. They rise before God.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the angel took the censer and filled it with fire from the altar and threw it on the earth, and there were peals of thunder, rumblings, flashes of lightning, and an earthquake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel fills the censer with fire from the altar and throws it on the earth, bringing thunder, lightning and an earthquake.

Prayers answered. The same altar that received prayer sends judgment. God answers his people’s cries for justice.

Ezekiel 10:2. Coals scattered over the city.

For worship. Praise God that prayer moves history.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 6: the seven angels prepare to blow. Verse 7: the first trumpet brings hail and fire mixed with blood, and a third of the earth, a third of the trees and all green grass are burned. Verses 8–9: the second brings something like a great mountain, burning, thrown into the sea — the image Jeremiah used of Babylon as a burnt mountain (Jer. 51:25) — and a third of the sea becomes blood, a third of its creatures die, a third of the ships are destroyed. For seven churches on the coast of Asia the sea was the economy, not the scenery.

Verses 10–11: the third trumpet drops a blazing star, Wormwood, on the fresh water, and many people died from the water, because it had been made bitter. Apsinthos is bitter rather than poisonous, and it is the prophets’ standing image for judgment that makes the sweet unswallowable (Jer. 9:15; 23:15; Lam. 3:19) — most pointedly in Amos, where men turn justice to wormwood (Amos 5:7) and here find their own wells undrinkable.

Verse 12: the fourth strikes a third of the sun, moon and stars, so that a third of the light is darkened — the ninth plague on Egypt (Ex. 10:21–23), aimed at a nation whose chief god was the sun and whose Pharaoh was his son.

Verse 13 closes with an eagle at the zenith, where everyone can see it, crying Woe, woe, woe to those who dwell on the earth — one woe for each trumpet still to come. Four trumpets have struck earth, sea, fresh water and sky, the whole created order. The remaining three will fall on people.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Trumpets Are the Plagues of Egypt

Hail and fire, water turned to blood, bitterness and darkness strike earth, sea, fresh water and sky — each limited to a third. As in Egypt, the aim is to expose false gods and bring God’s people out.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: For coastal churches, a stricken sea meant a stricken economy.

Now: Do not decode these as headlines; see in them the failure of every false security, and the warning to repent.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the seven angels who had the seven trumpets prepared to blow them. The first angel blew his trumpet, and there followed hail and fire, mixed with blood, and these were thrown upon the earth. And a third of the earth was burned up, and a third of the trees were burned up, and all green grass was burned up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angels prepare to blow, and at the first trumpet hail and fire mixed with blood burn up a third of the earth, the trees and the green grass.

The plagues of Egypt. Hail and fire (Exodus 9:23–25). The trumpets echo the exodus: judgment on oppressors, rescue for God’s people.

A third. Partial. The trumpets are warnings calling people to repent (9:20–21).

Where Christians differ: when and how literal? Some apply the trumpets to the fall of Jerusalem or Rome, others to a future tribulation. Verdict: they are symbolic pictures of God’s partial judgments on the world throughout the age between Christ’s comings, warning of the final judgment.
verseByVerse.note: The trumpet plagues echo the plagues on Egypt, but each strikes only a third — judgment still held back.

verseByVerse.quote: The second angel blew his trumpet, and something like a great mountain, burning with fire, was thrown into the sea, and a third of the sea became blood. A third of the living creatures in the sea died, and a third of the ships were destroyed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the second trumpet a burning mountain is thrown into the sea, a third of the sea becomes blood, a third of sea creatures die and a third of ships are destroyed.

The Nile turned to blood. Exodus 7:20.

A burning mountain. Perhaps a picture of a fallen kingdom (Jeremiah 51:25, of Babylon).

Ships. Trade and commerce are struck (compare 18:17–19).

verseByVerse.quote: The third angel blew his trumpet, and a great star fell from heaven, blazing like a torch, and it fell on a third of the rivers and on the springs of water. The name of the star is Wormwood. A third of the waters became wormwood, and many people died from the water, because it had been made bitter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the third trumpet a blazing star called Wormwood falls on a third of the rivers and springs, making them bitter, and many die.

Wormwood. A bitter plant, used by Jeremiah of the bitterness of judgment (Jeremiah 9:15).

Bitter water. The reverse of Marah, where God made bitter water sweet (Exodus 15:23–25).

On a Tuesday. What the world drinks to satisfy it turns bitter without God.
verseByVerse.note: Wormwood is a bitter plant, used by the prophets as a picture of bitter judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: The fourth angel blew his trumpet, and a third of the sun was struck, and a third of the moon, and a third of the stars, so that a third of their light might be darkened, and a third of the day might be kept from shining, and likewise a third of the night. Then I looked, and I heard an eagle crying with a loud voice as it flew directly overhead, "Woe, woe, woe to those who dwell on the earth, at the blasts of the other trumpets that the three angels are about to blow!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the fourth trumpet a third of the sun, moon and stars are darkened, and an eagle cries woe on the earth’s inhabitants because of the three trumpets still to come.

Darkness. The ninth plague (Exodus 10:21–23).

Woe, woe, woe. The last three trumpets are worse: they strike people directly.

Those who dwell on the earth. In Revelation, this means unbelievers, whose home and hope are in this world.

Textual note. Later manuscripts read “angel” rather than “eagle”. The words are similar in Greek; “eagle” is earlier and better attested.

For worship. Thank God that his warnings come before his final judgment.

8.text: <sup>1</sup>When the Lamb opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour.<sup>2</sup>Then I saw the seven angels who stand before God, and seven trumpets were given to them.<sup>3</sup>And another angel came and stood at the altar with a golden censer, and he was given much incense to offer with the prayers of all the saints on the golden altar before the throne,<sup>4</sup>and the smoke of the incense, with the prayers of the saints, rose before God from the hand of the angel.<sup>5</sup>Then the angel took the censer and filled it with fire from the altar and threw it on the earth, and there were peals of thunder, rumblings, flashes of lightning, and an earthquake.<sup>6</sup>Now the seven angels who had the seven trumpets prepared to blow them.<sup>7</sup>The first angel blew his trumpet, and there followed hail and fire, mixed with blood, and these were thrown upon the earth. And a third of the earth was burned up, and a third of the trees were burned up, and all green grass was burned up.<sup>8</sup>The second angel blew his trumpet, and something like a great mountain, burning with fire, was thrown into the sea, and a third of the sea became blood.<sup>9</sup>A third of the living creatures in the sea died, and a third of the ships were destroyed.<sup>10</sup>The third angel blew his trumpet, and a great star fell from heaven, blazing like a torch, and it fell on a third of the rivers and on the springs of water.<sup>11</sup>The name of the star is Wormwood. A third of the waters became wormwood, and many people died from the water, because it had been made bitter.<sup>12</sup>The fourth angel blew his trumpet, and a third of the sun was struck, and a third of the moon, and a third of the stars, so that a third of their light might be darkened, and a third of the day might be kept from shining, and likewise a third of the night.<sup>13</sup>Then I looked, and I heard an eagle crying with a loud voice as it flew directly overhead, “Woe, woe, woe to those who dwell on the earth, at the blasts of the other trumpets that the three angels are about to blow!”

9.title: The Fifth and Sixth Trumpets: The Demonic and the Deadly
9.overview:
Chapter 9 is among the most vivid and terrifying in Revelation. The fifth trumpet releases demonic locusts from the abyss — creatures drawn from Joel 2 and shaped like scorpions, with the faces of humans and the hair of women and the teeth of lions. The sixth trumpet releases four angels bound at the great Euphrates river, who command an army of two hundred million mounted troops. The devastation escalates from the bounded third of the earlier trumpets to something more comprehensive and more personal: now humanity itself is directly targeted.

The two woe-trumpets of chapter 9 share a common theme: demonic power unleashed. The fifth trumpet releases the army of the abyss, led by “the angel of the bottomless pit” whose name in Hebrew is Abaddon and in Greek Apollyon — “Destroyer.” The sixth releases an army from beyond the Euphrates — the frontier from which Israel’s ancient enemies (Assyria, Babylon) had always come. The locust-army of the fifth trumpet torments but does not kill; the cavalry of the sixth kills a third of humanity. The escalation is purposeful: God is turning up the pressure on a world that refuses to repent.

The chapter’s most sobering verse is its final one: “The rest of mankind, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent.” The purpose of the trumpet judgments — like the purpose of the Exodus plagues — was to break the hardness of heart that keeps humanity from turning to God. Pharaoh’s hardness repeated in every generation: even faced with the unmistakable signs of divine judgment, even watching a third of their companions die, the survivors “did not repent of the works of their hands nor give up worshiping demons.” The judgment does not automatically produce repentance; only grace can break what judgment cannot.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Fifth Trumpet: The Locusts from the Abyss
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2: a star fallen from heaven — a perfect participle, an event already complete — who is immediately a he, and who was given the key to the shaft of the bottomless pit. He opens it, and before anything comes out the light goes: smoke like the smoke of a great furnace darkens the sun and the air (cf. Gen. 19:28).

Verses 3–4: locusts come up out of the smoke with the power of scorpions — and are told not to touch grass, plant or tree, which is the one thing locusts exist to do. Their only target is those who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads: the first cash-out of chapter 7, and the doorpost of the Exodus Passover moved from the house to the person (cf. Ex. 8:22; 10:23).

Verses 5–6: they are allowed to torment for five months — about the life cycle of a locust swarm — but not to kill. And then the hardest sentence in the chapter: people will seek death and will not find it. They will long to die, but death will flee from them (cf. Job 3:21; Jer. 8:3).

Verses 7–10 describe them in eight comparisons, each introduced by like: horses prepared for battle (Joel 2:4), what looked like crowns of gold, human faces, women’s hair, lions’ teeth (Joel 1:6), iron breastplates, wings like many chariots, and scorpion tails in which their power to hurt resides.

Verses 11–12: Proverbs 30:27 says locusts have no king; these have one — the angel of the bottomless pit, named in both languages, Abaddon (Hebrew for destruction, Job 26:6; 28:22; Prov. 15:11) and Apollyon (Greek for destroyer). Then a line of bookkeeping: the first woe has passed; behold, two woes are still to come.
verseByVerse.theology:
On a Permission

A fallen star is given the key to the abyss; the locusts are told whom they may not touch and allowed five months. Their king is Abaddon, Apollyon, the destroyer — a creature on a leash, not God’s rival.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The torment fell on those without God’s seal, and it ended when the season ended.

Now: If you have longed to die, you are in the company of Job, Moses and Elijah, not under condemnation — tell another believer.

verseByVerse.quote: And the fifth angel blew his trumpet, and I saw a star fallen from heaven to earth, and he was given the key to the shaft of the bottomless pit. He opened the shaft of the bottomless pit, and from the shaft rose smoke like the smoke of a great furnace, and the sun and the air were darkened with the smoke from the shaft.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the fifth trumpet John sees a fallen star given the key to the bottomless pit; he opens it, and smoke pours out and darkens the sun and air. From here the judgments fall on people, and even the powers of the abyss act only when God permits — but evil’s first effect is to darken.

The target changes. Four trumpets struck earth, sea, fresh water and sky; an eagle cried three woes. Now the trumpets fall on people.

A star fallen. John doesn’t see a star fall but a star “fallen” — a completed event whose result still stands. And the star at once becomes “he”: an object turns into a person mid-sentence.

Who is the fallen star? Many take him as Satan, with strong support: “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10:18); Isaiah’s taunt, “How you are fallen from heaven, O Day Star, son of Dawn!” (Isaiah 14:12), read that way since the early church; and the dragon thrown down to earth in 12:9. Others take him as an angel on commission, since 20:1 shows an angel descending with the key of the bottomless pit, plainly no enemy. The more likely reading is that he is Satan or a fallen angel, allowed by God to release this judgment. Either way, the point that matters is settled: “he was given the key.” Keys in this book are kept in one place — “I have the keys of Death and Hades” (1:18). Even opening the abyss is a delegated act.

The abyss. In the Greek Old Testament the word is used for the deep of Genesis 1:2. In the New Testament it is where demons are kept and don’t want to go: the legion begged Jesus “not to command them to depart into the abyss” (Luke 8:31); Peter and Jude speak of rebel angels kept in chains for judgment (2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6). And it has a shaft — a mouth that can be shut, and is shut except when opened by permission.

First the light goes. Smoke “like the smoke of a great furnace” — as Abraham saw over Sodom, “the smoke of the land went up like the smoke of a furnace” (Genesis 19:28). Before anything comes out, the light goes. That is exactly what evil does. It rarely arrives arguing. It arrives as a haze: things once clear stop being clear, obvious distinctions go soft, and after a while no one can see far enough to be sure of anything. A test: where has your moral vision gone hazy — something you once called sin that you now just call complicated? Bring it back into the light of Scripture.

verseByVerse.quote: Then from the smoke came locusts on the earth, and they were given power like the power of scorpions of the earth. They were told not to harm the grass of the earth or any green plant or any tree, but only those people who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Locusts with scorpion-like power come out of the smoke, but they are forbidden to harm vegetation and may touch only those without God’s seal on their foreheads. Demonic forces are real and terrible, but God sets their limits, and his seal marks a boundary they cannot cross.

Locusts. The ancient image of total devastation. Joel built a prophecy on them: an army that darkens the land, runs like war horses, leaps walls, and leaves Eden looking like a desert (Joel 1:4–7; 2:1–11). There is nothing to fight. They come as a shadow on the horizon, and when they lift nothing green is left.

Wrong in every particular. These come out of the abyss, not off the fields. They have scorpions’ power, which locusts lack. And they are told not to touch grass, the one thing locusts exist to eat. This isn’t an infestation. It is what comes up when the pit is opened, wearing the shape of the most feared plague of the ancient world.

A scorpion’s sting. Rarely fatal to a healthy adult, and agonising; Rehoboam used it as a picture of intensified cruelty (1 Kings 12:11). This judgment doesn’t kill, and isn’t therefore lesser.

Three fences. “They were told” — the divine passive again. A fence around the vegetation; and a fence around people, drawn along one line: “only those people who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads.”

What the seal does. The first time chapter 7’s sealing is cashed out. It doesn’t exempt anyone from the great tribulation (7:14), and it didn’t spare the martyrs under the altar. It sets a limit on what can be done to a sealed person and by whom. The powers of the abyss have a list, and the list has a boundary, drawn before the shaft was opened.

Egypt again. God drew a line through Egypt: “I will set apart the land of Goshen, where my people dwell, so that no swarms of flies shall be there” (Exodus 8:22); in the darkness “all the people of Israel had light where they lived” (Exodus 10:23); and at Passover the doorposts were marked with blood. The seal on the forehead is the doorpost of Exodus, moved from the house to the person.

An honest fear answered. The seal isn’t a promise that nothing will happen to you. Christians get cancer, lose jobs, are lied about, go to prison, and die. What it guarantees is that nothing can reach past it to what you actually are — you remain God’s. A test: are you afraid of spiritual powers? You needn’t be. If you are Christ’s, you carry his seal, and the abyss has been told where its boundary is.

verseByVerse.quote: They were allowed to torment them for five months, but not to kill them, and their torment was like the torment of a scorpion when it stings someone. And in those days people will seek death and will not find it. They will long to die, but death will flee from them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The locusts may torment the unsealed for five months but not kill them, and people will long to die yet not find death. Life without God becomes its own torment for those who refuse him, yet God limits even this judgment in time.

Two boundaries. “Allowed” again. They may torment, not kill — and for five months, not a day more.

Why five months? The plainest answer: a locust’s life cycle, roughly a summer season. Not a code, but a bounded, recognisable stretch every farming society could measure. It will feel endless while it lasts. It isn’t.

Seeking death. “People will seek death and will not find it. They will long to die, but death will flee from them.” Job spoke of those “who long for death, but it comes not” (Job 3:21); Jeremiah of survivors who would prefer death to life (Jeremiah 8:3). This is existence itself become punishment, with the one exit closed.

If you know this country. Some read this from outside, as a future horror. Others recognise it. There are Christians who have lain awake wishing quite specifically not to wake up. If that is you, this verse isn’t describing your condemnation. Three things, plainly. First, wanting to die isn’t the same as being abandoned by God. Moses asked God to kill him (Numbers 11:15); Elijah asked to die the day after his greatest victory (1 Kings 19:4); Jonah asked twice (Jonah 4:3, 8); Job longed for it. God rebuked none of them. He fed Elijah and let him sleep. Second, this torment falls expressly on those without God’s seal (v. 4) — people being handed the end of their refusal, existence without him — not on his struggling children. Third, despair says the darkness is permanent and there is no door. This whole book announces a door opened from the other side at enormous cost, by the One who holds the keys of Death and Hades (1:18). If you are in this territory, tell another Christian this week, and a doctor or pastor if the thoughts are pressing; don’t carry it alone. That isn’t weakness; it is what the body of Christ is for.

The true horror. Rightly read, the horror isn’t that God is cruel but that there is a state worse than dying, which human beings can reach by their own steady choosing. The mercy in the chapter is the five-month fence around it, put there by God.
verseByVerse.note: Five months is roughly the life span of a locust, or the season in which they swarm.

verseByVerse.quote: In appearance the locusts were like horses prepared for battle: on their heads were what looked like crowns of gold; their faces were like human faces, their hair like women's hair, and their teeth like lions' teeth; they had breastplates like breastplates of iron, and the noise of their wings was like the noise of many chariots with horses rushing into battle. They have tails and stings like scorpions, and their power to hurt people for five months is in their tails.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John describes the locusts in a cascade of “like”s: war horses, false golden crowns, human faces, women’s hair, lions’ teeth, iron breastplates, roaring wings and scorpion tails. This is spiritual evil given a body — intelligent, armoured, falsely crowned, and stinging from behind — yet still under God’s time limit.

Impossible to draw. Eight comparisons in four verses, each with “like.” John isn’t describing a species; he is telling a congregation what it felt like to look at.

Horses and counterfeit crowns. “Like horses prepared for battle” — as Joel said, “Their appearance is like the appearance of horses” (Joel 2:4); a locust’s head does look like a tiny horse’s, and the Italian word for grasshopper, cavalletta, means little horse. On their heads, “what looked like crowns of gold” — not crowns. A counterfeit, and John won’t let it pass. Everything genuinely crowned in this book is crowned by God.

Faces and teeth. Human faces: the worst detail — whatever this is has intelligence and intent, and looks back at you. Long hair, perhaps a locust’s streaming antennae. Lions’ teeth, from Joel 1:6.

Armour and noise. Iron breastplates: nothing gets through. Wings “like the noise of many chariots with horses rushing into battle”: a swarm is heard before it is seen, a dry roar that fills the sky.

The sting from behind. “Their power to hurt people… is in their tails.” The sixth trumpet repeats it (v. 19). Twice in one chapter the injury comes from behind, after the thing seems to have passed. That is how much evil works: the damage is rarely done at the moment of encounter, but afterwards, by what was left in the wound.

Not a weapon to identify. A man’s face and a lion’s teeth; armour and a crown that isn’t one; a locust that won’t eat grass, a horse that isn’t a horse. Every category slips. Every generation that has identified these with a weapon — cavalry, cannon, helicopters, drones — has been confident, and overtaken by the next generation’s equally confident guess.

What is permanent. The anatomy of spiritual evil: intelligent, armoured, untouchable by those it torments, crowned with an authority it didn’t earn, deafening, stinging from behind. A congregation living near “where Satan’s throne is” (2:13) didn’t need it decoded. They needed to know it comes up on a permission and goes down on a timetable. A test: where are you being stung by something you thought was over — an old sin, an old wound? Name it to Christ, who sets the timetable.

verseByVerse.quote: They have as king over them the angel of the bottomless pit. His name in Hebrew is Abaddon, and in Greek he is called Apollyon. The first woe has passed; behold, two woes are still to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The locusts’ king is the angel of the bottomless pit, named Abaddon in Hebrew and Apollyon in Greek — Destruction, the Destroyer. Evil has an organiser, but he can only destroy, and he is a creature on God’s leash, not God’s equal.

A king. Proverbs says “the locusts have no king” (Proverbs 30:27) — part of what makes a swarm so unnerving. These have one. The chaos is organised and has a commander, named twice so that both halves of the congregation catch it.

Two names. Abaddon is Hebrew for destruction, an Old Testament name for the realm of the dead: “Sheol is naked before God, and Abaddon has no covering” (Job 26:6; cf. Job 28:22; Proverbs 15:11). Apollyon is Greek for the destroyer. Two languages, one meaning: this figure isn’t a local problem.

A barb at Apollo? Probably. Apollo was a great god of the Greek world, sometimes linked with the locust, and emperors from Augustus on associated themselves with him. A Christian in Ephesus might well hear it: the god the empire boasts in sounds like the Destroyer, and what he really rules is a pit.

He can only unmake. His name is his job description. He can’t create or build. Set him beside the One on the throne, praised in chapter 4 because “you created all things” (4:11), and the asymmetry is total. One makes things out of nothing; the other unmakes what someone else made, and can be shut in a shaft.

Not two matched powers. Many thoughtful Christians quietly fear that good and evil are roughly matched, wrestling for the world with the outcome uncertain. Revelation never allows it. The destroyer is the subject of passive sentences: he is given a key, allowed five months, told what he may not touch. He isn’t God’s opposite number. He is a creature with a leash and a name. A test: do you live as if the outcome is in doubt? Pray today as one who knows who is on the throne.

“The first woe has passed.” One verse of bookkeeping, doing two things. It confirms the eagle’s three woes (8:13) are the fifth, sixth and seventh trumpets. And it says “has passed.” The five months ended; whatever came up went back down. That matters to people inside something. Every affliction in this book is announced, measured, and reported finished. The One who keeps the register holds the keys, and he has never lost count.
verseByVerse.note: Abaddon means “destruction” and Apollyon “destroyer.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–21 — The Sixth Trumpet: The Army from the Euphrates
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 13–14: the sixth trumpet, and a voice from the four horns of the golden altar — the incense altar, where the prayers of all the saints were offered in 8:3–4 and from which fire was thrown down in 8:5. The order it gives is Release the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates. They are bound; they must be released; the order comes from the altar where the church prays. The Euphrates was the empire’s eastern frontier and the direction every invasion of Israel had come from.

Verse 15: the four had been prepared for the hour, the day, the month, and the year — one article in the Greek governs all four, so this is a fixed moment rather than a duration — and are released to kill a third of mankind. The fraction has moved from things to people. Verse 16 gives the number of mounted troops as twice ten thousand times ten thousand, with the telling clause I heard their number, exactly as at 7:4.

Verses 17–19: breastplates the colour of fire, sapphire and sulfur — the same three things the horses breathe. Lions’ heads; fire, smoke and sulfur from their mouths, the substance of Sodom (Gen. 19:24) and of the lake of fire (19:20; 20:10). A third of mankind killed by these three plagues. And the power is in mouths and in tails, the tails being like serpents with heads — the word John reserves for the dragon (12:9; 20:2).

Verses 20–21 give the verdict the whole sequence was building toward. The rest of mankind, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent — not of the works of their hands, not of worshipping demons and idols of gold, silver, bronze, stone and wood which cannot see or hear or walk (Ps. 115:4–8), and not of their murders, sorceries, sexual immorality or thefts.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Order Comes from the Altar

The voice that releases the four angels comes from the altar where the saints’ prayers are offered. They were prepared for the hour, day, month and year. Yet the survivors did not repent of their idols, sorceries and sins.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Beyond the Euphrates lay the invader every Roman province feared.

Now: Judgement alone does not change hearts; we become like what we worship.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the sixth angel blew his trumpet, and I heard a voice from the four horns of the golden altar before God, saying to the sixth angel who had the trumpet, "Release the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates."
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the sixth trumpet a voice from the horns of the golden altar orders the release of four angels bound at the Euphrates. God’s judgments answer his people’s prayers, and even the most feared invading forces are held back until he gives the word.

From the altar. The golden altar is the incense altar. In 8:3–4 an angel offered incense there with the prayers of all the saints; in 8:5 its fire was thrown to earth. Now a voice from its four horns releases the sixth trumpet.

Refuge and blood. An altar’s horns were the corner projections a man grasped when he fled for sanctuary (1 Kings 1:50–51), and on which atoning blood was smeared (Leviticus 4:7, 18). The order to release destroying angels comes from the altar where the church’s prayers are burned.

The third time. For the third time in two chapters: God’s judgments on the world aren’t arbitrary spasms; they answer his people’s praying, issued from where that praying is received. A congregation that has prayed for years about wickedness no one seems to stop is being told where its prayers went and what they are doing.

Bound, then released. They are bound — and somebody had to bind them. They are released by an order, from an altar, at a set moment. The pattern hasn’t varied for four chapters: nothing hostile moves except on a permission issued from the throne room.

The Euphrates. The eastern edge of Rome’s empire and of Israel’s world before it. Every great invasion that threatened Jerusalem came from beyond it — Assyria, then Babylon. In John’s day the terror there was Parthia, the one power Rome never subdued, whose mounted archers had destroyed a Roman army at Carrhae. To say “the Euphrates” was to say what a border means to any country invaded across one: the direction the end comes from.

Who are the four angels bound at the Euphrates? Because they are bound and then released to kill, they are most likely fallen angels, held in restraint until God’s appointed hour (cf. 2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6). Even their release is under his control: they were “prepared for the hour, the day, the month, and the year” (v. 15).

On a rope. Whatever we think about history’s invasions, this verse says something about all of them: the horde crossing the border was on a rope, the rope was in God’s hand, and the hand let go at a moment of its own choosing. A test: what force do you most fear crossing into your life or your nation? Pray to the One who holds the rope.
verseByVerse.note: The Euphrates was the eastern frontier of the Roman world, beyond which lay the feared Parthians.

verseByVerse.quote: So the four angels, who had been prepared for the hour, the day, the month, and the year, were released to kill a third of mankind. The number of mounted troops was twice ten thousand times ten thousand; I heard their number.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The four angels, prepared for a precise hour, are released to kill a third of mankind with a cavalry numbering twice ten thousand times ten thousand. Even catastrophe happens at a moment God has appointed, and the vast forces against his small church are still under his command.

A diary entry. “The hour, the day, the month, and the year” — one article governs all four, making them one appointed moment, not a span. Not for a year, month, day and hour, but for the hour, on the day, in the month, of the year.

Time-stamped in advance. The most steadying sentence in the chapter. The moment was fixed before the angels were bound; they were “prepared” — made ready and standing ready. The catastrophe that comes without warning and seems to prove nobody is steering has a time stamp applied in advance. That isn’t to call catastrophe good; Scripture never does. It is to say history isn’t a run of accidents occasionally interrupted by providence. Every hour has been counted, including the ones nobody would choose. A test: what hour of your life seemed to prove no one was steering? It too was counted.

A third of mankind. The horsemen had a fourth; the first trumpets a third of earth, sea, water and light; now a third of people. Judgment escalates from things to people — and still two-thirds are untouched, for a reason v. 20 states bluntly.

Two hundred million? “Twice ten thousand times ten thousand.” As arithmetic, two hundred million; almost certainly not meant so. A myriad, ten thousand, was the largest number Greek had a word for, so myriads of myriads is the language reaching its ceiling, used already of the angels around the throne (5:11) and by Daniel (Daniel 7:10). Doubling it means “and twice that again.” The whole Roman empire may have numbered sixty million.

“I heard their number.” John didn’t count them; he was told — exactly as with the 144,000: “I heard the number of the sealed” (7:4). Given the same way, the two numbers should be read the same way, as figures of overwhelming completeness.

Proportion. The church in Asia was a few thousand people in seven towns, meeting in houses, with no standing at all. The forces against them run off the end of the counting system — and the whole host is on the far side of a river, tied up, waiting for a word from an altar.

verseByVerse.quote: And this is how I saw the horses in my vision and those who rode them: they wore breastplates the color of fire and of sapphire and of sulfur, and the heads of the horses were like lions' heads, and fire and smoke and sulfur came out of their mouths. By these three plagues a third of mankind was killed, by the fire and smoke and sulfur coming out of their mouths. For the power of the horses is in their mouths and in their tails, for their tails are like serpents with heads, and by means of them they wound.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John sees the horses and riders: breastplates of fire, sapphire and sulfur; lion-headed horses breathing fire, smoke and sulfur that kill a third of mankind; and serpent-headed tails that wound. The judgment smells of hell itself, and the serpent’s sting comes from behind, after the danger seems past.

A vision. John reminds the reader mid-description: “in my vision.” He isn’t claiming to have watched cavalry through a telescope.

Wearing what they breathe. Breastplates of fire-red, dark blue and sulfur-yellow — the colours of the fire, smoke and sulfur pouring from the horses’ mouths.

Sulfur. Brimstone has one address in Scripture: “the LORD rained on Sodom and Gomorrah sulfur and fire from the LORD out of heaven” (Genesis 19:24). It is the smell of judgment, and the book uses it again for the lake of fire (19:20; 20:10; 21:8). What comes from these mouths is the substance of hell.

Mouths. “By these three plagues” — Exodus vocabulary again. And the killing is by what comes out of a mouth, which in this book is never accidental: Christ’s weapon is the sword from his mouth (1:16; 19:15). Two mouths, two kinds of word, both decisive. What comes from a mouth kills or saves.

Tails with heads. Twice now the tail is the dangerous end (v. 10), and here the tails have heads — it bites in both directions, the second bite after you think it has passed. The word for serpent belongs in this book to one owner: “that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan” (12:9; 20:2). John has signed the picture. And readers in Asia would think of the Parthian archers, famous for shooting backwards as they rode away.

Ruin from behind. That is how ruin often arrives in a life. The moment of the encounter is rarely the moment of the damage. The affair ended years ago; the consequences are only now walking through the door. The drink was put down; the liver wasn’t consulted. The words were said one bad evening; the son hasn’t called since. Evil does its worst work with its back turned. A test: what sin are you toying with because it seems to have no consequences yet? The sting is in the tail. Turn from it now.

verseByVerse.quote: The rest of mankind, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent of the works of their hands nor give up worshiping demons and idols of gold and silver and bronze and stone and wood, which cannot see or hear or walk, nor did they repent of their murders or their sorceries or their sexual immorality or their thefts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The survivors of these plagues still refuse to repent of their idols or of their murders, sorceries, sexual immorality and thefts. Suffering alone does not change hearts: people cling to what they worship, and the root of every visible sin is idolatry — yet the door to repent stays open.

“The rest.” Two-thirds survived. Every fraction in four chapters — a fourth, a third, a third — existed for those left, and this verse says what they did with the mercy of being alive. They didn’t repent.

Wouldn’t a catastrophe convince them? Many assume that if God made himself unmistakable, people would believe. Revelation says it has been tried: the sky darkened, the water turned bitter, a third of the race died, and the survivors went back to what they were doing. Suffering doesn’t automatically produce repentance; it hardens as often as it softens. Pharaoh, whose plagues these are, is the proof: plague after plague he hardened his heart, and in the end his army drove into a sea God had opened.

Blind idols, blind worshippers. Gold, silver, bronze, stone and wood “which cannot see or hear or walk” — almost word for word the Psalm: “They have mouths, but do not speak; eyes, but do not see… Those who make them become like them” (Psalm 115:5–8; cf. Daniel 5:23). That last line is the sting. You become like what you worship; worship something blind and deaf and in the end you can’t see or hear either — exactly what this chapter has described.

Demons behind them. John calls the idols demons, as Paul said: “what pagans sacrifice they offer to demons and not to God” (1 Corinthians 10:20). The statue is wood; what is served through it isn’t nothing.

Ordinary sins. Murders, sorceries, sexual immorality, thefts. “Sorceries” is pharmakeia — magic, spells, and the potions used in them. It isn’t a verse about medicine, and reading it so is a misuse. It names the attempt to control life, luck, love and death by technique rather than trust in God: pay the right practitioner, use the right substance, say the right words.

Root and fruit. Idolatry is the root; murder, manipulation, immorality and theft the fruit. Whoever has replaced God will end up taking his neighbour’s life, body, marriage or property, because nothing is left to stop him. None of the four is exotic; each is available on an ordinary Tuesday.

A test. Not “Do I own a statue?” An idol is whatever you couldn’t give up. Take the thing you have already been warned about — by your body, your bank, your spouse, a friend who risked saying it — and notice how expertly you have explained the warning away. That is v. 20 happening in a life, at a scale where it can still be repented of. Do it today.

A door left unused. The judgments were fractional so someone would be left to turn; the trumpets were warnings, not the end; an eagle cried three woes in daylight before the first landed. God went to extraordinary lengths to be heard, and the chapter’s last word is that they did not repent — not that they could not.

They will long to die, but death will flee from them.<sup>7</sup>In appearance the locusts were like horses prepared for battle: on their heads were what looked like crowns of gold; their faces were like human faces,<sup>8</sup>their hair like women’s hair, and their teeth like lions’ teeth;<sup>9</sup>they had breastplates like breastplates of iron, and the noise of their wings was like the noise of many chariots with horses rushing into battle.<sup>10</sup>They have tails and stings like scorpions, and their power to hurt people for five months is in their tails.<sup>11</sup>They have as king over them the angel of the bottomless pit. His name in Hebrew is Abaddon, and in Greek he is called Apollyon.<sup>12</sup>The first woe has passed; behold, two woes are still to come.<sup>13</sup>Then the sixth angel blew his trumpet, and I heard a voice from the four horns of the golden altar before God,<sup>14</sup>saying to the sixth angel who had the trumpet, “Release the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates.”<sup>15</sup>So the four angels, who had been prepared for the hour, the day, the month, and the year, were released to kill a third of mankind.<sup>16</sup>The number of mounted troops was twice ten thousand times ten thousand; I heard their number.<sup>17</sup>And this is how I saw the horses in my vision and those who rode them: they wore breastplates the color of fire and of sapphire and of sulfur, and the heads of the horses were like lions’ heads, and fire and smoke and sulfur came out of their mouths.<sup>18</sup>By these three plagues a third of mankind was killed, by the fire and smoke and sulfur coming out of their mouths.<sup>19</sup>For the power of the horses is in their mouths and in their tails, for their tails are like serpents with heads, and by means of them they wound.<sup>20</sup>The rest of mankind, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent of the works of their hands nor give up worshiping demons and idols of gold and silver and bronze and stone and wood, which cannot see or hear or walk,<sup>21</sup>nor did they repent of their murders or their sorceries or their sexual immorality or their thefts.

10.title: The Angel and the Little Scroll
10.overview:
Chapter 10 is the second great interlude of Revelation — this one inserted between the sixth and seventh trumpets (as chapter 7 was inserted between the sixth and seventh seals). The interlude performs the same function: it pauses the judgment sequence to reorient the reader to the prophetic commission of the church. Before the seventh trumpet sounds and the final woe arrives, John is given a little scroll to eat and recommissioned to prophesy.

A mighty angel descends from heaven clothed with a cloud, with a rainbow over his head, his face like the sun, his legs like pillars of fire — imagery that deliberately echoes the description of Christ in chapter 1. He stands on sea and land (claiming sovereignty over the whole earth), holds a little open scroll, and cries out with a loud voice like a lion’s roar. Seven thunders respond — and John is told not to write what the thunders said. This is the only thing in Revelation that is sealed rather than revealed: some of God’s purposes remain hidden until their time.

John eats the little scroll at the angel’s command. It is sweet in his mouth but bitter in his stomach — an echo of Ezekiel’s commissioning (Ezekiel 2:8–3:3) and Jeremiah’s experience of the word (Jeremiah 15:16). The word of God is sweet to receive — it is the good news of grace, the promise of the kingdom, the comfort of the gospel. But the prophetic task is bitter: to speak God’s word to a world that does not want to hear it, to witness to the truth in the face of hostility, to suffer for the testimony of Jesus. The whole book of Revelation is this little scroll: sweet with the glory of the Lamb, bitter with the suffering of faithful witness.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Angel and the Little Scroll
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Six trumpets have sounded; the seventh does not sound until 11:15. Everything between is an interlude, exactly as chapter 7 stood between the sixth and seventh seals — a repetition that is itself an argument about how John builds his sevens.

Verses 1–2: another mighty angel comes down wrapped in a cloud, with a rainbow over his head, a face like the sun and legs like pillars of fire — every detail borrowed from the descriptions of God and of Christ (1:7, 15, 16; 4:3; Ex. 13:21). He holds a little scroll, and it is already open, unlike the sealed scroll of chapter 5. He sets his right foot on the sea and his left on the land: the conqueror’s posture (Josh. 1:3), with one foot on each of the two places the beasts of chapter 13 will rise from.

Verse 3: he calls out like a lion roaring — the prophets’ image for God speaking (Amos 3:8; Hos. 11:10; Joel 3:16) — and the seven thunders sound, the definite article suggesting a known set, most likely the sevenfold voice of the LORD in Psalm 29. Verse 4: John, pen in hand and about to write, is stopped: Seal up what the seven thunders have said, and do not write it down.

Verses 5–7: the angel raises his right hand and swears — the posture of Daniel 12:6–7 — by the one who lives for ever and who made heaven, earth and sea, that there would be no more delay, and that at the seventh trumpet the mystery of God would be fulfilled, just as he announced to his servants the prophets.

Verses 8–10: John is sent to take the open scroll and told Take and eat it; it will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be sweet as honey — Ezekiel’s commission exactly (Ezek. 2:9–3:3; cf. Jer. 15:16). He eats, and reports the tastes in the order he met them: sweet first, bitter after. Verse 11 sends him back to work: You must again prophesy about many peoples and nations and languages and kings.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Sealed Thunders and the Swallowed Scroll

A mighty angel in his master’s glory stands on sea and land. What the seven thunders said is sealed — the one sealed sentence in an unsealed book. The angel swears there will be no more delay, and John must eat the little scroll: sweet in the mouth, bitter in the stomach.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: An exiled old man was recommissioned to prophesy to peoples, nations and kings.

Now: Do not claim to know what God has withheld; and expect the gospel to be sweet to receive and costly to carry.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw another mighty angel coming down from heaven, wrapped in a cloud, with a rainbow over his head, and his face was like the sun, and his legs like pillars of fire. He had a little scroll open in his hand. And he set his right foot on the sea, and his left foot on the land,
verseByVerse.commentary:
A mighty angel comes down from heaven, robed in cloud, crowned with a rainbow, face like the sun, holding an open little scroll, and plants one foot on the sea and one on the land. Before the darkest chapters, God’s messenger is shown claiming the whole world for him.

An interlude again. Six trumpets have sounded; the seventh waits until 11:15. Everything between is an interlude, as chapter 7 stood between the sixth and seventh seals. John doesn’t rush his sevens. Twice, just when a reader braces for the end, the vision stops and turns to the church.

Is this angel Christ? Every detail has been met before: the cloud Christ comes with (1:7), the rainbow around the throne (4:3), a face like the sun (1:16), legs like pillars of fire, recalling his bronze feet (1:15) and Israel’s pillar of fire (Exodus 13:21). So some serious readers conclude this is Christ himself. Three things tell against it. He is “another mighty angel,” another of the same kind as the mighty angel of 5:2. In v. 6 he swears by the One who lives forever, which Christ doesn’t need to do (cf. Hebrews 6:13). And Revelation never calls Christ an angel, though it names him a hundred other things. The more likely reading is that he is a herald dressed in his master’s livery. When an ambassador arrives in the king’s colours, the point isn’t that he is the king, but whose message he carries.

A little scroll, open. Little — a different word from the great sealed scroll of chapter 5. And open. That scroll had seven seals no one could break; this one lies unrolled in an angel’s hand, and John will soon be told to take it. Whether it is part of the great scroll or a separate commission isn’t stated. It is small enough to hold, open enough to read, and about to be handed to a man.

A foot on each. Sea and land: everywhere. Planting a foot on territory is what a conqueror does: “Every place that the sole of your foot will tread upon I have given to you” (Joshua 1:3). He stands on the world — one foot on the sea the beast will rise from (13:1), one on the earth the second beast will rise from (13:11).

Hold that when it gets dark. Before the dragon or either beast appears, a messenger from heaven stands with a foot on each of the places they come from, holding an open scroll under a covenant rainbow. A test: when evil seems to own the world, do you remember whose foot is already on it?

verseByVerse.quote: and called out with a loud voice, like a lion roaring. When he called out, the seven thunders sounded. And when the seven thunders had sounded, I was about to write, but I heard a voice from heaven saying, "Seal up what the seven thunders have said, and do not write it down."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel roars like a lion, the seven thunders speak, and when John starts to write he is told, “Seal up what the seven thunders have said, and do not write it down.” God has revealed what we need, and he has deliberately kept some things back — so we should neither demand nor claim more than he has given.

A lion’s roar. Not a warning shot; it carries for miles and announces possession of territory. “The lion has roared; who will not fear? The Lord GOD has spoken; who can but prophesy?” (Amos 3:8; cf. Hosea 11:10; Joel 3:16). In this book there is one Lion, of Judah, who turned out to be a Lamb (5:5–6). The angel roars with his master’s voice.

The seven thunders. “The” seven thunders, as if readers should know which. The likeliest background is Psalm 29, where “the voice of the LORD” thunders seven times over the waters, breaking cedars and shaking the wilderness, until in his temple “all cry, ‘Glory!’” Another full series of divine speech. And John understood it — a man doesn’t reach for a pen to write down noise. Then it is taken from him, and from every reader since.

Once told not to write. The reverse of every other instruction John receives. “Write what you see in a book and send it to the seven churches” (1:11); “Write therefore the things that you have seen” (1:19); “Write this down, for these words are trustworthy and true” (21:5). Twelve times he is told to write; once, not to. And the pen was already moving: “I was about to write.”

The one sealed sentence. Daniel was told to seal his book until the end (Daniel 12:4, 9); John at the close is told, “Do not seal up the words of the prophecy of this book, for the time is near” (22:10). Revelation is the unsealed book. It holds exactly one sealed sentence, and we don’t have it. Why? Suggestions abound — judgments cancelled in mercy, the bowls held back until chapter 16, the days shortened. None can be proved. Nobody knows, because the point is that we weren’t told.

A boundary God set. “The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children forever, that we may do all the words of this law” (Deuteronomy 29:29). Both categories are God’s decision. And the revealed things are for doing, not just knowing. That has an edge for anyone hungry for more than is given — the date, the identity, the exact sequence, the name behind the number. John, an apostle in the Spirit with the information in his ears, was refused permission to pass it on. Anyone claiming to have recovered what the thunders said claims something John was forbidden. A test: is your reading of Revelation driven by curiosity about what is hidden, or by obedience to what is revealed?

Unanswered questions. For the believer who has asked God for years: Why did that happen? Why no child? Why did a good man’s prayer come to nothing? This verse doesn’t say the answer doesn’t exist. The thunders spoke; there was content; John understood it. The answer exists and hasn’t been given, and the withholding is deliberate. Being told no by God about information isn’t the same as there being nothing there. Trust him with the sealed things.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel whom I saw standing on the sea and on the land raised his right hand to heaven and swore by him who lives forever and ever, who created heaven and what is in it, the earth and what is in it, and the sea and what is in it, that there would be no more delay, but that in the days of the trumpet call to be sounded by the seventh angel, the mystery of God would be fulfilled, just as he announced to his servants the prophets.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel raises his hand and swears by the eternal Creator that there will be no more delay: at the seventh trumpet God’s mystery — his whole saving purpose announced through the prophets — will be fulfilled. The long wait of God’s people has a fixed end, guaranteed by God himself.

An oath from Daniel. The scene comes from Daniel 12, where a man in linen above the waters raises his hands to heaven and swears “by him who lives forever” how long until the end (Daniel 12:6–7). Readers who knew Daniel would recognise the posture before the content.

The ground belongs to him. The One sworn by lives forever and made heaven, earth and sea and all in them. Not decoration: the angel stands on sea and land and swears by the One who made them. Whatever the beasts rising from them will claim, the ground under this oath belongs to Someone else.

No more delay. The King James rendered it “there should be time no longer,” and many took it as the end of time itself. The word can mean either; the context settles it. This answers the souls under the altar: “how long?” (6:10). They were told to rest a little longer. Here, under oath, an angel announces that the little longer has run out.

The hardest thing. Waiting has been the hardest thing in this book, and in the Christian life — not only the suffering but its open-endedness, not knowing if it lasts a month or forty years. This verse doesn’t say when. It says the when is fixed and sworn to by the Creator, and the postponement is over. A test: what are you waiting on God for? Wait as one whose end date is sworn in heaven.

The mystery of God. In the New Testament a mystery isn’t an unsolvable puzzle but a secret now disclosed (Ephesians 3:3–6; Colossians 1:26–27). Here it is God’s whole purpose: in Christ to gather up all things, judge evil, redeem a people from every nation, and put creation right. It “would be fulfilled” — brought to completion.

Nothing new. “Just as he announced to his servants the prophets.” What the seventh trumpet completes is the programme God published through Isaiah, Daniel, Amos and the rest (Amos 3:7). And “announced” is the verb behind “gospel”: he preached its good news to them in advance.

The reassurance needed here. Six trumpets have sounded and the world is worse; two-thirds of mankind refuse to repent; the beasts haven’t even arrived. And an angel with a foot on sea and land swears that God’s plan will be finished, on time, exactly as advertised.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the voice that I had heard from heaven spoke to me again, saying, "Go, take the scroll that is open in the hand of the angel who is standing on the sea and on the land." So I went to the angel and told him to give me the little scroll. And he said to me, "Take and eat it; it will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be sweet as honey." And I took the little scroll from the hand of the angel and ate it. It was sweet as honey in my mouth, but when I had eaten it my stomach was made bitter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John is told to take the little scroll and eat it; it is sweet as honey in his mouth but bitter in his stomach. God’s word must be taken deep into us before we speak it, and it is both sweet — because it is his — and bitter, because of the judgment and suffering it announces.

An errand. The voice that told him not to write now tells him to move, and John does something rather charming: he walks over and asks the angel for the scroll. He doesn’t snatch it.

Ezekiel’s commission. Ezekiel received this exactly, nearly seven centuries earlier: a scroll of “lamentation and mourning and woe,” and the command, “Son of man, eat whatever you find here. Eat this scroll, and go, speak to the house of Israel.” “Then I ate it, and it was in my mouth as sweet as honey” (Ezekiel 2:9–3:3). Jeremiah: “Your words were found, and I ate them, and your words became to me a joy and the delight of my heart” (Jeremiah 15:16).

Why eating. A herald could be handed a script and read it out. This isn’t that. No one delivers a message by digesting it. Eating makes a thing part of you — slowly, inwardly, irreversibly. God’s word isn’t first material to transmit but food to take in until it is in the blood, and only then does one speak. A test: do you read Scripture to pass it on, or to be fed by it first?

Sweet first. The angel warned bitter-then-sweet; John tasted sweet-then-bitter. Sweet because it is God’s word, and nothing is better: “sweeter also than honey and drippings of the honeycomb” (Psalm 19:10; cf. 119:103).

Then bitter. Because of what is in it. John is about to see two witnesses killed in the street, a dragon hunting a woman, a beast conquering the saints, and a city drunk on martyrs’ blood. No one takes that in and feels nothing. Ezekiel went from his scroll “in bitterness in the heat of my spirit” and sat stunned among the exiles seven days (Ezekiel 3:14–15).

The order of the tastes. Every honest Christian eventually recognises it. The gospel is sweet on the way in and costly on the way down. No one is converted by being told what it will require; they are converted by being told they are loved and forgiven, and it is honey. The bitterness comes later, and isn’t a sign something went wrong. It is the taste of truth being absorbed by someone who must now live in a world that doesn’t want it.

The taste of ministry. Anyone who has had to say a true thing that would cost a friendship knows the sequence: the delight of knowing it, then the churning at two in the morning before the conversation. A preacher who finds Scripture only sweet hasn’t noticed what is in it; one who finds it only bitter has forgotten why he started. The prophet gets both, in that order, from one scroll.

Why Revelation is hard. It was never meant to be comfortable. It is sweet — the Lamb reigns, the martyrs are vindicated, God wipes every tear — and bitter, because the road there runs through chapters 11 to 20. John had to swallow both before he was allowed to speak.
verseByVerse.note: Like Ezekiel, John eats God’s message: sweet to receive, bitter because it announces judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: And I was told, "You must again prophesy about many peoples and nations and languages and kings."
verseByVerse.commentary:
John is told he must prophesy again about many peoples, nations, languages and kings. God commissions an old, exiled, powerless man with a message for the whole world — and his usefulness to God was not over.

Who is told this. An old man on a bare island of about thirteen square miles, under Roman banishment, with no congregation, property, pulpit or way home. He has written the seven letters and seen the throne, the Lamb, the seals and the trumpets. By any reckoning his work is behind him.

“You must.” The word of divine necessity, used in 1:1 of what “must soon take place,” and by Jesus of his own suffering. Not an invitation or a career step but a commission, and John isn’t asked whether he would like it.

The whole world. “Many peoples and nations and languages and kings” — the fourfold phrase for humanity since 5:9, with “kings” replacing “tribes,” because from chapter 11 the book turns to the powers of the earth. A prisoner with no legal standing receives a preaching commission covering every nation and its rulers, and his only equipment is a small scroll he has eaten.

About, or against. The preposition can mean either. Prophecy in Scripture is rarely prediction for its own sake. It is God’s verdict on the present, spoken aloud, usually to people who didn’t ask for it.

Not finished. For any Christian who has concluded his useful years are over — through age, illness, a job that ended, or a church that no longer asks. John’s circumstances were worse than most: exiled, elderly, isolated. Heaven’s word was “again.” The most extraordinary assignment of his life came after everything that looked like his ministry was taken away. A test: what has God given you to do in this season, however small it looks? Do it this week.

The shape of every commission. A messenger in his master’s glory plants his feet on the world. Seven thunders speak and are sealed, so the church learns there is a limit to what it will be told. An oath by the Creator says the waiting is over and the mystery will be finished as promised. And a scroll is handed to a man, who eats it — honey and bitterness — and is sent back to work. God doesn’t hand out information to be relayed. He feeds a person with his word until it is inside him, then sends him out to say it.

And he set his right foot on the sea, and his left foot on the land,<sup>3</sup>and called out with a loud voice, like a lion roaring. When he called out, the seven thunders sounded.<sup>4</sup>And when the seven thunders had sounded, I was about to write, but I heard a voice from heaven saying, “Seal up what the seven thunders have said, and do not write it down.”<sup>5</sup>And the angel whom I saw standing on the sea and on the land raised his right hand to heaven<sup>6</sup>and swore by him who lives forever and ever, who created heaven and what is in it, the earth and what is in it, and the sea and what is in it, that there would be no more delay,<sup>7</sup>but that in the days of the trumpet call to be sounded by the seventh angel, the mystery of God would be fulfilled, just as he announced to his servants the prophets.<sup>8</sup>Then the voice that I had heard from heaven spoke to me again, saying, “Go, take the scroll that is open in the hand of the angel who is standing on the sea and on the land.”<sup>9</sup>So I went to the angel and told him to give me the little scroll.
