11.title: The Two Witnesses and the Seventh Trumpet
11.overview:
Chapter 11 is the most compressed chapter in Revelation, covering the entire church age from two angles: the measuring of the temple (the church’s preservation), the ministry of the two witnesses (the church’s prophetic witness), their death and resurrection (the church’s apparent defeat and vindication), and the seventh trumpet (the declaration of the kingdom consummated). It is also one of the most contested chapters in the book.

The measuring of the temple in vv. 1–2 has generated enormous debate. Dispensationalists understand it as a prophecy of a literal rebuilt temple in Jerusalem during the tribulation, the outer court given over to Gentile domination for 42 months. The amillennial reading understands the temple as the church (following Paul’s regular use of temple-language for the believing community — 1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:21; 2 Corinthians 6:16) and the measuring as God’s preservation of his people. The outer court “given over to the nations” represents the church’s visible vulnerability to worldly power — it will be trampled — while the inner sanctuary (the true community of the redeemed) is preserved.

The two witnesses of vv. 3–13 are the most important image in the chapter. Their identity has been debated endlessly: Moses and Elijah (because of the specific powers: turning water to blood = Moses, shutting the sky = Elijah), Elijah and Enoch (the two who did not die), or — the majority Reformed reading — the whole witnessing church across the church age. The number two is the number of legal testimony (Deuteronomy 17:6; 19:15; Matthew 18:16); the two witnesses represent the complete testimony of the church to the gospel of Jesus Christ. Their supernatural powers (fire from their mouths, power over rain and waters) are the powers of the prophetic word: proclamation that both judges and saves.

The seventh trumpet of vv. 15–19 does not release a new woe but sounds the final declaration of the kingdom: “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever.” This is the answer to the Lord’s Prayer (“Your kingdom come”) and the goal toward which all of history moves. The kingdom is announced as already accomplished — the aorist tense of the verb (“has become”) indicates a completed action. What will still unfold in chapters 12–22 is the working out of what has already been declared from the throne.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2: John is given a measuring rod and told to measure the temple, the altar and the worshippers — but expressly not the outer court, which is given over to the nations to trample for forty-two months. Measuring in the prophets is a legal owner marking out what is his (Ezek. 40–42; Zech. 2:1–5). Something is claimed and something is deliberately left out, and both are God’s decision.

Verses 3–4: two witnesses are granted authority to prophesy 1,260 days in sackcloth — the coarse black goat hair of mourning, not the uniform of a triumphant movement. They are the two olive trees and the two lampstands of Zechariah 4, where two olive trees feed oil straight into a lampstand and the governing word is not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit (Zech. 4:6).

Verses 5–6 give their powers, and they are two men’s résumés side by side: fire from the mouth (cf. Jer. 5:14), shutting the sky so that no rain falls — Elijah, for three and a half years (1 Kings 17:1; Luke 4:25) — and turning water to blood and striking with plagues, which is Moses in Egypt (Ex. 7:17–20).

Verses 7–8: when they have finished their testimony, the beast from the bottomless pit makes war on them, conquers them and kills them, and their bodies lie in the street of the great city that symbolically is called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified. John supplies the interpretive key himself: pneumatikōs, symbolically. Verses 9–10: for three and a half days the world gazes at the bodies, refuses them burial, and throws the only party in the book — making merry and exchanging presents, because these two prophets had been a torment.

Verses 11–12: a breath of life from God enters them and they stand on their feet (Ezek. 37:10), and a loud voice says Come up here! — the words spoken to John at 4:1 — and they go up in a cloud and their enemies watched them. Verse 13: an earthquake takes a tenth of the city and seven thousand people, and the rest were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven. Verse 14 closes the section: the second woe has passed.
verseByVerse.theology:
Measured, Trampled, Raised

God measures his temple and leaves the outer court to be trampled for a bounded time. His two witnesses prophesy in sackcloth, are killed when their testimony is finished, lie unburied while the world celebrates, and are raised and called up in their enemies’ sight.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Plagues had not moved the world; the witnesses’ death and vindication did.

Now: No faithful witness is cut off before his testimony is finished, and a witness that troubles nobody may not be one.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I was given a measuring rod like a staff, and I was told, "Rise and measure the temple of God and the altar and those who worship there, but do not measure the court outside the temple; leave that out, for it is given over to the nations, and they will trample the holy city for forty-two months.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John is told to measure God’s temple, altar and worshippers but leave out the outer court, which is given to the nations to trample the holy city for forty-two months. God claims and protects his true people, while allowing them to suffer outwardly for a limited time.

To measure is to claim. Measuring in the prophets isn’t surveying; it is an owner marking out what is his and what he will protect. Ezekiel watched a man measure a temple chapter after chapter (Ezekiel 40–42). Zechariah saw a man measuring Jerusalem and heard God say, “I will be to her a wall of fire all around” (Zechariah 2:5).

What temple is measured? The literal reading, held by Walvoord and MacArthur, takes it as a temple building in Jerusalem, rebuilt in the future, with these events in a future tribulation; it takes the words at their plain sense. Its difficulty is that John likely wrote around AD 95, a quarter-century after the temple was destroyed, so it requires a temple that doesn’t yet exist. The symbolic reading takes the temple as the people of God, the standing New Testament usage: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple?” (1 Corinthians 3:16; cf. Ephesians 2:21; 1 Peter 2:5). The New Testament says nothing of a rebuilt temple. The more likely reading is that the measured temple is the true people of God, kept safe by him — the sealing of chapter 7 in another figure — while the outer court and trampled city picture the church suffering outwardly in the world.

Measured and unmeasured. The pastoral heart on any reading. Something is measured and something deliberately left out, and both are God’s decision. He doesn’t say the outer court is beyond his reach; he says “leave that out,” and it “is given over” — the trampling is licensed. So the church isn’t promised that nothing can be trampled, but that what the trampling reaches isn’t the temple. Buildings burn, reputations are ruined, denominations collapse, believers are imprisoned and killed. None of it touches the sanctuary, the altar or the worshippers. A test: what of yours is being trampled — your reputation, your comfort, your church’s standing? Ask whether it is outer court or temple. What is truly yours in Christ has been measured.

Forty-two months. The book’s most repeated number, in three forms: forty-two months (11:2; 13:5), 1,260 days (11:3; 12:6), and “a time, and times, and half a time” (12:14). All are three and a half years, from Daniel, where the little horn oppresses the saints “for a time, times, and half a time” (Daniel 7:25; cf. 12:7). Three and a half is half of seven: a period real and severe, and definitely incomplete — broken off before it can run its course. However it is read, its message is why John repeats it: this time is bounded, and Someone has written down when it stops.
verseByVerse.note: Forty-two months, 1,260 days (v. 3) and “a time, and times, and half a time” (12:14) are all three and a half years — Daniel’s limited time of trouble.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will grant authority to my two witnesses, and they will prophesy for 1,260 days, clothed in sackcloth." These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God grants authority to his two witnesses, who prophesy for 1,260 days in sackcloth; they are the two olive trees and two lampstands standing before the Lord. God gives his church power to bear witness in a time of trouble, sustained not by its own strength but by his Spirit.

Who are the two witnesses? Some take them as Moses and Elijah, since the powers in vv. 5–6 are theirs and they stood with Christ at the transfiguration (Matthew 17:3). Some as Enoch and Elijah, the two who didn’t die (Genesis 5:24; 2 Kings 2:11). Some as two literal prophets of a future tribulation. Many take them as the church in its witnessing role, for three reasons from the text: v. 4 calls them “the two lampstands,” and this book has defined lampstands as churches (1:20); two is the legal minimum for valid testimony — “Only on the evidence of two witnesses or of three witnesses shall a charge be established” (Deuteronomy 19:15); and seven lampstands becoming two suits a church reduced but still lawfully testifying. The more likely reading is the last. On any reading the substance is the same: God has witnesses; they are given authority; they speak for a bounded time; they are killed; and they are raised.

Are the 1,260 days a literal three and a half years? Futurist readers take them as the second half of a future seven-year tribulation. But John uses the three forms interchangeably for one period (11:2–3; 12:6, 14; 13:5), in which the church witnesses, is nourished in the wilderness, and is persecuted by the beast. The more likely reading is that they describe the whole age between Christ’s comings — a limited time, cut short, under God’s control.

Sackcloth. Coarse goat hair, the dress of mourning and repentance, worn by Jacob for a lost son and by Nineveh at Jonah’s preaching. Not the uniform of a triumphant movement but of people grieved by what they see and calling others to repent. That is the tone of the church’s testimony in this age. Not swagger; mourning. A test: when you speak of the world’s sin, do you sound grieved or superior?

Olive trees and lampstands. Lifted from Zechariah 4: a golden lampstand fed oil directly by two olive trees, explained as “the two anointed ones who stand by the Lord of the whole earth” (Zechariah 4:14) — there Joshua the priest and Zerubbabel the governor, rebuilding a ruined temple in a ruined city. The word at the centre of that vision: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the LORD of hosts” (Zechariah 4:6). A lampstand can’t make light or oil; it holds up what is poured in. The church in sackcloth isn’t running on its own reserves.

Too small? Every serious Christian knows the discouragement: the church seems too small, tired and compromised to say anything the world will hear. The witnesses are two, in mourning dress, in a city that will kill them — and connected to an inexhaustible supply, with authority that was granted. Pray for the Spirit’s oil, and speak.

verseByVerse.quote: And if anyone would harm them, fire pours from their mouth and consumes their foes. If anyone would harm them, this is how he is doomed to be killed. They have the power to shut the sky, that no rain may fall during the days of their prophesying, and they have power over the waters to turn them into blood and to strike the earth with every kind of plague, as often as they desire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever tries to harm the witnesses is consumed by fire from their mouths, and they can shut the sky and turn water to blood like Elijah and Moses. God’s word in the mouths of his people carries real power — the same power seen in the law and the prophets.

Fire from the mouth. Not from the hand. In this book that is settled: the sword comes from Christ’s mouth (1:16; 19:15), and God told Jeremiah, “behold, I am making my words in your mouth a fire, and this people wood, and the fire shall consume them” (Jeremiah 5:14). The weapon is the word. What these witnesses do is speak.

A standing rule. Said twice, like a law: harm them, and this follows. And the second half is passive — “he is doomed to be killed” — so the witnesses aren’t executioners. They speak; the judgment falls from elsewhere.

Two men’s résumés. Shutting the sky is Elijah exactly, who told Ahab there would be no dew or rain except by his word (1 Kings 17:1) — for three and a half years, as Luke and James both note (Luke 4:25; James 5:17), the very number of this chapter. Turning water to blood and striking with plagues is Moses in Egypt (Exodus 7:17–20).

The law and the prophets. Moses and Elijah stand behind the witnesses whether or not they are the witnesses. They are the two halves of the Old Testament, and they spoke with Christ on the mountain about his departure (Luke 9:30–31). The church testifies to the whole word of God, doing what they did: standing before a Pharaoh and an Ahab and saying the true thing.

Power and death together. “As often as they desire” shouldn’t be softened: God doesn’t ration his witnesses’ authority. But hold it beside v. 7: people with power to shut the sky are about to be killed in the street. Both are true at once — the church’s experience in every century. God’s word in believers’ mouths has real, world-altering force, and those who carry it are often overpowered, humiliated and killed. Anyone told only the first half will be shattered by the second; anyone who has seen only the second won’t believe the first. John gives both, two verses apart. A test: do you underestimate the word you carry because the world seems not to listen? Speak it anyway.
verseByVerse.note: Their powers recall Elijah (fire, drought) and Moses (water to blood, plagues).

verseByVerse.quote: And when they have finished their testimony, the beast that rises from the bottomless pit will make war on them and conquer them and kill them, and their dead bodies will lie in the street of the great city that symbolically is called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the witnesses finish their testimony, the beast from the abyss makes war on them, conquers and kills them, and their bodies lie in the street of the great city where their Lord was crucified. God’s witnesses can be defeated and killed — but never before their work is done, and they share their Lord’s path.

“When they have finished.” The beast doesn’t interrupt them. He can’t touch them until the testimony is complete. No witness in this book is silenced before saying what he was sent to say. That is a promise to lean on, though not the one most want. It doesn’t say the witness will be protected; it says he will be finished. No one in God’s service is cut off mid-sentence by accident, and the believer who dies at forty with half his work apparently undone has, on this verse, completed it. A test: are you anxious about leaving things unfinished? Do today’s faithful work, and trust him with the length.

The beast’s first appearance. Introduced casually, with “the,” two chapters before he is described. He rises from the bottomless pit opened in 9:1–2 — not a rival from somewhere else, but something come up out of a hole unlocked with a key someone was given.

“Conquer.” The verb that ends every letter as a promise to the faithful, used of Christ at 5:5 — here used of the beast against the saints, successfully, as again at 13:7. Revelation doesn’t pretend the church always wins its battles. It loses visibly, in public, to a power permitted to defeat it. And the book exists to redefine what that means, because the defining case of conquering by being killed is the Lamb standing with his throat cut (5:6). The beast conquers by killing witnesses; the Lamb conquered by being killed. Same verb, opposite direction.

“Symbolically.” John supplies the key himself: the city is called Sodom and Egypt “symbolically” — spiritually. These are not addresses. “Where their Lord was crucified” points to Jerusalem; Sodom is the byword for depravity (Isaiah called Jerusalem’s rulers “you rulers of Sodom,” Isaiah 1:10); Egypt is the house of slavery; and “the great city” is this book’s name for Babylon (17:18; 18:10). Four identities on one city: wherever God’s people are opposed, that place becomes Sodom and Egypt and Babylon and the city that killed the Lord. It has a branch in every generation.

In the street. Not in a prison or tomb, but in the open where the traffic goes. Whatever public humiliation looks like in a given century, John spares no detail.

verseByVerse.quote: For three and a half days some from the peoples and tribes and languages and nations will gaze at their dead bodies and refuse to let them be placed in a tomb, and those who dwell on the earth will rejoice over them and make merry and exchange presents, because these two prophets had been a torment to those who dwell on the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For three and a half days people from every nation gaze at the witnesses’ bodies, refuse them burial, and celebrate with gifts, because these prophets had tormented them. The world may rejoice at silencing God’s witnesses, but its triumph is brief — and a witness that troubles no one is probably not a witness.

Days, not years. Three and a half days against three and a half years elsewhere. The humiliation is real and brief — the same shape as the ministry, without its length.

Unburied. In the ancient world, leaving a body unburied was the last insult, saying the person didn’t count as human; burial was owed even to an enemy. And the fourfold phrase — peoples, tribes, languages, nations — is the one used since 5:9 of the ransomed, now used of the spectators. The same world the Lamb bought stands in the street staring at the bodies.

Gazing. Not glancing. They come and stand and look, for days. Any generation that has watched a humiliation circulate for days will recognise the appetite.

The world’s party. Every other celebration in these chapters is in heaven; this one is on earth, held because two preachers are dead. “Exchange presents” makes it unbearable: the language of a public holiday. Someone declares a day off, and people send gifts.

A torment. “Because these two prophets had been a torment” — the word used of the locusts in 9:5. The witnesses had no army or legal standing, only a message, and the message was intolerable. Ahab said it to Elijah’s face: “Is it you, you troubler of Israel?” (1 Kings 18:17).

A warning and a comfort. The same sentence. The warning: if the world is entirely comfortable with what your church says, it isn’t saying what these two said. A witness that torments no one probably isn’t a witness. The comfort: when Christians are treated as a problem to be removed rather than a view to be debated, that isn’t evidence something has gone wrong. It is what the two witnesses received, and their Lord in the same city. A test: is there anything in your witness that would trouble a world settled on the earth?

Earth-dwellers. Twice in one verse: those whose whole account is settled here (8:13). They hold a party for three and a half days, and the next verse begins with “But.”

verseByVerse.quote: But after the three and a half days a breath of life from God entered them, and they stood up on their feet, and great fear fell on those who saw them. Then they heard a loud voice from heaven saying to them, "Come up here!" And they went up to heaven in a cloud, and their enemies watched them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After three and a half days the breath of life from God enters the witnesses; they stand up, great fear falls on the onlookers, and a voice calls them up to heaven in a cloud while their enemies watch. God publicly vindicates his faithful witnesses by raising them, as he raised Christ.

Dry bones. The wording is Ezekiel’s valley, where breath entered the bones “and they lived and stood on their feet, an exceedingly great army” (Ezekiel 37:10). The word for breath is also the word for Spirit, as in Ezekiel’s Hebrew.

The party stops. What a crowd declared finished, refusing it burial, stands up in the street. “Great fear fell on those who saw them.” Three and a half days of gazing at corpses, and the corpses stand.

Their Lord’s path. “Come up here!” is what the voice said to John at 4:1. “In a cloud” is how Christ ascended (Acts 1:9) and will return (1:7). The witnesses receive their Lord’s death, in his city, then his resurrection and ascension, in that order.

“Their enemies watched them.” When Jesus rose, the world didn’t see; the guards saw an empty tomb and were paid to say otherwise, and he appeared only to his own. Here the vindication is public, and those who arranged the deaths stand in the street with their gifts still in their hands.

Vindication comes after. The pattern isn’t that faithful witness avoids humiliation, but that vindication comes later, before the same audience. Every Christian written off, misrepresented, quietly removed or made ridiculous for saying something true is shown the end of the story — not a private consolation, but a summons heard aloud and a departure the accusers must watch.

What they don’t do. They don’t argue, retaliate or explain. They stand, are called, and go. Vindication in Scripture is rarely achieved; it is done to a person by Another, usually later than he would choose. Peter told churches in these same provinces: “Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God so that at the proper time he may exalt you” (1 Peter 5:6). A test: where are you trying to vindicate yourself? Leave it to him.

verseByVerse.quote: And at that hour there was a great earthquake, and a tenth of the city fell. Seven thousand people were killed in the earthquake, and the rest were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven. The second woe has passed; behold, the third woe is soon to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At that hour an earthquake destroys a tenth of the city and kills seven thousand, and the rest, terrified, give glory to the God of heaven. Where plagues failed, the faithful witness, death and resurrection of God’s people lead many to turn to God.

The proportions reversed. A fourth was struck in chapter 6, a third repeatedly in chapters 8–9. Here a tenth, and seven thousand — and the other nine-tenths do what no group in Revelation has yet done.

Same phrase, opposite outcome. At 9:20, “The rest of mankind… did not repent.” Here, “the rest… gave glory to the God of heaven.” The trumpets struck a third of mankind and produced nothing. Two witnesses prophesied in sackcloth, were killed and raised — and nine-tenths of a city gave glory to God.

Is this genuine conversion? Some read it as terror rather than repentance, noting that at 16:9 people who refuse to repent are said not to give God glory, so the contrast may be only formal. Others take it at face value: “give glory” to God is what Revelation says of real worship (14:7; 19:7), and this is the one place in the book where a mass of ordinary people turns to God. The more likely reading is the second.

How the world is reached. If so, the chapter makes an argument about how the world is actually reached, and it isn’t the one most churches would make. Plagues didn’t do it. Cosmic catastrophe didn’t do it. A third of mankind dying didn’t do it. What did it was two witnesses in mourning dress, refusing to stop talking, being killed for it, and being raised. A test: are you hoping the world will be shaken into faith, or are you bearing faithful witness yourself, whatever it costs?

Seven thousand. Perhaps an echo of Elijah, who stands behind these witnesses. When he complained he alone was left, God said, “I will leave seven thousand in Israel, all the knees that have not bowed to Baal” (1 Kings 19:18). There, seven thousand were the preserved remnant. Here seven thousand fall and the great majority turn. The arithmetic of grace is turned the other way up.

Two woes past. The bookkeeping again, matching 9:12. The third woe is “soon,” and the next verse sounds the seventh trumpet — which contains no woe John records, only the announcement of a kingdom.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 15: the seventh trumpet sounds and brings no plague at all, only an announcement — The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever. Singular kingdom, not plural: one worldly system under many governments, and it has changed hands. And the verb is aorist, a completed act: not will become but has become.

Verses 16–17: the twenty-four elders come off their own thrones onto their faces, giving thanks to Lord God Almighty, who is and who was — and the threefold title of 1:4, 1:8 and 4:8 has lost its third term. The one who is to come has come, and the future tense drops out of the name of God. You have taken your great power and begun to reign: not been given, but taken. He was always sovereign; what changes is that the reign becomes visible and unopposed.

Verse 18 quotes Psalm 2:1 in the past tense — the nations raged, and it is over — and lists what the moment contains: wrath; the dead judged; the servants rewarded, the prophets and saints, and those who fear your name, both small and great; and destroying the destroyers of the earth, an exact reciprocity using the same root twice.

Verse 19 opens the temple in heaven, and the ark of his covenant was seen within his temple — the object that stood behind the veil, seen by one man once a year, and lost when Babylon destroyed the temple in 586 BC. Then the storm signs, now five of them: lightning, rumblings, thunder, earthquake and heavy hail.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Kingdom Has Come

The seventh trumpet announces that the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ. God is now praised as the one who is and who was — the one to come has come — and the ark of his covenant is seen in his temple.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The outcome was declared with eleven chapters still to run.

Now: Believers live inside a victory already won and not yet seen; small and great alike will be rewarded.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the seventh angel blew his trumpet, and there were loud voices in heaven, saying, "The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever." And the twenty-four elders who sit on their thrones before God fell on their faces and worshiped God, saying, "We give thanks to you, Lord God Almighty, who is and who was, for you have taken your great power and begun to reign.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The seventh trumpet sounds and heaven proclaims, “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever,” and the elders worship God for taking his power and beginning to reign. The outcome of history is settled: Christ’s kingdom has already won, and it will be fully visible at his coming.

An announcement. Six trumpets brought hail, blood, wormwood, darkness, locusts and cavalry. The seventh brings an announcement — the sentence the whole book has climbed toward. Those who know Handel have heard it sung; the singing can carry a person past what it actually says.

One kingdom. “The kingdom of the world” — singular, not “kingdoms” as older translations had it. One worldly system under many governments, and it has changed hands.

“Has become.” A completed act. Heaven doesn’t say the world will become God’s or is becoming his, but announces a transfer already made — a herald reading out a result, not a forecast.

The ending first. Eleven chapters remain. The dragon hasn’t appeared, neither beast has risen, Babylon hasn’t fallen, the white horse hasn’t ridden out. The outcome is declared before the conflict is described — the single most important structural fact about Revelation. It isn’t a thriller with the ending in doubt, but the account of a war whose result was announced at the halfway point, and before that at an empty tomb.

Living inside a victory. The first hearers were told the empire would worsen, a beast would rule every tribe, and they would be conquered and killed. And in the middle: the kingdom of the world has already changed owners. They weren’t asked to hope for a victory but to live inside one not yet made visible. A test: do you face this week as one hoping Christ might win, or as one who knows he has?

A word left out. The divine title has been threefold from the start: “who is and who was and who is to come” (1:4, 8; 4:8). Here it is twofold: “who is and who was.” The third term is gone. Not an oversight: the One who is to come has come. The title held a future tense while there was a future to wait for, and at the seventh trumpet it drops out of God’s name.

Taken. “You have taken your great power and begun to reign.” He was always sovereign; what changes is that his reign becomes visible and unopposed. And the elders’ response isn’t analysis. Twenty-four figures with thrones of their own get off them and put their faces on the floor.

verseByVerse.quote: The nations raged, but your wrath came, and the time for the dead to be judged, and for rewarding your servants, the prophets and saints, and those who fear your name, both small and great, and for destroying the destroyers of the earth." Then God's temple in heaven was opened, and the ark of his covenant was seen within his temple. There were flashes of lightning, rumblings, peals of thunder, an earthquake, and heavy hail.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The elders sing that the nations raged but God’s wrath has come: the time to judge the dead, reward his servants great and small, and destroy the destroyers of the earth. Then God’s heavenly temple opens and the ark of his covenant is seen. God will judge justly, reward every faithful servant, and keep his covenant forever.

The raging answered. “The nations raged” quotes Psalm 2: “Why do the nations rage and the peoples plot in vain?” — kings set against the LORD and his Anointed, God laughing and installing his King on Zion. Revelation has quoted that psalm since 2:27. Here it reports the raging in the past tense. It was answered.

Wrath and judgment. “Your wrath came” — one clause, not dwelt on, in a book that has spent six chapters on judgment. Then “the time for the dead to be judged”: everyone, including all who died thinking the matter closed. Nothing has been filed away.

Rewards for small and great. The longest clause, and its generosity is the point. Prophets, saints, and simply “those who fear your name” — and then a phrase that won’t let anyone be ranked out: “both small and great.” No tiers. The witnesses who shut the sky and the widow who kept praying and never told anyone are in the same sentence. And it is “rewarding”: God means to give people things for what they did, and the New Testament isn’t embarrassed about it (Matthew 6:4; 1 Corinthians 3:14; Hebrews 11:6). Grace doesn’t abolish reward; it is why reward is possible at all. A test: what hidden faithfulness are you tempted to think goes unnoticed? He has it in his book.

Destroying the destroyers. The same root twice, as the English keeps it. Those who ruined the world are ruined. The sentence is the crime, said back.

The ark. For a Jewish reader the most astonishing sentence in the chapter. The ark stood in the Most Holy Place, seen by one man once a year. It vanished when Babylon destroyed the temple in 586 BC, and Jeremiah had said a day would come when no one would speak of it or miss it (Jeremiah 3:16). For nearly seven hundred years Israel’s holiest object had simply been gone. Here it is, in the temple in heaven, in plain view, doors open. The ark held the covenant tablets under a lid where blood was sprinkled yearly. To see it is to be told the covenant was never lost when the building fell, that God has kept his side, and that the place where blood was applied for sin is still in the room. The chapter that began by measuring a temple and leaving part to be trampled ends by opening the real one.

The storm grows. Lightning, rumblings, thunder, earthquake, hail: three elements at 4:5, four at 8:5, five here. The nations raged; his wrath came; the covenant stands open in the light.

12.title: The Woman, the Dragon, and the War in Heaven
12.overview:
Chapter 12 is the theological heart of Revelation. Everything that has come before — the seals, the trumpets, the witnesses — and everything that follows — the beasts, the bowls, Babylon’s fall — is explained here. We are shown the cosmic backstory: the war between the dragon and the woman, the birth of the child who will rule all nations, the war in heaven that cast Satan down, and the dragon’s fury against the woman’s offspring. This is the explanation for why the church is persecuted: the dragon, having failed to destroy the child, turns his fury on those who “hold to the testimony of Jesus.”

The great sign in heaven — the woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet and a crown of twelve stars — draws on Genesis 37:9 (Joseph’s dream where the sun, moon, and eleven stars bowed down to him, representing his family) and on the Old Testament imagery of Israel as the bride/mother of God’s people (Isaiah 54; Jeremiah 6:2). The woman is not Mary (though the imagery encompasses the incarnation). She is the messianic community — Israel who gave birth to the Messiah, and the church who is the continuation and expansion of that community. She is clothed with cosmic glory; she is in labor.

The great red dragon with seven heads and ten horns and seven diadems is Satan himself, identified explicitly in v. 9: “that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world.” His seven heads and ten horns anticipate the beast of chapter 13, which mirrors the dragon’s appearance — the beast is the dragon’s instrument, Rome as the embodiment of satanic opposition to Christ. The dragon’s tail sweeping down a third of the stars has been interpreted as the fall of the angels who followed Satan in the primordial rebellion.

The cosmic war of vv. 7–12 is one of the most dramatic scenes in Revelation: Michael and his angels fight the dragon and his angels; the dragon is thrown down. The war in heaven is won. The announcement that follows is the theological explanation: they conquered “by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death.” The cross — not Michael’s sword — is the decisive weapon. The dragon is thrown down because the Lamb was slain.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Woman and the Dragon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2: a great sign — John says so before he describes anything — a woman clothed with the sun, the moon under her feet, a crown of twelve stars, pregnant and screaming in labour. The sun, moon and twelve stars come from Joseph’s dream, where Jacob himself supplies the key (Gen. 37:9–10): this is the covenant people, from whom the Messiah comes.

Verses 3–4: another sign, a great red dragon with seven heads, ten horns and seven diadems — royal crowns, not the victor’s wreath the woman wears, and the crowns that belong by right to the rider of 19:12. His tail sweeps down a third of the stars, and he stands in front of the woman waiting to devour the child.

Verse 5: she bears a male child who is to rule all the nations with a rod of iron (Ps. 2:9) — and the child is caught up to God and to his throne. Between the birth and the throne there is nothing: no Galilee, no cross, no empty tomb. Thirty-three years pass in a comma, because from the dragon’s side there is nothing to report but total failure.

Verse 6: the woman flees into the wilderness, where she has a place prepared by God, to be nourished for 1,260 days. The child is safe on the throne; the mother is in the desert — which is the position of the church between the ascension and the end.
verseByVerse.theology:
The War Behind the War

The woman — the covenant people, Israel and the church — bears the Messiah, while the dragon waits to devour the child. The child is caught up to God’s throne, and the woman is kept and fed in the wilderness for a measured time.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Every attack on the promised line, from Pharaoh to Herod, was the dragon at the woman’s feet.

Now: The church’s wilderness is hard, but it is a place prepared by God.

verseByVerse.quote: And a great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars. She was pregnant and was crying out in birth pains and the agony of giving birth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A great sign appears in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, the moon under her feet, crowned with twelve stars, crying out in labour. She is the people of God — Israel from whom the Messiah came, continued in the church — glorious in heaven’s sight and suffering on earth, with pain that is going somewhere.

The war behind the war. Chapters 1–11 showed what happens on earth and in heaven as the scroll opens; chapter 12 pulls the curtain back further and shows why. From here to chapter 20 the reader watches the dragon, his two beasts and their city, and this chapter introduces them.

A sign. John says so before describing anything — his standing courtesy: this stands for something; read it as a sign.

Who is she? Joseph dreamed of the sun, moon and eleven stars bowing to him, and his father understood at once: Jacob, his mother, and the brothers (Genesis 37:9–10). Add Joseph and there are twelve. Sun, moon and twelve stars is Israel, the covenant people from whom the Messiah comes. Some take the woman as Mary, and she is in the picture: a real woman bore the child of v. 5. But this woman outlives the child’s ascension, flees to the wilderness, is pursued for 1,260 days, and has other offspring “who keep the commandments of God” (v. 17). That isn’t a biography. She is God’s covenant people — Israel, out of whom Christ came, and the church, the same people continued.

Glory and agony at once. Clothed with the sun, and crying out in birth pains. That is the whole doctrine of the people of God in one picture. From heaven the church is clothed with the sun and crowned with stars. From the street she is a woman in labour, making a great deal of noise, with something enormous waiting for her. Both are accurate. A believer shown only the first won’t recognise his own church; one who has seen only the second won’t believe there is anything else to see.

Pain with an outcome. Birth pain in Scripture is never mere suffering. Isaiah used it of Israel in exile (Isaiah 26:17–18; 66:7–9); Jesus of the troubles before the end — “All these are but the beginning of the birth pains” (Matthew 24:8); Paul of creation “groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now” (Romans 8:22). The pain is real, severe, and going somewhere. A test: when your church struggles, do you see only a woman in labour, or also the sun she is clothed with?
verseByVerse.note: The sun, moon and twelve stars recall Joseph’s dream of Israel’s family. The woman seems to be the people of God, from whom the Messiah came.

verseByVerse.quote: And another sign appeared in heaven: behold, a great red dragon, with seven heads and ten horns, and on his heads seven diadems. His tail swept down a third of the stars of heaven and cast them to the earth. And the dragon stood before the woman who was about to give birth, so that when she bore her child he might devour it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A great red dragon with seven heads, ten horns and seven crowns sweeps a third of the stars down and stands ready to devour the woman’s child the moment he is born. Satan is a real, personal enemy who claims a sovereignty he doesn’t have, and all through history he has tried to destroy the promised Christ.

What Satan is. Another sign. This isn’t what Satan looks like but what he is. The dragon in the Old Testament is the chaos-monster of the deep — Leviathan, the twisting serpent God alone can master (Job 41; Psalm 74:13–14; Isaiah 27:1) — and Ezekiel called Pharaoh “the great dragon that lies in the midst of his streams” (Ezekiel 29:3).

A counterfeit crown. Seven heads: God’s number of completeness, worn by the dragon. Ten horns: power. Seven diadems — the sharpest detail. A diadem is a royal crown, unlike the victor’s wreath; the woman wears a wreath of stars, the dragon seven royal crowns. He claims a sovereignty he doesn’t hold, and at 19:12 the rider on the white horse appears wearing “many diadems,” settling whose crowns they really are.

A third of the stars. Read naturally alongside vv. 7–9, these are the angels who fell with him. A third again: even in his greatest success the dragon gets a limited portion, and two-thirds stayed.

The plot of the Old Testament. “The dragon stood before the woman… that… he might devour it.” Right after the fall God promised enmity between the serpent and the woman’s offspring: “he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel” (Genesis 3:15). Everything after is the serpent trying to reach the child first. Cain kills Abel. Pharaoh orders Hebrew boys into the Nile. Athaliah destroys Judah’s royal family and misses one baby hidden in a bedroom (2 Kings 11:1–3). Haman obtains a decree against every Jew in the empire. And when the child is born, Herod kills the boys of Bethlehem (Matthew 2:16). Matthew reports the massacre as history; John shows what was underneath it.

The second layer. The events are real — a real decree, a real sword, real children — and something behind them is also real, hostile, personal, and has been at this a long time. Paul says it without the picture: “we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the cosmic powers over this present darkness” (Ephesians 6:12). A test: when you face opposition to the gospel, do you fight people, or pray against the powers behind them?

How little he does. He stands, waiting, with crowns he didn’t earn and a mouth open for a child not yet born. In the next verse the child is taken to God’s throne, and the dragon doesn’t lay a finger on him.

verseByVerse.quote: She gave birth to a male child, one who is to rule all the nations with a rod of iron, but her child was caught up to God and to his throne, and the woman fled into the wilderness, where she has a place prepared by God, in which she is to be nourished for 1,260 days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The woman bears a son who will rule the nations with a rod of iron; he is caught up to God’s throne, and she flees into the wilderness to a place God has prepared, where she is fed for 1,260 days. Christ has escaped the dragon’s grasp and reigns, while the church lives through this age in a hard place where God provides for her.

The child is Jesus. The quotation settles it: “You shall break them with a rod of iron and dash them in pieces like a potter’s vessel” (Psalm 2:9), the Messiah’s coronation psalm, applied in this book to Christ (19:15) and to those who conquer (2:27).

A life in a comma. Between “she gave birth” and “caught up to God and to his throne” there is nothing — no childhood, Galilee, sermons, miracles, cross or empty tomb. The whole Gospel passes in a comma. Because this chapter isn’t telling the story of Jesus but the story of the dragon’s attempt on him, and from the dragon’s side there is nothing to report between the birth and the throne except total defeat. He stood with his mouth open, and the child went straight past him to God’s seat.

Caught up. Snatched, seized with force — the word for the man “caught up to the third heaven” (2 Corinthians 12:2) and the church “caught up” to meet the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4:17). A rescue at speed.

Not avoiding the cross. The compression could mislead. The cross is everywhere in this book — the Lamb standing as though slain is its central image, and v. 11 says the saints conquered “by the blood of the Lamb.” The point is that the cross wasn’t a victory for the dragon. He devoured nothing. The child went to the throne, by a route through a grave that couldn’t hold him.

The mother in the desert. The child is safe on the throne; the mother is in the wilderness. That is the church’s position between the ascension and the end. The wilderness is where Israel went after the exodus — dangerous, without resources, and the place of daily provision, where a nation was fed forty years by bread arriving each morning; where Elijah was fed by ravens and an angel (1 Kings 17:6; 19:5–8). A hard address, and not abandonment.

A place prepared. “Prepared by God” — the verb Jesus used of the place he goes to prepare (John 14:2). The desert wasn’t an accident of flight; the accommodation was booked. “She is to be nourished” — by an unnamed hand, for the 1,260 days the book keeps repeating. A test: in your own wilderness stretch, have you noticed how you are being fed? Name one provision and thank him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — Satan Thrown Down to Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 7–8: war in heaven, Michael and his angels against the dragon and his; the dragon fights back, is defeated, and there was no longer any place for them in heaven. Michael appears in Scripture only in Daniel, Jude and here — the great prince who has charge of your people (Dan. 12:1), and the archangel who would not pronounce a blasphemous judgment against the devil but said The Lord rebuke you (Jude 9).

Verse 9 gives him four names in one sentence, and each is a job description: the great dragon, raw destructive power; that ancient serpent, the same one, from the garden; the devil, diabolos, slanderer; and Satan, Hebrew for adversary or accuser. Two of the four mean the same thing. He is also the deceiver of the whole world, and the verb thrown down is repeated three times in the verse.

Verse 10 explains it, and the explanation is a court case: the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down, who accuses them day and night before our God. Verse 11 defines the book’s central verb in three clauses — they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death. Verse 12 gives the two reactions: heaven rejoices, earth and sea are warned, for the devil has come down to you in great wrath, because he knows that his time is short.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Accuser Thrown Down

Satan, the accuser who stood as prosecutor before God, is thrown down. The saints conquer him by the blood of the Lamb, by the word of their testimony, and by not loving their lives even to death.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Congregations that had buried martyrs were told those deaths were victories.

Now: The voice reciting your record has lost its standing, because the charges were paid. His fury is the fury of one whose time is short.

verseByVerse.quote: Now war arose in heaven, Michael and his angels fighting against the dragon. And the dragon and his angels fought back, but he was defeated, and there was no longer any place for them in heaven. And the great dragon was thrown down, that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world—he was thrown down to the earth, and his angels were thrown down with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
War breaks out in heaven; Michael and his angels defeat the dragon, and Satan — the ancient serpent, the devil, the deceiver of the whole world — is thrown down to the earth with his angels. Through Christ’s victory, Satan has lost his place in heaven, though he still rages on earth.

Michael. Named only in Daniel, Jude and here. In Daniel, “the great prince who has charge of your people” (Daniel 12:1; cf. 10:13, 21). Jude calls him an archangel who, disputing with the devil, “did not presume to pronounce a blasphemous judgment, but said, ‘The Lord rebuke you’” (Jude 9). A creature, and a careful one.

What was Satan doing in heaven? The Old Testament answers plainly, and it is the key to the chapter. In Job he presents himself among the sons of God and accuses a righteous man: “Does Job fear God for no reason?” (Job 1:9). In Zechariah he stands to accuse the high priest, who is in filthy garments — and the accusation is true (Zechariah 3:1–4). Satan’s place in heaven was never a throne. It was a prosecutor’s bench.

When was Satan thrown down? Some place it before creation, linking Isaiah 14 and Ezekiel 28; futurists place it in the middle of a coming tribulation. But the song that follows says it happened when “the salvation and the power and the kingdom of our God and the authority of his Christ have come,” and the saints conquered “by the blood of the Lamb” (vv. 10–11). Jesus spoke the same way: “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10:18); and on his last night, “Now is the judgment of this world; now will the ruler of this world be cast out” (John 12:31). The more likely reading is that Satan was cast down at the cross. He lost his place as accuser; he didn’t lose his rage. That is why “your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion” (1 Peter 5:8), and why he knows his time is short (v. 12).

Four names, four jobs. “The great dragon”: raw destructive power. “That ancient serpent”: the same one from the garden, connected to Genesis 3 without help. “The devil”: slanderer. “Satan”: adversary, accuser. Two of the four mean much the same, and the next verse makes that the point.

The deceiver. His method hasn’t changed since the garden, where the first move wasn’t a threat but a question: “Did God actually say…?” (Genesis 3:1). He isn’t chiefly described here as torturer or tempter but as a liar with a legal practice. A test: what lie about God are you most tempted to believe this week — that he is holding out on you, or that he won’t forgive? Answer it with what God has actually said.

Thrown down, three times. “Thrown down… thrown down… thrown down with him.” He didn’t withdraw or resign. He was removed, by force, and the sentence won’t stop saying so.

verseByVerse.quote: And I heard a loud voice in heaven, saying, "Now the salvation and the power and the kingdom of our God and the authority of his Christ have come, for the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down, who accuses them day and night before our God. And they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death. Therefore, rejoice, O heavens and you who dwell in them! But woe to you, O earth and sea, for the devil has come down to you in great wrath, because he knows that his time is short!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Heaven rejoices that the accuser of believers has been thrown down; they conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and the word of their testimony, not loving their lives even to death. Satan can no longer condemn those whose sins Christ has paid for, and his fury on earth is that of a defeated enemy whose time is short.

A court case. Heaven explains what happened, entirely in legal terms. The dragon is called “the accuser of our brothers… who accuses them day and night before our God.” Take it literally, because it explains what many Christians feel and can’t name. A voice in God’s presence was reciting a list — and not inventing charges. That is the terrible part: the file in Zechariah 3 was accurate. The accusations against you are, on the whole, true.

Thrown out. Not because the charges failed or God stopped listening. The next sentence gives the reason, and defines the book’s central verb, promised to all seven churches. Here is what conquering consists of.

By the blood of the Lamb. First, and the ground of the rest. The accuser wasn’t defeated by argument, or by the saints’ record. He was defeated because the charges were paid. A prosecutor whose every allegation has been settled by someone else has nothing to do in the room. There is no case left (Romans 8:33–34). A test: when your conscience replays your sins, do you argue your record, or point to the blood?

By the word of their testimony. Second, following from the first. Not what they achieved but what they said — the true thing about Christ, before people who didn’t want it. That saying is a weapon.

Not loving their lives. Third, the cost. Not hatred of living, but that when it came to a choice between their lives and their testimony, the testimony won (cf. John 12:25). Some died. A person not clinging to his own life has nothing left that can be threatened.

The shape of courage. It doesn’t begin with bravery. It begins with a verdict already delivered in blood, produces speech, and only then costs something. No one here is asked to be fearless first.

Rejoice — and woe. Heaven celebrates; earth is warned. And the devil’s great wrath isn’t because he is winning but “because he knows that his time is short!” That reframes much Christian experience. The pressure a believer feels isn’t an advancing enemy but the fury of one thrown out of court, who has read the timetable. A cornered animal is dangerous because it is cornered. And “short” as heaven measures it isn’t always short as a suffering church measures it — but it is short.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–17 — The Dragon Pursues the Woman
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 13: when the dragon saw that he had been thrown down, he pursued the woman. The logic matters — he goes after the mother because he cannot reach the child, who is on the throne, and cannot go back to the courtroom.

Verse 14: the woman was given the two wings of the great eagle to fly into the wilderness, to be nourished for a time, and times, and half a time. The wings are the exodus — I bore you on eagles’ wings and brought you to myself (Ex. 19:4; cf. Deut. 32:11; Isa. 40:31) — and the time is Daniel 7:25, the third form of the same number John has now used three ways in two chapters.

Verses 15–16: the serpent pours a river out of his mouth to sweep her away, and the earth came to the help of the woman and swallowed it — as the ground opened on Korah (Num. 16:31–33) and the sea closed over Pharaoh’s chariots.

Verse 17: the dragon, furious, goes off to make war on the rest of her offspring — reaching back to Genesis 3:15 — defined by exactly two marks: those who keep the commandments of God and hold to the testimony of Jesus. And the chapter ends on a quiet, ominous line: And he stood on the sand of the sea.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Complete Exodus

Thrown down, the dragon pursues the woman, but she is given eagle’s wings and carried to the wilderness to be fed. The flood from his mouth is swallowed by the earth, and he turns on her children — those who keep God’s commandments and hold to the testimony of Jesus.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The church under Rome was living inside the story of Exodus, and knew how it ended.

Now: Persecution is the rage of a defeated accuser, and the wilderness is where God feeds his people.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the dragon saw that he had been thrown down to the earth, he pursued the woman who had given birth to the male child. But the woman was given the two wings of the great eagle so that she might fly from the serpent into the wilderness, to the place where she is to be nourished for a time, and times, and half a time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thrown down to earth, the dragon pursues the woman, but she is given the two wings of the great eagle to fly to her place in the wilderness, where she is nourished for a time, and times, and half a time. Persecution of the church is the rage of a defeated enemy, and God carries and feeds his people through it, as in the exodus.

Displaced rage. He goes after the woman because he has been thrown down. He can’t reach the child on the throne or return to the courtroom, so he turns on the mother. The church’s persecution in this age is the displaced rage of a defeated prosecutor. That doesn’t make it less real, and this book never pretends it does. But it settles what it means: not evidence the dragon is gaining ground, but that he lost the only ground that mattered.

Eagles’ wings. The exodus: “You yourselves have seen what I did to the Egyptians, and how I bore you on eagles’ wings and brought you to myself” (Exodus 19:4; cf. Deuteronomy 32:11). The chapter now holds a complete exodus: a tyrant killing children, a child rescued, a flight, a wilderness, a place prepared, food from an unnamed hand, eagles’ wings, and next a water-crossing where the enemy is undone by his own flood. John tells seven congregations under Roman pressure that they are living in Exodus — and they know how it ends.

Given. She doesn’t grow the wings or buy them. Isaiah promised the same to exhausted people: “they who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings like eagles” (Isaiah 40:31).

A time, and times, and half a time. The third form of the same number, taken directly from Daniel 7:25. Forty-two months, 1,260 days, a time and times and half a time — used interchangeably within two chapters, itself a strong sign John means one period by them.

Where God feeds without competition. For the second time the wilderness is a place of nourishment, not exposure (cf. v. 6). The desert is where the dragon can’t follow and the food arrives anyway. Any Christian who has been through a stretch with nothing in it — no prospects, company or visible progress — is told what that place is for. It isn’t where God loses track of his people. It is where he feeds them without competition. A test: in a barren season, are you looking for the food he sends — his word, his people, his presence?

verseByVerse.quote: The serpent poured water like a river out of his mouth after the woman, to sweep her away with a flood. But the earth came to the help of the woman, and the earth opened its mouth and swallowed the river that the dragon had poured from his mouth. Then the dragon became furious with the woman and went off to make war on the rest of her offspring, on those who keep the commandments of God and hold to the testimony of Jesus. And he stood on the sand of the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The serpent pours a river from his mouth to sweep the woman away, but the earth swallows it; furious, the dragon makes war on her other offspring — those who keep God’s commandments and hold to the testimony of Jesus — and stands on the seashore. Satan attacks with floods of lies, God rescues by unexpected means, and the marks of his people are simple: obedience and confession.

Two mouths. The dragon’s mouth pours a river; the earth’s mouth swallows it. What comes from the dragon’s mouth is what always has — he is “the deceiver of the whole world” (v. 9), and his one method is speech. The flood is a torrent of lies.

A flood of words. In the Psalms, overwhelming waters picture slander and hostile testimony: “Save me, O God! For the waters have come up to my neck… and the flood sweeps over me” (Psalm 69:1–2). That is how a reputation is destroyed: not one accusation, which can be answered, but a volume arriving faster than anyone can respond, until the truth is under water.

Help from the ground. The rescue comes from the least likely place. The earth in this book is usually where the trouble is. Here it opens its mouth and swallows a river, as the ground swallowed Korah (Numbers 16:31–33) and the sea closed over Pharaoh’s chariots. God isn’t limited to the instruments a believer would expect. He has used a pagan king’s decree, a famine, a shipwreck and an earthquake in a prison to protect his people, and here the ground. A test: are you dictating to God how he must rescue you? Watch for his unexpected help.

The rest of her offspring. Frustrated with the mother, he turns on the children, and John defines them precisely, reaching back to Genesis 3:15. Two marks only. “Keep the commandments of God”: obedience — ordinary, unglamorous, in what God has actually commanded, not what we would prefer to be judged on. “Hold to the testimony of Jesus”: confession — they haven’t let go of what they say about him.

A short list. Not those who understand this book, or identified the beast correctly, or never suffered. Obedience and confession, held on to. That is what the dragon makes war on, and all it takes to be on his list. A test: are you marked by those two things this week?

On the beach. “And he stood on the sand of the sea.” (Some manuscripts read “I stood”; the ESV notes it, and “he” is the better reading.) The dragon walks to the shoreline and looks out at the water — and the next sentence is “And I saw a beast rising out of the sea.” He is calling something up. But the reader now has everything needed to watch without panic: the child is on the throne; the accuser is thrown out with no case to bring; the woman is fed in a place prepared; the saints conquer by blood already shed and words already spoken. The dragon on that beach is a defeated prosecutor with a short time, doing the only thing left to him.
