13.title: The Two Beasts: The Dragon's Earthly Instruments
13.overview:
Chapter 13 is the political theology chapter of Revelation. The dragon, standing on the seashore, summons two beasts — one from the sea, one from the land — and delegates to them his authority, his throne, and great power. Together the dragon and the two beasts form a Satanic trinity that parodies the Holy Trinity: the dragon parodies the Father, the beast from the sea parodies the Son (including a parody death and resurrection), and the beast from the land parodies the Spirit (pointing away from itself to the first beast, as the Spirit points away from himself to the Son). The unholy trinity is the political and religious power structure of every totalitarian system that demands ultimate allegiance.

Interpretive flag — The Beast from the Sea: This is the third major structural decision point. The preterist reading identifies the beast as Nero Caesar — and the gematria (numerical value of letters) of “Nero Caesar” in Hebrew adds up to 666. The mortal wound that was healed (v. 3) refers to the Nero redivivus myth: rumors after Nero’s death in AD 68 that he had survived and would return from the east with the Parthian army. The historicist reading has identified the beast with various historical powers including the papacy. The futurist/dispensational reading sees a still-future individual world ruler, a literal Antichrist who will arise in the last days, be given global political power, and demand global worship. The idealist/amillennial reading understands the beast as the pattern of totalitarian political power that demands ultimate allegiance in every age — with Rome as the first-century embodiment and every subsequent empire that makes similar demands as its successor. The idealist position is followed here, while the specific Nero/Rome referent is fully acknowledged as the primary first-century layer.

Interpretive flag — 666: Three readings predominate. (1) Gematria: “Neron Kaisar” in Hebrew letters (nun-resh-vav-nun / qoph-samek-resh) adds to 666; the spelling without the final n adds to 616, which is the reading of some early manuscripts. The specific first-century referent. (2) The number of incompleteness: six is one less than seven (the number of divine completeness); 666 is the triple intensification of falling short of the divine — the beast is humanity at its most grandiose, still falling short of the glory of God. (3) The number of humanity: six was associated with humanity in some traditions (created on the sixth day). The beast is the ultimate expression of humanity’s totalitarian self-divinization. All three readings illuminate the symbol; none is exhaustive.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2: a beast rises out of the sea with the dragon’s own features — seven heads, ten horns, royal diadems — and blasphemous names on its heads, which is what Roman coins and inscriptions actually gave the emperors. It is like a leopard, with a bear’s feet and a lion’s mouth: Daniel’s four beasts (Dan. 7:2–7) compressed into one. And the dragon gave it his power, his throne and great authority — the offer Christ refused in the desert (Luke 4:6).

Verses 3–4: one head has a mortal wound that was healed, and the whole earth marvels. The Greek uses the same participle used of the Lamb at 5:6, so the parody is deliberate. The world worships dragon and beast together, chanting Who is like the beast, and who can fight against it? — the song of the exodus (Ex. 15:11) with a different object, and the meaning of the name Michael turned to the wrong address.

Verses 5–6: the beast was given a mouth of haughty and blasphemous words and was allowed authority for forty-two months (cf. Dan. 7:8, 25). It blasphemes God’s name and his dwelling — and John glosses the dwelling himself: that is, those who dwell in heaven.

Verses 7–8: it was allowed to make war on the saints and to conquer them, with authority over every tribe and people and language and nation; and all the earth-dwellers worship it, everyone whose name has not been written from the foundation of the world in the book of life of the Lamb who was slain. Verses 9–10 turn to the reader: If anyone has an ear, let him hear — captivity to captivity, sword to sword (cf. Jer. 15:2) — Here is a call for the endurance and faith of the saints.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Beast from the Sea

The dragon gives the beast his power, throne and authority. It mimics the Lamb’s death and resurrection, wins the world’s worship because it seems unbeatable, and is allowed to speak blasphemies and make war on the saints for forty-two months.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Rome’s emperors bore divine titles on coins and inscriptions.

Now: Worship of power begins as a calculation that resistance is pointless. The saints’ calling is endurance and faith; their names are in the Lamb’s book.

verseByVerse.quote: And I saw a beast rising out of the sea, with ten horns and seven heads, with ten diadems on its horns and blasphemous names on its heads. And the beast that I saw was like a leopard; its feet were like a bear's, and its mouth was like a lion's mouth. And to it the dragon gave his power and his throne and great authority.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A beast rises from the sea, with ten horns, seven heads, ten crowns and blasphemous names, combining leopard, bear and lion, and the dragon gives it his power, throne and authority. Satan works through political power that claims divine honours — the same beast in every age, wearing different costumes.

The dragon’s likeness. The dragon stood on the beach at the end of chapter 12; this is what he calls up. Seven heads, ten horns, royal crowns — exactly the dragon of 12:3. What comes out of the water is what the dragon looks like when he takes a form that can hold public office.

Two pointed differences. The dragon wore seven crowns on his heads; the beast wears ten on its horns — more crowns, worn on the instruments of force. And blasphemous names on its heads. To a first-century reader that wasn’t a metaphor: coins and inscriptions across Asia gave emperors titles like divine, son of god, saviour of the world, and lord and god. The beast is wearing them.

Daniel’s four beasts in one. Daniel saw four beasts from the sea — a lion with eagles’ wings, a bear, a leopard, and a terrifying fourth with ten horns (Daniel 7:2–7): four kingdoms. John names three in reverse order and gives their features to one animal. What Daniel saw as a succession of empires, John compresses into a single creature. The point isn’t chronology but that there has only ever been one beast in different national costumes. Babylon, Persia, Greece and Rome aren’t four problems but four appearances of one thing, which reappears in every century. Anyone who has decided the beast is one particular regime should notice John has just merged four.

Who or what is the beast from the sea? In John’s day it was the Roman empire demanding worship. The Reformers saw it in the papacy; futurists see a final world ruler. The more likely reading is that it is the persecuting power of the state set against God, which took its first shape in Rome, has reappeared again and again in history, and will come to a final form before Christ returns.

A throne from the dragon. “To it the dragon gave his power and his throne and great authority.” The devil offered Christ the same in the desert: “To you I will give all this authority and their glory, for it has been delivered to me” (Luke 4:6). Christ refused; the beast accepts. That is the whole difference between the two kingdoms in this book: one takes a throne from the dragon, the other a cross from his Father. And “gave” — everything the dragon has, he was permitted to have. Throughout the chapter the beasts are given or allowed things (vv. 5, 7, 14, 15); the chain of permission runs past the dragon to the throne.

From the sea. The sea is chaos, frozen flat before God’s throne (4:6) and gone in the new creation (21:1). Empires come up out of the churn. A test: when a government demands the loyalty that belongs to God, do you recognise the beast’s face, whatever flag it flies?
verseByVerse.note: This beast combines the four beasts of Daniel 7 — leopard, bear, lion and the ten-horned beast.

verseByVerse.quote: One of its heads seemed to have a mortal wound, but its mortal wound was healed, and the whole earth marveled as they followed the beast. And they worshiped the dragon, for he had given his authority to the beast, and they worshiped the beast, saying, "Who is like the beast, and who can fight against it?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of the beast’s heads seems mortally wounded but is healed, and the whole world marvels, follows it, and worships both the dragon and the beast: “Who is like the beast, and who can fight against it?” Satan imitates Christ’s death and resurrection to win worship, and people worship power because it seems unbeatable.

A counterfeit resurrection. “Mortal wound” is literally “slain to death,” using the same word as the Lamb “standing, as though it had been slain” (5:6). The beast is a deliberate parody: a figure with a death-wound, alive anyway, demanding the worship that belongs to the One who really died and rose.

Satan copies. The key to this chapter and the next two. A beast with a resurrection; a second beast with horns like a lamb; a mark on the forehead; an image that speaks; a city called great. Satan invents nothing. He copies, and the copies are close enough to fool people who haven’t looked carefully.

What is the healed wound? Some link it with the legend that Nero, who killed himself in AD 68, would return from beyond the Euphrates — a rumour that produced several impostors. Others with the empire’s near-collapse in the civil wars of AD 68–69, when four emperors ruled in a year, and its full recovery under Vespasian. Others with a future event. The more likely reading is that it is a parody of the Lamb who was slain and lives: the persecuting power seems destroyed, rises again, and the world marvels. The wound is what makes the beast credible.

The world’s hymn. “Who is like the beast?” parodies the song at the sea: “Who is like you, O LORD, among the gods? Who is like you, majestic in holiness…?” (Exodus 15:11). Same sentence, different object. And Michael, who threw the dragon out of heaven, means “Who is like God?” The beast’s worshippers chant the archangel’s name at the wrong address.

Worship of power. “Who can fight against it?” No one claims the beast is kind, just or true. They worship it because it can’t be beaten — the reasoning of someone who has decided that whatever is strongest must be obeyed.

Not an exotic sin. Very few people consciously decide to worship a tyrant. They conclude that resistance is pointless, that the thing is too big to oppose, and that a sensible person accommodates himself to it. That conclusion, reached quietly and without ceremony, is what the verse describes. The first act of worship is usually a calculation. A test: where have you quietly decided that something — a culture, an employer, a movement — is too big to stand against, and so gone along?

verseByVerse.quote: And the beast was given a mouth uttering haughty and blasphemous words, and it was allowed to exercise authority for forty-two months. It opened its mouth to utter blasphemies against God, blaspheming his name and his dwelling, that is, those who dwell in heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The beast is given a mouth for proud blasphemies and allowed authority for forty-two months; it slanders God’s name and his dwelling — the people who dwell in heaven. The beast’s power is on a limited licence from God, its main weapon is its mouth, and attacking God’s people is attacking God.

Given; allowed. Two divine passives in one verse, the reason a Christian can read this chapter without despair. The beast didn’t acquire its mouth; it was given one. It didn’t seize its term; it was allowed one. Its authority is on licence, and the licence has an expiry date.

The same clock. Forty-two months — the number of chapter 11, of the woman in the wilderness, and of Daniel’s little horn (Daniel 7:25). The beast’s authority runs exactly as long as the church’s testimony (11:3) and the woman’s protection (12:6, 14). One clock governs the persecuting and the preserving.

Daniel’s mouth. Of the little horn: “in this horn were eyes like the eyes of a man, and a mouth speaking great things” (Daniel 7:8); “He shall speak words against the Most High, and shall wear out the saints of the Most High” (Daniel 7:25).

God’s dwelling is his people. It blasphemes God’s name, and “his dwelling, that is, those who dwell in heaven” — John’s own gloss, in case anyone imagines a building. Slandering the church is slandering God, the logic of the Damascus road: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). What is done to the body is done to the head.

The beast talks. Ten horns, the dragon’s authority, a healed death-wound — and both verses describing its activity are about its mouth. That should recalibrate how a believer expects pressure to come. The great opposition in this book isn’t chiefly a police force but a narrative: a version of reality, repeated with enormous confidence and reach, in which God is small, his people contemptible, and the beast the only realistic option. Christians braced for a knock at the door are sometimes overwhelmed instead by forty years of being told, pleasantly, that what they believe is ridiculous. A test: whose story about the world are you absorbing most hours of the week?

A mouth against a mouth. Against a mouth, the church is issued a mouth: “the word of their testimony” (12:11), and behind it the sword from Christ’s mouth (1:16; 19:15). Keep speaking his word.

verseByVerse.quote: Also it was allowed to make war on the saints and to conquer them. And authority was given it over every tribe and people and language and nation, and all who dwell on earth will worship it, everyone whose name has not been written from the foundation of the world in the book of life of the Lamb who was slain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The beast is allowed to make war on the saints and conquer them, and is given authority over every nation; all earth-dwellers worship it — everyone whose name is not written in the Lamb’s book of life. Faithfulness doesn’t guarantee survival, but those whose names the slain Lamb has written will not worship the beast.

The hardest sentence. Permitted to make war on Christians, and permitted to win. The verb is “conquer” — the promise that ends every letter, used of Christ at 5:5 and of the saints at 12:11 — here used of the beast against them, as at 11:7. Revelation won’t tell the church faithfulness guarantees survival. It says the opposite, twice. Congregations are overrun; believers imprisoned and executed. The beast wins, visibly, for forty-two months.

Two kinds of victory. Hold it beside 12:11: “they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death.” Same verb, same people, opposite outcome, resolved in the last clause. The beast conquers their bodies; they conquer him by dying without letting go. Two victories run at once, and only one is visible from the street.

The bought territory. “Every tribe and people and language and nation” — the fourfold phrase of 5:9. The beast’s reach is universal, given, and covers exactly the territory already bought by Someone else.

Earth-dwellers. John’s term (8:13) for those whose whole account is settled here — not geography; the saints live on earth too and are never called that.

The register. The most reassuring clause in the chapter. There is a book, belonging to “the Lamb who was slain.” Names were written in it “from the foundation of the world” — before anyone had done anything to deserve entry or exclusion. And those whose names are in it don’t worship the beast.

Could I be deceived into worshipping the beast? The verse says the opposite. The worshippers are those whose names are not written; those whose names are written are kept. That isn’t a promise that a believer will never be frightened, waver or fail — Peter denied Christ three times in a courtyard. It is a promise about who does the holding: “no one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:28). The register isn’t a list of people who held out. It belongs to the One with the wounds, and the entries were made before the world existed. A test: is your confidence resting on your grip on Christ, or his grip on you?

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone has an ear, let him hear: If anyone is to be taken captive, to captivity he goes; if anyone is to be slain with the sword, with the sword must he be slain. Here is a call for the endurance and faith of the saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John calls each listener to hear: whoever is appointed to captivity or the sword will go to it — this calls for the saints’ endurance and faith. Christians shouldn’t expect escape from every suffering; God calls us to stay faithful and keep trusting him through it.

For you personally. The formula closed all seven letters, always with “what the Spirit says to the churches.” Here those words are gone. Having described a beast conquering the saints, John turns to whoever is listening: this part is for you.

A sentence already passed. The saying comes from Jeremiah: “Those who are for pestilence, to pestilence, and those who are for the sword, to the sword; those who are for famine, to famine, and those who are for captivity, to captivity” (Jeremiah 15:2).

Not fatalism. The verse’s last sentence rules that out. It means a Christian facing the beast shouldn’t expect an escape route, spend his strength hunting one, or conclude when arrest comes that something has gone wrong with God’s arrangements. If captivity is appointed, that is where you are going. No fourth option is being withheld.

Bleak? Only until it is set against the alternative: a Christianity that promises deliverance from every hard thing, and so leaves a believer, when the door actually opens, concluding God has failed. This verse removes that conclusion in advance. Nothing done to a Christian by the beast is outside what was appointed, and none of it surprises the One who holds the keys.

Endurance and faith. The Christian response to the beast in two words. Endurance: holding a position under weight. Faith — or faithfulness; the word covers both, and both fit.

What isn’t on the list. Not resistance, organisation, clever manoeuvring, political leverage, or withdrawal into a compound. The beast has the dragon’s authority and the worship of the whole earth, and the instruction to the church is: stay where you are and keep trusting him.

The refusal to move. Any Christian under long pressure will recognise the realism. Most of what the New Testament asks of believers in trouble isn’t spectacular; it is the refusal to move. A similar call returns at 14:12. Twice, at the darkest points, the reader is told what is asked of him is endurance and faith, and nothing else. A test: what would faithful endurance look like in your hardest situation this week? Not escape — staying, and trusting.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 11–12: a second beast rises out of the earth — the opposite element, so that between them the dragon has the whole world covered. It has two horns like a lamb and it spoke like a dragon. Named three times later as the false prophet (16:13; 19:20; 20:10), its entire function is to make the world worship the first beast.

Verses 13–15: it performs great signs, including fire from heaven — Elijah’s credential on Carmel (1 Kings 18:38) — and by the signs it is allowed to work it deceives the earth-dwellers, telling them to make an image for the beast. It is allowed to give the image breath so that it speaks and orders the death of anyone who will not worship it. Behind this stands Daniel 3: an image on a plain, an order to bow at a signal, and a furnace — and three men who said But if not (Dan. 3:17–18).

Verses 16–17: it marks all — small and great, rich and poor, free and slave — on the right hand or the forehead, so that no one can buy or sell without the mark, that is, the name of the beast or the number of its name. Verse 18 sets the puzzle: let the one who has understanding calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a man, and his number is 666.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Beast from the Land

A second beast with horns like a lamb and a voice like a dragon makes the world worship the first. It works signs, gives the image a voice, and requires a mark — the beast’s name — without which no one can buy or sell. Its number, 666, is the number of a man.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Local notables ran the imperial cult, and refusing it cost a tradesman his living.

Now: The mark is an allegiance, not a device; nobody takes it by accident. Test teachers by what they say, not by how familiar they look.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw another beast rising out of the earth. It had two horns like a lamb and it spoke like a dragon. It exercises all the authority of the first beast in its presence, and makes the earth and its inhabitants worship the first beast, whose mortal wound was healed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A second beast rises from the earth, with two horns like a lamb but speaking like a dragon, and it makes the world worship the first beast. False religion looks gentle and familiar, but its message is the dragon’s — and its job is to win worship for the beast.

Land and sea covered. The first beast came from the sea, this one from the land. Between them the dragon has the world covered — exactly what the angel of 10:2 contested, one foot on each.

The unholy trinity. The dragon, the sea beast, and this one, later named “the false prophet” (16:13; 19:20; 20:10). Set against Father, Son and Spirit, the parody is exact. The dragon gives authority to the beast, as the Father gives all things to the Son. The beast bears a death-wound, lives, and is worshipped. And the false prophet draws no attention to himself; his whole function is to make the world worship the beast — just what the Spirit does for Christ (John 16:14).

Lamb’s horns, dragon’s voice. The most useful sentence in the chapter for recognising deception. It looks like a lamb — horns like the Lamb at the centre of this book. From a distance it is harmless, even familiar. Then it opens its mouth, and out comes the dragon. Jesus: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves” (Matthew 7:15). Paul: Satan disguises himself as an angel of light, and his servants as servants of righteousness (2 Corinthians 11:14–15). The New Testament warning about deception isn’t that it will look frightening, but familiar — and the test isn’t appearance but speech.

A usable test. Don’t ask whether a teacher, movement or message feels Christian, looks Christian, or uses Christian words — the horns are convincing. Ask what it actually says when it speaks at length, and whether that is what the dragon says: that God isn’t to be taken at his word, that his commands are a cage, that safety lies in accommodation. Apply it to the voices you listen to this week.

A department, not a rival. It works “in its presence” with the first beast’s authority, and its business is organising worship. In Asia this had a concrete shape: the imperial cult was run by a provincial council of local notables, and its priests weren’t Romans from abroad but leading men of the cities — neighbours, patrons, people the church knew. The pressure to worship didn’t arrive from the sea. It came up out of the local ground.
verseByVerse.note: This second beast is later called “the false prophet.”

verseByVerse.quote: It performs great signs, even making fire come down from heaven to earth in front of people, and by the signs that it is allowed to work in the presence of the beast it deceives those who dwell on earth, telling them to make an image for the beast that was wounded by the sword and yet lived. And it was allowed to give breath to the image of the beast, so that the image of the beast might even speak and might cause those who would not worship the image of the beast to be slain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second beast performs great signs, even calling fire from heaven, deceives the earth-dwellers, has them make an image of the first beast, and gives it breath to speak and to kill those who won’t worship it. Miracles alone prove nothing; deception uses religion and wonders to make false worship plausible, and faithful people must refuse even at the cost of their lives.

Real signs. The word is the one John’s Gospel uses for Jesus’ miracles. This isn’t mere conjuring. Scripture is consistent that supernatural power proves nothing by itself: Pharaoh’s magicians duplicated the first plagues (Exodus 7:11, 22); Moses warned that a prophet’s sign might come true while he led Israel to other gods, and that God was testing them by it (Deuteronomy 13:1–3); Jesus said false christs and false prophets would “perform great signs and wonders” (Matthew 24:24). A test: are you drawn to a ministry chiefly by its wonders? Test it by its words about Christ.

Elijah’s fire. Fire from heaven was Elijah’s sign on Carmel, when it settled who the true God was before a nation (1 Kings 18:38). The false prophet reproduces the credential of Israel’s greatest prophet, and the two witnesses of chapter 11 had Elijah’s powers too. Both sides have fire. Only one has the truth.

Allowed. Even the deceiving miracles run on a licence.

An idol that talks. The Old Testament mocks idols because they can’t: “They have mouths, but do not speak; eyes, but do not see. They have ears, but do not hear” (Psalm 115:5–6), the psalm John used at 9:20. Here this idol talks back, and what it says is a death sentence. How it speaks — ancient temples did use hidden speaking-tubes and moving statues — doesn’t matter. The demand is the same either way: bow, or die.

Daniel 3. An image on a plain, an order to bow at a signal, a furnace for refusers. Three men said no, in words that could be carved over this chapter: “our God whom we serve is able to deliver us… But if not, be it known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods” (Daniel 3:17–18). “But if not” is the endurance of the saints in three words.

Force needs plausibility. The first beast supplies the force; the second the plausibility — signs, wonders, reasons, respectable local men explaining it is only a formality. Raw power alone has never commanded worship. It needs someone with lamb’s horns to make the case. A test: what “only a formality” are you being asked to perform that would deny Christ? Say “but if not” — and refuse.

verseByVerse.quote: Also it causes all, both small and great, both rich and poor, both free and slave, to be marked on the right hand or the forehead, so that no one can buy or sell unless he has the mark, that is, the name of the beast or the number of its name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second beast makes everyone — small and great, rich and poor, free and slave — receive a mark on the right hand or forehead, so that no one can buy or sell without the mark, the beast’s name or number. The mark is not a device but an allegiance, a counterfeit of God’s seal, enforced by economic pressure — and no believer takes it by accident.

Everyone. Three pairs covering every social division: status, wealth, legal condition. No one is exempt by being important or overlooked for being insignificant. The demand reaches the senator and the slave in one sentence.

A counterfeit seal. The original was shown first: God’s servants sealed on their foreheads (7:3), the 144,000 with the Lamb’s and the Father’s name written there (14:1). Everyone in this book is marked; there is no unmarked category. The only question is whose name is on you.

Hand and forehead. Israel was told to bind God’s words “as a sign on your hand, and they shall be as frontlets between your eyes” (Deuteronomy 6:8). Hand and forehead: what you do and what you think. The beast demands what God demanded, in the same two places — a parody, not merely an atrocity.

Buy or sell. Here the chapter stops being theoretical for most readers. The pressure isn’t chiefly death but trade. Keep your convictions and lose your livelihood, or make one small formal gesture and go on feeding your family. In Asia that was real: a tradesman who wouldn’t join the guild ritual lost the guild’s work, probably the pressure behind the letters to Pergamum and Thyatira. Later, under Decius, a certificate that one had sacrificed — copies survive on papyrus — was the difference between a working life and ruin. A test: what would you give up to stay faithful at work? Decide before the pressure comes.

Not a barcode. The mark isn’t a barcode, microchip, credit card, vaccine or implant. Every generation since printing has identified it with its newest technology, and every one has been wrong, with no loss of confidence. The text rules out the technological reading: the mark is “the name of the beast or the number of its name.” Not a device but an identity — a declaration of who owns you and whose name you will say. Whatever administrative form loyalty takes in a given century, what is demanded is worship, and what is at stake is allegiance.

What if I take it by accident? No one in this chapter takes it by accident. It is the visible sign of worship already given, by people who have already marvelled, worshipped, and decided no one can fight the beast. No one stumbles into it. And those whose names are in the Lamb’s book are not the ones at that counter.

verseByVerse.quote: This calls for wisdom: let the one who has understanding calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a man, and his number is 666.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John calls for wisdom to calculate the beast’s number — the number of a man — 666. The number most likely pointed John’s first readers to Nero and marks the beast as humanity making itself god, always falling short of God’s perfection — not a code for guessing a future name.

A puzzle with a key. No verse has been used more irresponsibly, so start with what it says. It invites calculation: “let the one who has understanding calculate.” John sets a puzzle to people who had the key. And “the number of a man” may mean a particular man or a number characteristic of humanity; both are grammatically possible.

Letters as numbers. In Hebrew and Greek the letters double as numerals, so every name has a numerical value. It was a common game; graffiti from Pompeii reads, in effect, “I love her whose number is 545.” First-century readers knew at once what John was asking.

What does 666 mean? The most widely held identification is Nero: his Greek name and title, “Neron Kesar,” written in Hebrew letters, add up to 666. And some ancient manuscripts read 616 — exactly the total of the Latin form, “Nero Caesar,” without the final n. A variant that shifts the number by precisely one dropped letter is hard to explain as coincidence; early readers apparently knew the name and adjusted to their spelling. The historicist tradition of the Reformation applied it to the papacy. The futurist tradition takes it as the name of an Antichrist still to come, calculable only when he appears. And a reading that needs no name: six is one short of seven, the number of completeness; six three times is falling short raised to the highest pitch. The more likely reading combines these: the number marks the beast as the height of human self-deification, which in John’s day had Nero’s face. It is a portrait, not a code for calculating a future name.

A magnificent almost. Whatever the beast is and whenever it appears, it is a world-conquering almost. Seven heads it didn’t earn, ten crowns it was given, a resurrection it counterfeited — and it can’t reach seven.

A history of confident error. Every century has found its man — emperors, popes, sultans, Napoleon, Hitler, and a line of modern politicians made to fit by ingenious arithmetic. What all these identifications shared was certainty. John asks for wisdom and understanding, not cleverness, and they aren’t the same. A test: does your interest in this verse make you wiser and more faithful, or just more speculative?

What to take away. Not a name but a recognition. The beast is whatever demands the allegiance that belongs to God, backed by force, made plausible by religion, enforced through the power to buy and sell. It has worn many costumes and will wear more. Every one is a six — gigantic, unopposable to look at, worshipped by the whole earth, and one short of the number that belongs to the Lamb.
verseByVerse.note: Letters also served as numbers. Many think 666 spells “Neron Caesar” (the Greek form) in Hebrew letters; some manuscripts read 616, which fits the Latin spelling of the name. Others see 666 as falling short of seven again and again.

And to it the dragon gave his power and his throne and great authority.<sup>3</sup>One of its heads seemed to have a mortal wound, but its mortal wound was healed, and the whole earth marveled as they followed the beast.<sup>4</sup>And they worshiped the dragon, for he had given his authority to the beast, and they worshiped the beast, saying, “Who is like the beast, and who can fight against it?”<sup>5</sup>And the beast was given a mouth uttering haughty and blasphemous words, and it was allowed to exercise authority for forty-two months.<sup>6</sup>It opened its mouth to utter blasphemies against God, blaspheming his name and his dwelling, that is, those who dwell in heaven.<sup>7</sup>Also it was allowed to make war on the saints and to conquer them. And authority was given it over every tribe and people and language and nation,<sup>8</sup>and all who dwell on earth will worship it, everyone whose name has not been written from the foundation of the world in the book of life of the Lamb who was slain.<sup>9</sup>If anyone has an ear, let him hear:<sup>10</sup>If anyone is to be taken captive, to captivity he goes; if anyone is to be slain with the sword, with the sword must he be slain. Here is a call for the endurance and faith of the saints.<sup>11</sup>Then I saw another beast rising out of the earth. It had two horns like a lamb and it spoke like a dragon.<sup>12</sup>It exercises all the authority of the first beast in its presence, and makes the earth and its inhabitants worship the first beast, whose mortal wound was healed.<sup>13</sup>It performs great signs, even making fire come down from heaven to earth in front of people,<sup>14</sup>and by the signs that it is allowed to work in the presence of the beast it deceives those who dwell on earth, telling them to make an image for the beast that was wounded by the sword and yet lived.<sup>15</sup>And it was allowed to give breath to the image of the beast, so that the image of the beast might even speak and might cause those who would not worship the image of the beast to be slain.<sup>16</sup>Also it causes all, both small and great, both rich and poor, both free and slave, to be marked on the right hand or the forehead,<sup>17</sup>so that no one can buy or sell unless he has the mark, that is, the name of the beast or the number of its name.<sup>18</sup>This calls for wisdom: let the one who has understanding calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a man, and his number is 666.

14.title: The Lamb, the Harvest, and the Three Angels
14.overview:
Chapter 14 is a triptych of three visions, each answering the terror of chapter 13 with a counter-vision of divine certainty. First: the Lamb on Mount Zion with the 144,000 — the redeemed in their completeness, standing where the beast could not reach them. Second: three angels flying in midheaven, each with a message that together constitute the gospel, the judgment, and the warning. Third: the great harvest of the earth — the grain harvest of the redeemed and the grape harvest of the wicked, two harvests that together depict the final judgment in all its terrible binary clarity.

The chapter is the hinge of Revelation. Behind it lies the cosmic backstory (chapters 12–13) and the long unfolding of the seals and trumpets (chapters 6–11). Before it lies the bowl judgments, Babylon's fall, the Rider on the white horse, and the new creation. Chapter 14 stands at the center and declares: the outcome is certain. The Lamb is on Mount Zion. The harvest is coming. The one who endures to the end will be saved.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The Lamb and the 144,000 on Mount Zion
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Chapter 13 ended with a mark on the hand or forehead and a number; chapter 14 opens with a different forehead and a different name. Verse 1: on Mount Zion stands the Lamb, and with him the 144,000 sealed in chapter 7, complete, wearing his name and his Father’s. Everyone in this book is marked; the alternative to the beast’s mark is not an unmarked crowd.

Verses 2–3: a voice like the roar of many waters and loud thunder — and, in the same breath, like harpists playing on harps. They sing a new song before the throne, and no one could learn that song except the 144,000 who had been redeemed from the earth. Not because the words are difficult, but because a song about being ransomed cannot be sung truly by someone who has not been.

Verses 4–5 describe them: they have not defiled themselves with women, for they are virgins; they follow the Lamb wherever he goes; they are firstfruits (aparchē, the first sheaf that both belongs to God and guarantees more is coming); and in their mouth no lie was found, for they are blameless — language taken from the servant of Isaiah 53:9 and the remnant of Zephaniah 3:13, and amōmos, the word for a sacrificial animal without defect.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lamb on Mount Zion

Against the beast’s mark stand the 144,000 with the Lamb’s name on their foreheads, singing a new song only the redeemed can learn. They follow the Lamb wherever he goes, and are blameless because they were bought.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Not one of those sealed in chapter 7 is missing.

Now: Ask whether the song of the cross is a statement you admire or your own account.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I looked, and behold, on Mount Zion stood the Lamb, and with him 144,000 who had his name and his Father's name written on their foreheads. And I heard a voice from heaven like the roar of many waters and like the sound of loud thunder. The voice I heard was like the sound of harpists playing on their harps, and they were singing a new song before the throne and before the four living creatures and before the elders. No one could learn that song except the 144,000 who had been redeemed from the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John sees the Lamb standing on Mount Zion with the 144,000, who bear his and his Father’s name on their foreheads and sing a new song that only the redeemed can learn. In contrast to the beast’s marked followers, Christ’s people are complete, secure with him, and worship from the experience of being ransomed.

A different forehead. Chapter 13 ended with a mark and a number; chapter 14 opens with a different forehead and a different name. Everyone in this book is marked. The alternative to the beast isn’t an unmarked crowd but a marked one, wearing a different name in the same place.

Mount Zion. The hill where, in the Psalms, God installs his King in the teeth of the raging nations: “As for me, I have set my King on Zion, my holy hill” (Psalm 2:6). Hebrews says Christians have already come there: “you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem” (Hebrews 12:22). Earthly hill or heavenly city, the sense is the same: where the King stands and the enemy doesn’t.

None missing. In 13:1 a beast rose from the sea; here the Lamb simply stands, and his company is counted and complete. Not one of the 144,000 sealed in chapter 7 is missing. The sealing worked. They are the same as in chapter 7: the complete people of God, sealed with the name of the Lamb and his Father — not a literal number from ethnic Israel, nor the special class of “anointed” taught by Jehovah’s Witnesses.

Waters, thunder and harps. “The roar of many waters” is the voice of the risen Christ (1:15) and of God’s glory returning (Ezekiel 43:2); thunder is God’s voice at Sinai; and in the same breath, harps, the most delicate sound of the ancient world. Overwhelming and beautiful at the same volume. Nothing in human music does both; a waterfall isn’t tender and a harp can’t be heard over one. Any picture of heaven’s worship that is merely soothing has lost half of it.

A new song. Sung when God has done something unprecedented (Psalm 96:1), and sung once before in this book (5:9): “by your blood you ransomed people for God.” That is this song’s subject too.

No one else can learn it. Not because the words are hard; a song about being ransomed by blood can be printed and read by anyone. It can’t be sung truly by someone who hasn’t been ransomed. In chapter 5, myriads of angels praised the Lamb, but the new song was the song of the redeemed — things “into which angels long to look” (1 Peter 1:12).

A quiet test. In any ordinary service, when a hymn about the cross is sung, are you singing a true statement or your own account? The difference isn’t musical or emotional; someone can be moved by a tune he has no part in. The 144,000 sing what could only be learned by having it happen to them. Can you sing it that way this Sunday?

verseByVerse.quote: It is these who have not defiled themselves with women, for they are virgins. It is these who follow the Lamb wherever he goes. These have been redeemed from mankind as firstfruits for God and the Lamb, and in their mouth no lie was found, for they are blameless.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The 144,000 have not defiled themselves with women, follow the Lamb wherever he goes, are firstfruits redeemed for God, and have no lie in their mouths. Christ’s people keep themselves for him alone, follow him without conditions, belong to God as a pledge of the full harvest, and are truthful in a world of deceit.

What does “virgins” mean here? Three readings are held. First, literally, of celibate men. Whatever else is said, it can’t mean marriage defiles: “Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the marriage bed be undefiled” (Hebrews 13:4), and Paul calls forbidding marriage a teaching of demons (1 Timothy 4:1–3). Peter was married, and this book is addressed to ordinary households. Second, spiritual fidelity. In the prophets idolatry is adultery and God’s people a bride chasing lovers (Hosea 1–3; Jeremiah 3:6–10; Ezekiel 16). This book is about to describe a prostitute, Babylon, who intoxicated the nations (v. 8), and ends with a Bride. Paul used the image of a church: “I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:2). Third, holy-war imagery. The 144,000 came from a tribal muster, the way Israel counted an army, and soldiers on campaign abstained from sex: David’s men had kept themselves from women (1 Samuel 21:4–5); Uriah wouldn’t go home while the ark and army were in tents (2 Samuel 11:11; cf. Deuteronomy 23:9–10). The more likely reading is that the second and third are both in play, saying one thing: this company kept itself for one Lord in a world offering many. A test: what rival love is courting your heart this week?

Following wherever. “These follow the Lamb wherever he goes” — the simplest definition of a Christian in the book, startlingly plain after two chapters of beasts. “Follow me” was the first thing Jesus asked of fishermen and the last thing he said to Peter, twice (John 21:19, 22). The weight is on “wherever.” Following is easy while the road goes somewhere you would choose. The Lamb goes to a cross, through death, and meanwhile among lampstands in difficult towns. To follow wherever is to have surrendered the veto in advance — what distinguishes a disciple from an admirer. Where are you still holding a veto?

Firstfruits. The first sheaf, brought to God before the rest was gathered (Leviticus 23:10). A firstfruit belongs to God and guarantees more is coming. Paul calls Christ “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20).

No lie. Echoing the Servant, in whose mouth was no deceit (Isaiah 53:9), and the remnant of Zephaniah 3:13. In a book whose villain is “the deceiver of the whole world” (12:9), truthfulness isn’t a minor virtue. It is the mark of the other side. A test: where are you shading the truth to make life easier?

Blameless. The word for a sacrificial animal without defect — what is said of the Lamb. No one here achieved it. They were “redeemed,” bought (v. 3); the blamelessness was purchased and given.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 6–7: an angel flies directly overhead — at the zenith, where everyone can see — with an eternal gospel for every nation and tribe and language and people, and calls out three imperatives: fear God, give him glory, and worship him who made heaven and earth, the sea and the springs of water, because the hour of his judgment has come. The list is deliberate: those are the four things the first four trumpets struck (8:7–12).

Verse 8: a second angel announces Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great — Isaiah’s watchman’s cry (Isa. 21:9; cf. Jer. 51:8) — she who made all nations drink the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality. Babylon is announced as finished three chapters before she is even described.

Verses 9–11: a third angel warns that whoever worships the beast and takes its mark will drink the wine of God’s wrath, poured full strength into the cup of his anger, and be tormented with fire and sulfur in the presence of the holy angels and in the presence of the Lamb; and the smoke of their torment goes up for ever, and they have no rest, day or night.

Verse 12 turns to the reader with the sentence already used at 13:10: Here is a call for the endurance of the saints, those who keep the commandments of God and their faith in Jesus. Verse 13 gives the second of the book’s seven beatitudes, and one of the few sentences John is specifically commanded to write: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on — with the Spirit adding a comment of his own: that they may rest from their labors, for their deeds follow them.
verseByVerse.theology:
Gospel, Fall, and Warning

An angel flies overhead with an eternal gospel: fear God and worship the Creator. A second announces Babylon fallen. A third warns that worshippers of the beast will drink God’s wrath unmixed. Then: blessed are the dead who die in the Lord.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The empire was at its height when its fall was announced in the past tense.

Now: Fear God rather than the beast; the warning is given so that the saints endure, and their deeds follow them.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw another angel flying directly overhead, with an eternal gospel to proclaim to those who dwell on earth, to every nation and tribe and language and people. And he said with a loud voice, "Fear God and give him glory, because the hour of his judgment has come, and worship him who made heaven and earth, the sea and the springs of water."
verseByVerse.commentary:
An angel flies overhead with an eternal gospel for every nation, calling all people to fear God, give him glory and worship the Creator, because his hour of judgment has come. Even in judgment God sends the good news to everyone, and calls them to turn from false fears to the true God who made them.

Three angels, the gospel’s order. Three announcements follow, in the order the gospel always arrives: an appeal, a warning about the world, a warning about the alternative.

Overhead, to everyone. At the zenith, like the eagle of 8:13, where everyone below can see. No one will say the message was hard to come by. And it goes “to those who dwell on earth” — the very people who have settled for this world and worshipped the beast. The gospel is proclaimed to the group that has rejected it for eight chapters.

An eternal gospel. The only time the noun “gospel” appears in Revelation, and some question whether this is the gospel, since the cross isn’t mentioned. But its content — that the Judge of all the earth has come to do right, and his creatures may still turn to him — is good news of the most concrete kind to people under a beast. And the cross has already been proclaimed at length: chapter 5 is the gospel, and the slain Lamb has been at the centre of every scene since.

The ground is creation. “Fear God and give him glory… and worship him who made heaven and earth, the sea and the springs of water” — exactly the four things the first four trumpets struck (8:7–12). This is Paul’s argument to pagans without a Bible: “turn from these vain things to a living God, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and all that is in them” (Acts 14:15); “The God who made the world and everything in it” (Acts 17:24). Where there is no shared Scripture there is a shared sky, and everyone owes his existence to Someone. A test: when you speak to unbelieving friends, do you start where Paul started — with the God who made them?

Fear God. The command modern readers find hardest. Not terror, nor comfortable respect, but taking God seriously as what he is — the settled, awed recognition that there is Someone there of a different order. “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge” (Proverbs 1:7). And it is aimed at people who have spent the book terrified of a beast. The remedy for fearing the wrong thing isn’t fearlessness but fearing the right thing, which frees a person from everything else. What are you afraid of this week? Set the fear of God against it.

verseByVerse.quote: Another angel, a second, followed, saying, "Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great, she who made all nations drink the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A second angel announces, “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great,” who made all nations drunk on the wine of her immorality. The proud, godless world-city — Rome in John’s day and every such system since — is as good as fallen, because God has decided it, though it still seduces people with its pleasures.

The headline first. Babylon appears for the first time, in one verse, announced as finished. Chapters 17–18 describe her at length; this headline runs ahead of the story.

Isaiah’s watchman. “Fallen, fallen is Babylon; and all the carved images of her gods he has shattered to the ground” (Isaiah 21:9; cf. Jeremiah 51:8). The doubling is a herald’s shout, the way news of a great collapse actually gets called out.

The grammar of certainty. Babylon hasn’t fallen yet in the story; she isn’t even described for three chapters. The angel announces the collapse of an empire at the height of its power. Prophets do this constantly: what God has decided is reported as done, because from his side it is. That is what a Christian in Ephesus needed. The empire in front of him wasn’t wobbling; it was collecting his taxes, running his courts and threatening his trade. And the message read in his congregation used the past tense. A test: what power over your life do you need to hear announced as already fallen?

Who is Babylon? The historical Babylon had been ruins for centuries, so the name is a type, as Sodom and Egypt were at 11:8. For John’s readers it unmistakably meant Rome, which had destroyed the temple as Babylon did; Peter sends greetings from “She who is at Babylon” (1 Peter 5:13), almost certainly Rome. But the name is older than Rome and outlives it. Babylon begins at a tower built so that people could make a name for themselves (Genesis 11:4), and that project has never closed. Babylon is the city humanity builds without God — wherever it is, whatever it is called, however good its roads.

A glass, not a sword. “She who made all nations drink the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality.” Seduction, not conquest: the nations weren’t forced; they were poured a drink. And intoxication — lost judgment, the certainty at two in the morning that everything is fine. That is how the world’s system recruits, and why the church so often fails to notice. The beast comes with a sword and is obvious. Babylon comes with a glass, is charming, pays well, and doesn’t seem to ask for anything at all. A test: where is the world pouring for you — comfort, status, money, pleasure — and how much have you drunk?

verseByVerse.quote: And another angel, a third, followed them, saying with a loud voice, "If anyone worships the beast and its image and receives a mark on his forehead or on his hand, he also will drink the wine of God's wrath, poured full strength into the cup of his anger, and he will be tormented with fire and sulfur in the presence of the holy angels and in the presence of the Lamb. And the smoke of their torment goes up forever and ever, and they have no rest, day or night, these worshipers of the beast and its image, and whoever receives the mark of its name."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A third angel warns that whoever worships the beast and takes its mark will drink God’s undiluted wrath and be tormented with fire and sulfur in the Lamb’s presence, with no rest forever. Those who finally reject God for the beast face real, eternal judgment — a warning given only after the gospel has been proclaimed to all.

Without softening, without relish. The most terrible warning in the New Testament, to be read exactly as it stands.

Two cups. Babylon poured a drink; so does God. Those who drank hers will drink his. And “poured full strength”: ancient wine was nearly always mixed with water; unmixed wine was for getting drunk. The cup of God’s wrath is an Old Testament image — “in the hand of the LORD there is a cup with foaming wine, well mixed… all the wicked of the earth shall drain it down to the dregs” (Psalm 75:8; cf. Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15) — and here, for the first time, nothing softens it.

The water left out. Every judgment so far was diluted: a fourth, a third, a tenth, forty-two months, a limit on the locusts, a fence around the winds. That was the mixing — God’s patience. This is the cup with the water left out.

Two eternities. Fire and sulfur is Sodom (Genesis 19:24). Smoke rising forever is Isaiah’s picture of Edom (Isaiah 34:10). And “they have no rest, day or night” is the exact reverse of the living creatures who never cease worshipping (4:8) and the martyrs told to rest (6:11). Two eternities side by side; the difference is what a person is doing in them.

Is the punishment of the lost conscious and unending? Some evangelicals hold that the wicked are finally destroyed and cease to exist, pointing to the Bible’s language of destruction and perishing and arguing that the smoke rising forever describes a permanent result rather than a continuing experience. That view is held by people who love the Bible and want to be faithful to it. But the historic and majority position of the church, and the plain reading of these words, is that the punishment of the finally impenitent is conscious and unending, because “they have no rest, day or night” describes an experience, not a residue. That is the more likely reading.

In the presence of the Lamb. Not a distant dungeon God has forgotten. And the One present is the Lamb — who was slaughtered, wept at a tomb, and prayed for the men driving the nails. No one finally lost will be able to say the Judge didn’t offer himself first.

On whom it falls. Said twice: “these worshipers of the beast and its image, and whoever receives the mark of its name.” Not the unlucky or confused or never-asked. This warning is the third of three, and the first was an eternal gospel flown overhead to every nation. Nobody reaches v. 11 without being flown over by v. 6.

A particular face. For the reader thinking of someone he loves: Scripture doesn’t tell us the destination of anyone still alive and never invites us to work it out. It tells us the Judge is the Lamb, the gospel is still being flown overhead, and intercession is a priestly act — what you were made a priest to do (1:6). Pray, and keep praying. Remember that Paul once watched over the coats at Stephen’s death.

verseByVerse.quote: Here is a call for the endurance of the saints, those who keep the commandments of God and their faith in Jesus. And I heard a voice from heaven saying, "Write this: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on." "Blessed indeed," says the Spirit, "that they may rest from their labors, for their deeds follow them!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is a call for the saints to endure, keeping God’s commands and faith in Jesus; and a voice declares, “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord,” for they rest from their labours and their deeds follow them. Knowing God’s judgment helps believers stand firm, and Christians who die are blessed — at rest, and nothing they did for Christ is lost.

What it is for. A similar call came at 13:10, both times right after the darkest material — the beast conquering the saints, and now the undiluted cup. Twice John writes something almost unbearable, then turns to the reader: this is what it is for.

The same two marks. Keeping God’s commandments and holding faith in Jesus, as at 12:17. Obedience and trust. The list hasn’t grown, and won’t.

Not fear but endurance. After three verses about hell, the response asked for isn’t fear or a campaign. It is endurance — staying under the weight. Knowledge of judgment in this book is never given to frighten Christians, but to let them keep standing when the beast has every advantage, because they know how the accounts are finally settled.

A sentence heaven wanted written. “Write this: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on.” The second of Revelation’s seven blessings, and one of few sentences John is specifically commanded to write (cf. 19:9; 21:5). Not blessed are the strong, victorious or escaped. Blessed are the dead. To congregations that had buried people and expected to bury more, at the point where the beast is killing all who refuse the mark, God stops the vision to dictate a sentence about those who didn’t survive.

In the Lord. That carries everything. Death isn’t blessed in itself; it is “the last enemy” (1 Corinthians 15:26), thrown at last into the lake of fire (20:14). What is blessed is dying in him — Paul’s “dead in Christ” (1 Thessalonians 4:16).

The Spirit adds his word. “Blessed indeed… that they may rest from their labors, for their deeds follow them!” They rest — the word for exhausting toil, and the rest given the martyrs (6:11). Whatever heaven is, it is first described here as the end of being tired. And their deeds follow them — not going ahead as a credential, nor left behind as a legacy, but following, like servants walking behind their master into a house. Nothing done for Christ is left at the graveside: the visits no one recorded, giving that cost something, years of raising children in the faith, prayers in an empty kitchen. All of it walks in behind the one who did it (1 Corinthians 15:58).

For the funeral. This verse is for the graveside, for the person who knows he is dying, and for the one just home from the hospital who can’t think what to do next. The dead who die in the Lord are blessed; they are resting; and everything they did is on its way in after them. A test: what labour for Christ are you tempted to think is wasted? It will follow you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–20 — The Harvest of the Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 14–16: one like a son of man (Dan. 7:13; cf. Rev. 1:13) is seated on a white cloud with a golden crown and a sharp sickle. An angel comes out of the temple with word that the hour to reap has come, for the harvest of the earth is fully ripe, and he swings his sickle and the earth is reaped — in a single sentence, with no resistance recorded.

Verses 17–19: a second angel with a sharp sickle comes out of the temple, and a third comes from the altar, having authority over the fire, and orders the vintage: gather the clusters from the vine of the earth, for its grapes are ripe. The grapes are thrown into the great winepress of the wrath of God (cf. Isa. 63:3; Joel 3:13).

Verse 20: the winepress was trodden outside the city, and blood flowed from the winepress, as high as a horse’s bridle, for 1,600 stadia — about a hundred and eighty miles, roughly the length of Palestine, and four times four times a hundred, four being the number of the earth in this book. The figure means the whole world, completely.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Harvest of the Earth

One like a son of man reaps the ripe harvest, and the vintage of the earth is trodden in the winepress of God’s wrath outside the city. The timing is set by the one who has watched the field.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The order for the vintage came from the altar where the martyrs’ prayers were received.

Now: The delay was never indifference but patience; the judge who reaps is the one who was trodden outside the city for us.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I looked, and behold, a white cloud, and seated on the cloud one like a son of man, with a golden crown on his head, and a sharp sickle in his hand. And another angel came out of the temple, calling with a loud voice to him who sat on the cloud, "Put in your sickle, and reap, for the hour to reap has come, for the harvest of the earth is fully ripe." So he who sat on the cloud swung his sickle across the earth, and the earth was reaped.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John sees one like a son of man on a white cloud, crowned and holding a sharp sickle; an angel from the temple says the harvest is ripe, and he reaps the earth with one swing. Christ will gather the earth’s harvest at the hour the Father has set — the long delay was patience, waiting for the harvest to ripen.

The Son of Man. “One like a son of man” on a cloud is Daniel 7:13, the phrase used of the risen Christ in 1:13. A victor’s crown on his head — and in his hand, not a sword or sceptre, but a farm tool.

Is this Christ or an angel? Some take the figure as an angel, since in the next verse an angel tells him to start reaping — an odd thing for a creature to say to the Son of God. The objection is fair. But an angel coming “out of the temple” brings word from the Father’s presence, and Jesus said, “concerning that day or that hour, no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father” (Mark 13:32). A message from the sanctuary that the hour has come is exactly what the Son said he awaited. The more likely reading is that this is Christ.

Two harvests. Whether they are two pictures of one judgment or two gatherings is debated. The grain harvest here has not one hostile word: a sickle, a ripe field, a reaping. The grape harvest (vv. 17–20) is plainly wrath. So many take the first as the ingathering of the redeemed and the second as the judgment of the wicked, matching the parable of the wheat and weeds, where the reapers gather the wheat into the barn (Matthew 13:30, 39). Others take both as judgment, since Joel puts sickle and winepress together (Joel 3:13). The first is the more likely.

The right day. “The hour to reap has come, for the harvest of the earth is fully ripe” — literally dried out, over-ready. Anyone who has waited on a crop knows there is a right day. Cut too early and the grain is green and worthless; wait too long and it shatters on the ground. The point isn’t the violence of reaping but that a decision about timing is made by Someone who has been watching the field.

How long? The question running since 6:10. The delay was never indifference or failure of nerve, but a harvest not yet ready. Peter says what was ripening: the Lord “is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance” (2 Peter 3:9). A test: if the harvest came today, would you be gathered into the barn? Make sure of it now, while the patience lasts.

One swing. After thirteen chapters of seals, trumpets, beasts and dragons, the end arrives in a single sentence with no resistance recorded. No battle, no dialogue. The instrument that finishes the age is a sickle swung once by a man on a cloud.

verseByVerse.quote: Then another angel came out of the temple in heaven, and he too had a sharp sickle. And another angel came out from the altar, the angel who has authority over the fire, and he called with a loud voice to the one who had the sharp sickle, "Put in your sickle and gather the clusters from the vine of the earth, for its grapes are ripe." So the angel swung his sickle across the earth and gathered the grape harvest of the earth and threw it into the great winepress of the wrath of God. And the winepress was trodden outside the city, and blood flowed from the winepress, as high as a horse's bridle, for 1,600 stadia.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Another angel with a sickle gathers the vine of the earth at the command of the angel from the altar and throws it into the great winepress of God’s wrath, trodden outside the city, and blood flows for 1,600 stadia. God’s judgment on the wicked answers his people’s prayers and is terrible in scale — yet outside the city Christ has already been trodden for all who will trust him.

From the altar. The order comes from the angel “who has authority over the fire,” from the altar the reader has visited three times: where the saints’ prayers were burned with incense (8:3–4), where fire was thrown to earth (8:5), where the voice released the sixth trumpet (9:13). Beneath it the martyrs cried “how long?” (6:9–10). The vintage of God’s wrath is ordered from the place where the church’s prayers were received. The martyrs asked; this is the answer arriving.

The winepress. A stone trough where men trod grapes barefoot while the juice ran into a vat — hard, ordinary work, and one of the oldest pictures of judgment in Scripture. “I have trodden the winepress alone, and from the peoples no one was with me… their lifeblood spattered on my garments” (Isaiah 63:3); “Put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe. Go in, tread, for the winepress is full” (Joel 3:13). John quotes both.

Outside the city. The detail that should stop a Christian reader. That is where the sin offering was burned under the law, and where Jesus died: “So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood” (Hebrews 13:12). There are two treadings of that press outside that city. At the first, one man went in alone, and the blood was his own. Everyone at the second will have refused the first. That is the mercy hidden in the most violent verse in the book. A test: have you taken refuge in the first treading — his blood shed for you?

The scale. 1,600 stadia is about 184 miles, roughly the length of the land of Israel — a distance any reader could picture. And 1,600 is four times four times a hundred: four is the number of the earth in this book, and a hundred squares it — the whole world, completely. Blood as high as a horse’s bridle across a country isn’t a casualty forecast. It is a statement of scale and horror in the only register that can carry it.

Are the two harvests two different events? The more likely reading is that they are two sides of the one final coming: the grain harvest, the gathering of God’s people (Matthew 13:30), and the grape harvest, the judgment of the wicked. Jesus said, “the harvest is the end of the age, and the reapers are angels” (Matthew 13:39).

No comment. The chapter ends there, deliberately. Revelation doesn’t make judgment palatable or apologise for it. It sets it right after v. 13 — “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord” — so the reader holds both. The Lamb stands on Zion with his people, counted and complete; an eternal gospel flies overhead; Babylon is announced fallen while standing; the dead in the Lord rest, their deeds following them in; and the field has been watched by Someone who knows the day. The hand on the sickle has a wound in it.
verseByVerse.note: The 1,600 stadia (v. 20) are about 184 miles; a stadion was about 607 feet — roughly the length of the land of Israel.

The voice I heard was like the sound of harpists playing on their harps,<sup>3</sup>and they were singing a new song before the throne and before the four living creatures and before the elders. No one could learn that song except the 144,000 who had been redeemed from the earth.<sup>4</sup>It is these who have not defiled themselves with women, for they are virgins.
