21.title: All Things New: The New Heaven, New Earth, and New Jerusalem
21.overview:
Chapter 21 is the destination toward which every page of Revelation has been moving. Every sealed scroll, every trumpet, every suffering saint, every martyr’s cry of ‘How long?’ — all of it was moving toward this: “Behold, I am making all things new.” The new creation is not the consolation prize for a plan that nearly failed. It is the goal, the telos, the end for which the whole story was told.

The chapter falls into two great movements. The first (vv. 1–8) describes the new heaven and new earth from a distance — the cosmic renewal, the descent of the holy city, the voice from the throne declaring the end of tears and death, and the character of those who will inherit and those who will not. The second (vv. 9–27) zooms in: the angel takes John in the Spirit to a high mountain and shows him the new Jerusalem in breathtaking architectural detail — dimensions, gates, foundations, materials, light, temple, nations.

The key to the chapter is understanding what the new Jerusalem is. It is not primarily a city in the architectural sense; it is a person — “prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.” The new Jerusalem is the church, the bride of Christ, dwelling with God in the fullness of the covenant relationship that all of redemptive history has been building toward. The city and the bride are the same reality: the people of God in their final, perfected, glorified state, living in the presence of God as his dwelling place.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The New Heaven and the New Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2: a new heaven and a new earth, and the sea was no more; and the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband. The word for new is kainos, which usually means new in kind, renewed. And the direction is downward.

Verses 3–4: the dwelling place of God is with man — skēnē, a tent — with the covenant formula complete: they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God. Then four abolitions: He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore (cf. Isa. 25:8).

Verses 5–6: God the Father speaks in the first person for the second and last time in the book — Behold, I am making all things new; Write this down, for these words are trustworthy and true; It is done!; I am the Alpha and the Omega; and the offer, to the thirsty I will give from the spring of the water of life without payment (cf. Isa. 55:1; John 4:14).

Verses 7–8: the last promise to the conqueror — I will be his God and he will be my son, the Davidic promise of 2 Samuel 7:14 handed to anyone who holds on — and then the eight excluded categories, beginning startlingly with the cowardly and ending with all liars, whose portion is the second death.
verseByVerse.theology:
All Things New

A new heaven and earth — renewed, not replaced — and the holy city coming down as a bride. God dwells with his people and wipes away every tear; death, mourning, crying and pain are gone. He gives the water of life freely to the thirsty.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: John, cut off by the sea from his churches, hears that the sea will be no more.

Now: God answers grief not by explanation but by removal, with his own hand on the face.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away, and the sea was no more. And I saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John sees a new heaven and a new earth, with the first passed away and the sea gone, and the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down from God, prepared as a bride for her husband. God will not discard his creation but renew it, removing everything that threatens and separates, and he will bring his dwelling down to his people on a renewed earth.

The Bible’s destination. The whole Bible has been travelling toward this sentence. It opened, “In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth,” and now says it again with one word changed.

New, not replaced. John’s word for “new” usually stresses newness of quality rather than mere recency — new in kind, renewed — the same word he uses of the new Jerusalem, the new name, the new song. That is the difference between God scrapping his creation and renewing it. “The creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption and obtain the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (Romans 8:21) — set free, not replaced. Peter looks for “new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells” (2 Peter 3:13). The resurrection body is the pattern: the same body, transformed and glorified, with the wounds still in the hands. So the Christian hope isn’t escape from the material world into something vaporous. It is that this world — soil, water, weather, bodies, work, cities — will be put right. God doesn’t abandon what he made. A test: does your hope picture floating clouds, or a renewed earth? Let Scripture shape it, and treat God’s world accordingly now.

No more sea. This troubles people who love the sea, and deserves an answer. John isn’t making a statement about oceanography. In this book the sea is the ancient image of chaos — frozen flat before the throne (4:6), the beast’s birthplace (13:1), the grave of those with no graves (20:13). And John writes from an island; the sea is what keeps him from his churches. The promise isn’t that there will be no water, but that nothing will be left that separates, threatens or devours.

The city comes down. Watch the direction, because popular pictures of the Christian hope get it backwards. Nobody is going up. The Bible’s last movement isn’t humanity evacuated to heaven, but heaven arriving on a renewed earth — what Christians have always prayed without noticing: “your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven.”

The city is a bride. Not a bride’s residence: the city and the bride are the same, as v. 9 makes explicit when an angel offers to show John the Bride and shows him a city. The dwelling place turns out to be the people — why the description that follows can be architectural and personal at once, and why no one should try to draw it.

Two women. In 17:1 a bowl angel said, “Come, I will show you the judgment of the great prostitute,” and carried John into a wilderness. The same rank of angel, in almost the same words, now carries him up a mountain to see a Bride (v. 9). Two women, two cities, and the book has asked since chapter 17 which one the reader has been dressing for.

verseByVerse.quote: And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying, "Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God. He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A voice from the throne announces that God’s dwelling is now with mankind: he will live with them as their God, wipe away every tear, and end death, mourning, crying and pain forever. The goal of the whole Bible is God’s personal presence with his people, and he will heal every sorrow himself — not by explaining it, but by removing it.

God pitches his tent. “Dwelling place” is the word for a tent or tabernacle, and the verb matches: God will pitch his tent with them. Follow that word through the Bible and the whole story is on one thread. God walked with the man and woman in the garden, and they were sent out. He told Moses, “let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst” (Exodus 25:8). Solomon built a house and the glory filled it, and Ezekiel watched it leave. Then “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” — pitched his tent among us — written by the same John (John 1:14). Then the Spirit made a temple of ordinary people (1 Corinthians 3:16). And here is the end: no tent in a camp, no house on a hill, no veil, no exclusions. God with man, permanently, in the open.

The covenant fulfilled. “They will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God.” Said to Abraham, to Israel at Sinai, through Jeremiah and Ezekiel, always as a promise. Here it is reported as fact. And note “God himself” — not an angel or a representative or glory at a safe distance. What the whole Bible has been arranging isn’t improved circumstances for people. It is his presence. A test: is God himself the heart of your hope of heaven, or only the reunions and the relief?

Every tear. The second time in this book (7:17), and both times the same extraordinary thing: God does it himself, with his hand, on a face. Isaiah promised it: “He will swallow up death forever; and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from all faces” (Isaiah 25:8).

Four abolitions. Take them one at a time. Death: the thing that has taken everyone you have loved and will take you — gone, thrown into the lake (20:14). Mourning: the loud grief at the graveside. Crying: the private version, the sound someone makes alone in a car. Pain: the word covers both the body’s pain and the labour that wears a person out, reaching back to the curse of Genesis 3 and undoing it.

Removal, not explanation. No one here is told why it happened. The promise isn’t that the tears will finally make sense, but that God will wipe them from a face, that what caused them will be dead, and that “the former things have passed away.” This is the verse to hold when the reason for a grief has never arrived and probably never will. God doesn’t, in the end, argue with a bereaved person. He comes over and attends to the face.

Will we remember those we loved who are lost? Scripture doesn’t explain how, and we shouldn’t claim to know more than it says. But it does say we will be ourselves, known and knowing (1 Corinthians 13:12), and that God himself will wipe away every tear. We will see as God sees and share his perfect justice and perfect love. Whatever we remember, nothing will spoil the joy he gives. And that is a reason to pray for and speak to those we love while there is time.

verseByVerse.quote: And he who was seated on the throne said, "Behold, I am making all things new." Also he said, "Write this down, for these words are trustworthy and true." And he said to me, "It is done! I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end. To the thirsty I will give from the spring of the water of life without payment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God on the throne declares, “Behold, I am making all things new,” tells John to write it down because it is true, says “It is done!”, names himself the Alpha and Omega, and promises the thirsty the water of life free of charge. God is renewing his whole creation, his word is certain, and the gift of eternal life is offered freely to anyone who wants it.

God speaks. One of only two places in the book where God on the throne speaks in his own voice in the first person. At 1:8 he said who he is; here he says what he does. Two sentences, twenty chapters apart, bracketing the dragon, the beast, the bowls and the burning city.

All things new. “I am making” — present tense, happening, not merely scheduled. “All things” — nothing excepted. And not “I am making all new things,” but “I am making all things new.” Nothing is discarded and started over. The same things — this world, these people, the bodies in the ground — are made new. A test: what in your life looks beyond repair? Bring it to the One who makes all things new.

Write this down. The third and last time John is told to write a particular sentence: “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord” (14:13); “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb” (19:9); and this. Each is a promise a suffering church would find nearly impossible to believe, each with its own command to record it and guarantee of truth.

“It is done!” The same word as at the seventh bowl (16:17), echoing the cross: “It is finished” (John 19:30). The cross made the end of wrath bearable and the new world certain, and the same voice now says it over a finished world.

Alpha and Omega. The title of 1:8, waiting twenty chapters to be used again. He was the first letter when there was nothing to write about, and he is the last now that everything has been written.

A drink, given away. At the summit of the book, after the great white throne and the lake of fire, comes an offer. Not a reward, settlement or wage — a drink, given away. Isaiah’s words: “Come, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters; and he who has no money, come, buy and eat! Come, buy wine and milk without money and without price” (Isaiah 55:1). Christ’s words at a well (John 4:14) and at the feast: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37). “Without payment” is the word Paul uses of being “justified by his grace as a gift” (Romans 3:24).

The only qualification. “To the thirsty.” Not the deserving, the improved, or those who worked it out. The single requirement for the water of life is wanting it, and the book makes the offer once more with the doors held open (22:17). Are you thirsty? Come and drink.

verseByVerse.quote: The one who conquers will have this heritage, and I will be his God and he will be my son. But as for the cowardly, the faithless, the detestable, as for murderers, the sexually immoral, sorcerers, idolaters, and all liars, their portion will be in the lake that burns with fire and sulfur, which is the second death."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one who conquers will inherit all this, and God will be his God and he God’s son; but the cowardly, faithless, detestable, murderers, sexually immoral, sorcerers, idolaters and all liars will have their place in the lake of fire, the second death. The final reward is adoption into God’s family, while those who persist in unbelief and evil — not struggling believers — face final judgment.

The eighth promise. Seven times in chapters 2–3 something was promised to the one who conquers: the tree of life, escape from the second death, hidden manna and a white stone, authority and the morning star, white garments and a name confessed, a pillar in the temple, a seat on the throne. Here is the eighth and final one, and it isn’t a thing at all.

A son. “I will be his God and he will be my son.” God said it of David’s heir: “I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son” (2 Samuel 7:14) — the promise that made the royal line, applied in the New Testament to Christ (Hebrews 1:5). Here it is handed, without qualification, to anyone who conquers — whom chapter 12 defined as anyone who holds to Christ at cost. So the final reward isn’t real estate. It is adoption. Everything else on the list — the tree, the crown, the stone, the throne — was describing what belongs to a son in his father’s house (cf. Romans 8:17). A test: do you think of heaven mainly as a place, or as being God’s child at home?

The cowardly first. Eight categories, and the first stops any honest reader: not murderers or idolaters, but the cowardly, in a book written to people with every reason to be afraid. Handle it carefully, or it lands on the wrong person. It doesn’t mean a Christian who is afraid. If fear disqualified, the list would include Elijah under a broom tree, Peter in a courtyard, and every apostle on the night of the arrest. Christ said “Fear not” to John in chapter 1 precisely because John was on his face and terrified. What it names here is the person whose fear made the decision — who denied the name, took the mark, said the words about Caesar and went home safe. The opposite of the endurance the book calls for. Cowardice here isn’t an emotion; it is apostasy carried out for safety.

If this frightens you. A believer frightened by v. 8 shows by that reaction that it isn’t describing him; the people on this list aren’t troubled by it. And the escape is written two verses earlier in the widest terms in the Bible: “To the thirsty I will give from the spring of the water of life without payment.” Peter denied Christ three times with oaths and was given breakfast on a beach and a commission.

Does “all liars” mean that any lie damns, so that a Christian who has lied is lost? No. The list describes the settled character of those who belong to the lie and reject the truth (22:15), not believers who have sinned and repented. Every believer has lied; “the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin” (1 John 1:7). The warning is for those who make falsehood their way of life, and a call to everyone to come to Christ.

The loop of lies closed. The dragon is the deceiver of the whole world; the second beast deceives by signs; Babylon deceived the nations by sorcery. And of the redeemed on Mount Zion: “in their mouth no lie was found” (14:5). Two companies, and one thing that finally separates them is whether they told the truth.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 9–11: one of the seven bowl angels — the same rank, and almost the same words, as 17:1 — says Come, I will show you the Bride, the wife of the Lamb, and carries John to a great high mountain (17:3 was a wilderness). He promised a Bride and shows a city: the people are the place. It has the glory of God, radiant like jasper, clear as crystal — the description of the one on the throne at 4:3.

Verses 12–14: twelve gates, three on each side, bearing the names of the twelve tribes (cf. Num. 2; Ezek. 48:30–35); twelve foundations bearing the names of the twelve apostles (cf. Eph. 2:19–20). Verses 15–17: the city is measured with a golden rod — 12,000 stadia, about fourteen hundred miles, its length and width and height are equal — and its wall 144 cubits, twelve times twelve.

Verses 18–21: a wall of jasper and a city of gold like clear glass; twelve foundation stones named one by one, most of them from the high priest’s breastpiece (Ex. 28:17–21); twelve gates each made of a single pearl; and a street of gold like transparent glass.

Verse 22: And I saw no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb. Verses 23–25: no need of sun or moon, for the glory of God is its light and its lamp is the Lamb (cf. Isa. 60:19); the nations walk by that light and the kings bring their glory in; the gates never shut, and there is no night. Verses 26–27: they will bring into it the glory and the honor of the nations — and nothing unclean, detestable or false enters, but only those who are written in the Lamb’s book of life.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Bride, the City

The Bride is shown as a city coming down from God, bearing the names of the twelve tribes and the twelve apostles. It is a cube — the Most Holy Place enlarged — with no temple, for its temple is God and the Lamb; no sun, for the Lamb is its lamp; gates that never shut; and only those written in the Lamb’s book inside.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: What the high priest carried over his heart once a year is now the city’s foundation, and every gate is a pearl.

Now: Nobody will be nearer to God than anybody else, and there will be no night.

verseByVerse.quote: Then came one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls full of the seven last plagues and spoke to me, saying, "Come, I will show you the Bride, the wife of the Lamb." And he carried me away in the Spirit to a great, high mountain, and showed me the holy city Jerusalem coming down out of heaven from God, having the glory of God, its radiance like a most rare jewel, like a jasper, clear as crystal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A bowl angel invites John to see the Bride, the wife of the Lamb, carries him to a high mountain, and shows him the holy city Jerusalem coming down from God, shining with God’s glory like a crystal-clear jewel. God’s people are themselves the city, made by God and not by human ambition, and they will shine with his glory and reflect his likeness.

The same rank, a different woman. John gives the angel’s job description at length — “one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls” — so the reader makes the connection. At 17:1 the same rank said, “Come, I will show you the judgment of the great prostitute.” Same opening word, different woman.

Desert and mountain. To see the prostitute John was carried into a wilderness (17:3). To see the Bride, to “a great, high mountain,” where Ezekiel was taken to be shown a city (Ezekiel 40:2). One woman is seen in a desert; the other from a height.

The people are the place. He promised a Bride and showed a city, and John doesn’t treat that as a change of subject. The New Testament makes the same identification everywhere — the church is a building, a temple, a body, a household, a bride — which is why the measurements that follow can be enormous without being absurd.

Lowered into place. “Coming down out of heaven from God,” for the second time in nine verses. Not built up from the earth. Babylon began at a tower whose builders said, “let us build ourselves a city… and let us make a name for ourselves” (Genesis 11:4). Every human city since has been that project. This one is lowered into place, finished, by Someone else. A test: are you building your own name, or receiving the city God gives?

The glory as lighting. The first thing said isn’t its size or gates but that it has “the glory of God” — the weight of his presence that filled the tabernacle so Moses couldn’t enter and the temple so the priests couldn’t stand. What once had to be curtained off is now the city’s ordinary lighting.

She looks like him. “Like a jasper, clear as crystal” is how John described the One on the throne (4:3). The city looks like him. A bride wearing her husband’s likeness is not a bad definition of what the church is finally for — what Paul meant by being “transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another” (2 Corinthians 3:18).

verseByVerse.quote: It had a great, high wall, with twelve gates, and at the gates twelve angels, and on the gates the names of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel were inscribed— on the east three gates, on the north three gates, on the south three gates, and on the west three gates. And the wall of the city had twelve foundations, and on them were the twelve names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The city has a great high wall with twelve gates guarded by angels, named for Israel’s twelve tribes and facing all four directions, and twelve foundations bearing the names of the Lamb’s twelve apostles. God’s one people, Israel and the church together, live in a city that is secure from all spoiling and open to people from every direction.

Why a wall? Named first, and the strangest thing here. An ancient wall had one purpose: to keep an army out. This city has none to fear; the last enemy went into the lake a chapter ago (20:10, 14), and the gates are never shut anyway (v. 25). So what is a wall doing in the new creation? Not fear. A wall says this place has an inside, and v. 27 states the boundary: nothing unclean will ever enter. Measure that against everything you have loved. Every good thing you have known could be got at — the marriage, the friendship, the church, the health, a lifetime’s work; something always found a way in and spoiled it, usually from inside. Here at last is a good thing with a boundary that holds. The wall isn’t the anxiety of a besieged city but the settled fact of a city that will never be spoiled again.

Angels at open gates. The first time angels are posted in the Bible, they stand outside a garden with a flaming sword, keeping people out (Genesis 3:24). Here twelve stand at twelve gates that never close. The sentries are still at their stations, and there is nothing left for them to do but watch the nations walk in.

From every direction. Three gates on each side is the layout of Israel’s wilderness camp, three tribes on each side of the tabernacle (Numbers 2), and the plan of Ezekiel’s city with twelve gates named for the tribes (Ezekiel 48:30–35). A city with gates on one side has a preferred approach and a back. This one can be entered from anywhere — east where the exile went, north where the invasions came, south where Egypt was, west where Rome was. No one arrives at the wrong side. A test: do you think anyone is too far off, or came from the wrong direction, to enter?

Gates and foundations. Twelve tribes on the gates, twelve apostles in the foundations: Israel and the church built into one structure, neither bolted onto the other. Paul said it without the architecture: “the household of God, built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone” (Ephesians 2:19–20).

Names in the stonework. Every reader knows what those twelve were like: fishermen, a tax collector, a zealot, a man who denied Christ with oaths, a man who wouldn’t believe the resurrection without putting his hand in the wound. Their names are cut into the foundations of the new creation. Babylon’s great ones were her merchants (18:23). This city’s great ones are twelve provincial nobodies, many of whom died for saying a crucified man had come back.

verseByVerse.quote: And the one who spoke with me had a measuring rod of gold to measure the city and its gates and walls. The city lies foursquare, its length the same as its width. And he measured the city with his rod, 12,000 stadia. Its length and width and height are equal. He also measured its wall, 144 cubits by human measurement, which is also an angel's measurement.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel measures the city with a golden rod: a perfect cube, twelve thousand stadia in length, width and height, with a wall of 144 cubits. The whole city is God’s claimed and protected possession, with room for all his people, and it is the Most Holy Place expanded — all of God’s people living in his immediate presence.

Measured in full. Measuring in this book means claiming and protecting. At 11:1 John measured the temple and worshippers but not the outer court, which was trampled — a partial measuring, and a mercy. This one is total: city, gates and walls, with a rod of gold.

Room for all. Twelve thousand stadia is about 1,380 miles — roughly Jerusalem to Rome — in every direction, including up. No one is meant to picture it successfully. The figure answers a fear few Christians admit: whether there will be room. Twelve, the number of God’s people, times a thousand.

A cube. “Its length and width and height are equal.” The detail the chapter has been building to. There is exactly one cube in the Bible: the Most Holy Place in Solomon’s temple, twenty cubits long, wide and high (1 Kings 6:20). Where the ark stood behind the veil, which one man entered once a year with blood, having washed, and didn’t linger. The new Jerusalem is that room, expanded to the size of a continent, with everyone living inside it. That is the most important fact about the city, and it explains v. 22 in advance: no temple, because the city is the temple; no veil, because nothing is left to keep anyone out. A test: do you approach God as if the veil were still there? In Christ, you may come all the way in — now, in prayer.

The wall. 144 cubits, about 216 feet — twelve times twelve, the number of the 144,000. And “by human measurement, which is also an angel’s” tells the reader the figures aren’t in some other currency that would come out differently in heaven.

Deliberately impossible. A wall of 216 feet around a city 1,380 miles high wouldn’t keep anything out and couldn’t be seen from most of the city. That is the point: it isn’t for defence. Nothing is left to defend against. It is a boundary marking what is inside as holy, and its gates never close.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes give 12,000 stadia as about 1,380 miles; 144 cubits is about 216 feet. The city is a perfect cube, like the Most Holy Place in Solomon’s temple.

verseByVerse.quote: The wall was built of jasper, while the city was pure gold, like clear glass. The foundations of the wall of the city were adorned with every kind of jewel. The first was jasper, the second sapphire, the third agate, the fourth emerald, the fifth onyx, the sixth carnelian, the seventh chrysolite, the eighth beryl, the ninth topaz, the tenth chrysoprase, the eleventh jacinth, the twelfth amethyst. And the twelve gates were twelve pearls, each of the gates made of a single pearl, and the street of the city was pure gold, like transparent glass.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wall is jasper, the city pure gold like clear glass, the foundations adorned with twelve precious stones, each gate a single pearl, and the street transparent gold. The city reflects the beauty of God and carries his people as the high priest carried their names, and the things the world killed for become mere paving.

Gold you can see through. “Pure gold, like clear glass” — no material anyone has handled, and the street is the same (v. 21). The city’s most precious substance has stopped being opaque. Nothing in it casts a shadow or hides what is behind it.

Walking along a wall naming colours. Twelve stones, listed one by one with positions numbered, over a verse and a half. The slowness is the effect: a man walking along a wall naming colours.

The high priest’s breastpiece. The list has an address. Israel’s high priest wore a breastpiece of twelve stones, one for each tribe (Exodus 28:17–21), bearing their names “on his heart, when he goes into the Holy Place, to bring them to regular remembrance before the LORD” (Exodus 28:29). Most of John’s stones are on that list; several names differ only because the Greek Old Testament rendered them differently. So the city’s foundations are the breastpiece laid flat and built into the ground. What one man carried over his heart into the holy place is now the foundation everyone walks on. And jasper and carnelian are the two colours of the One on the throne (4:3). A test: do you know that Christ carries your name on his heart before the Father now?

Gates of pearl. A pearl is the one precious thing in the ancient world not mined or cut. An oyster makes it slowly, in response to an injury — a grain of grit it can’t expel, covered layer by layer for years until the wound is the treasure. Jesus told of a merchant who found one pearl of great value and sold everything to buy it (Matthew 13:45–46). The gate into the eternal city is that pearl, twelve times over, each a single stone — each one took a very long time and began with a wound.

Gold underfoot. The most valuable substance the ancient world knew, used for the surface people walk on. Babylon’s manifest began with gold, silver, jewels and pearls (18:12), and merchants wept when they couldn’t sell them. Here the same materials are paving. That isn’t to say wealth is unimportant but to set it in proportion. Everything the world killed for turns out, in the only city that lasts, to be surfacing — and someone who has spent a lifetime arranging his affairs around such things is shown what they are for. What are you arranging your life around?
verseByVerse.note: The twelve jewels recall the stones on the high priest’s breastpiece, engraved with the names of the tribes.

verseByVerse.quote: And I saw no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John sees no temple in the city, because its temple is the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb. The need for a special holy place, priests and barriers ends forever, because through the Lamb God’s people live directly in his presence.

The end of religion’s history. One sentence that overturns the religious history of the world. Every civilisation has built temples, and each answers the same problem: God is holy and people are not, so there must be a designated place, a mediating class, rules for approach, and a barrier between God and worshipper. Israel’s was the most carefully regulated: a court for the nations, beyond it a court for Israel, beyond that for men, beyond that for priests, and behind a curtain a room one man entered once a year with blood in his hands.

No temple. Ezekiel spent nine chapters on a temple (Ezekiel 40–48). The Jews of John’s day had watched theirs burn twenty-five years before and expected another. And John looks at the city of God and reports no temple in it.

The problem solved. Not because worship has ended, but because the arrangement a temple manages has ended. The problem a temple solves — how sinful people can be near a holy God without being destroyed — has been solved by Someone, and the verse names him: “its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb.”

Because there is a Lamb. When Jesus died, “the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom” (Matthew 27:51) — from the top, by Someone reaching down — and this verse is that tearing carried to its conclusion. He isn’t merely the priest or the sacrifice. He is the building (cf. John 2:19–21).

Everyone in the holy of holies. That is why the city is a cube. The Most Holy Place was the one room where God’s presence was unveiled, and the whole city is now that room. No outer court, no restricted section, no nearer and further; no one is closer to God than anyone else, and no one waits outside for a priest to come back and say it went well.

The end of distance. For every Christian who has felt that God is available only in certain places and times, that some people have better access, that the holy is somewhere he visits rather than lives — this verse ends it. The final state of the redeemed isn’t going to a holy place but living in one, with its Maker in the middle. A test: do you live as if access to God belongs to special people or places? Through the Lamb it is yours — use it today (cf. John 4:21–24).

verseByVerse.quote: And the city has no need of sun or moon to shine on it, for the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb. By its light will the nations walk, and the kings of the earth will bring their glory into it, and its gates will never be shut by day—and there will be no night there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The city needs no sun or moon, for God’s glory lights it and the Lamb is its lamp; the nations walk by its light, the kings bring their glory in, and its gates never shut, for there is no night. God himself will be his people’s light, what is truly good in human life will be gathered in, and every fear that comes with darkness will be gone.

No need of the sun. Genesis gives two great lights on the fourth day, and Isaiah promised: “The sun shall be no more your light by day, nor for brightness shall the moon give you light; but the LORD will be your everlasting light” (Isaiah 60:19). They aren’t destroyed; there is no need of them. A lamp isn’t a criticism of the sun; it is simply irrelevant at noon. The sun and moon have done a job on loan for all of history, and the owner has arrived.

The Lamb is the lamp. The word is a household lamp, the small clay dish that lit a room after dark. God’s glory is the city’s light, and the Lamb carries it — what he has been since chapter 1, “his face… like the sun shining in full strength” (1:16), and what he said: “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12).

The nations come. Isaiah 60 again: “nations shall come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your rising” (Isaiah 60:3); “the wealth of the nations shall come to you” (Isaiah 60:5). Startling in a book that spent nineteen chapters on kings committing immorality with a prostitute and warring on the Lamb. Those kings are dead; these aren’t the same men. This isn’t an amnesty for Babylon but the redemption of the nations as nations.

Their glory carried in. What is their glory? The text doesn’t say, and guessing is a poor substitute for reading. But the phrase implies that what the peoples of the earth have made and been isn’t simply erased. Something is carried in. That is a real word to anyone who wonders whether ordinary human work has any future — whether music, building, crops, children, languages and cities are all going into a fire. The gates are open, and something is brought in through them. A test: do you do your daily work as something that may count before God, or as merely passing time?

No night. Every walled city closed its gates at sundown; after dark, whatever was outside stayed outside, and whoever hadn’t got home wasn’t getting home. This city’s gates never shut, and John adds why: “there will be no night there.” The gates stay open because the hour of shutting never comes.

What is taken away. Anyone who has lain awake at three in the morning knows. Night in Scripture isn’t simply darkness: it is when the thief comes, the enemy moves, a person is alone with what he has done, the sick get worse and the frightened more frightened. None of it, ever again; the gates are open at what would have been midnight. Bring your night fears to him now, who will one day end them.

verseByVerse.quote: They will bring into it the glory and the honor of the nations. But nothing unclean will ever enter it, nor anyone who does what is detestable or false, but only those who are written in the Lamb's book of life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The glory and honour of the nations will be brought into the city, but nothing unclean, detestable or false will ever enter — only those written in the Lamb’s book of life. The city is open to the best of every people, yet only those made clean by belonging to the Lamb will be there.

Each guards the other. Verse 26 is the widest sentence in the chapter: the glory and honour of the nations — not of one nation, nor of the church only. Whatever is genuinely glorious in what people have made and become, from every people, is carried through those gates. The multitude of chapter 7 came “from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages,” and they don’t arrive empty-handed. Verse 27 at once shuts the door on sentimentality: “nothing unclean will ever enter.” The gates are always open, and not unguarded. This isn’t a city where everything is welcome, but where everything welcome has been made clean.

Three exclusions. Not a list of the worst crimes. “Unclean” is the ceremonial word: what couldn’t enter the sanctuary. “Detestable” is the Old Testament’s word for idolatry, written on the prostitute’s forehead (17:5). “False” closes the loop a last time: the dragon deceived, the false prophet deceived, Babylon deceived, and the redeemed are those “in their mouth no lie was found” (14:5).

Not a moral audit. Look how the sentence ends: “but only those who are written in the Lamb’s book of life.” The last mention of the book in Revelation lands where it did at the great white throne — not on what a person achieved but whether his name is in a register belonging to the Lamb who was slain, written from the foundation of the world (13:8; 17:8; 20:12, 15).

How the unclean become clean. So the two halves aren’t in tension. Nothing unclean enters — and the whole book has shown how the unclean become clean, in its most impossible image: “they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (7:14). No one walks in on his own record. Everyone who walks in has had something done to him first. A test: are you counting on your record to get through those gates, or on being washed?

The chapter in one view. A city fourteen hundred miles high, made of the Most Holy Place, with God’s glory for daylight and the Lamb for a lamp, its foundations set with the stones a high priest wore over his heart, its gates each a single pearl that began as a wound — and the gates never close, and those inside are the ones whose names were written before the world was made. God himself is with them. No temple, because he is there. No sun, because he is there. No night, because he is there. And no tears, because he has attended to their faces with his own hand.

22.title: Come, Lord Jesus: The River, the Tree, and the Final Invitation
22.overview:
The final chapter of Revelation — and of the entire Bible — has the quality of a great symphony resolving into its final chord. Everything that has been promised, everything that has been anticipated, every thread of the biblical story, gathers here and arrives. The river of the water of life. The tree of life with twelve kinds of fruit. The servants of God seeing his face. His name on their foreheads. No more night. And then, three times: ‘I am coming soon.’ And the great response of the church across all the ages: ‘Come, Lord Jesus.’

The chapter is framed by the river and tree (vv. 1–5) and the final testimony and invitation (vv. 6–21). The garden returns — but infinitely elevated. Eden had a river flowing from it (Genesis 2:10); the new Jerusalem has a river flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb. Eden had the tree of life (Genesis 2:9); the new Jerusalem has the tree of life bearing twelve kinds of fruit, one each month, its leaves for the healing of the nations. What was lost in the garden is restored in the city, but the city is greater than the garden: the tree is no longer guarded by cherubim with flaming swords (Genesis 3:24) — it stands in the middle of the street, its fruit available to all.

The closing testimony of the book weaves together three voices: the angel confirming the truth of what has been shown, Jesus speaking in the first person (‘I, Jesus, have sent my angel...’; ‘I am coming soon’), and the Spirit and Bride together issuing the great invitation: ‘Come.’ The book ends not with explanation but with longing — the longing of the church for her Lord, the longing of the Lord for his people, the longing of the Spirit for the consummation of all things. This is the last word of the Bible, and it is the word the whole church has been praying for two thousand years: Come.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The River and the Tree of Life
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2: the river of the water of life, bright as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb down the middle of the street; and on either side of it the tree of life, bearing twelve crops a year, and the leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations (cf. Ezek. 47:1–12). The Bible has been away from a river and a tree since Genesis 3, where cherubim with a flaming sword were set to guard the way to the tree of life (Gen. 2:9–10; 3:24). The promise made to Ephesus in the first letter (2:7) is being kept.

Verse 3: No longer will there be anything accursed — the sentence of Genesis 3:17–19 lifted — but the throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it, and his servants will worship him. Verse 4: They will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads. Verse 5: no night, no need of lamp or sun, for the Lord God will be their light, and they will reign forever and ever.
verseByVerse.theology:
The River and the Tree

The river of life flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb, and the tree of life stands open with fruit every month and leaves for the healing of the nations. The curse is gone, and his servants will see his face.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The way to the tree, guarded since Eden, stands open in the middle of the street.

Now: Heaven is not first a place but a face — seen at last, and lived through.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the angel showed me the river of the water of life, bright as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb through the middle of the street of the city; also, on either side of the river, the tree of life with its twelve kinds of fruit, yielding its fruit each month. The leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel shows John the river of the water of life flowing from the throne of God and the Lamb down the city’s street, with the tree of life on both sides, bearing fruit every month, its leaves for the healing of the nations. What was lost in Eden is restored and surpassed: unending life flows from God and the Lamb, and the divided nations are tended and made whole.

A river and a tree. Genesis 2 has a river flowing out of Eden and “the tree of life… in the midst of the garden” (Genesis 2:9–10). Genesis 3 ends with the man and woman put out and cherubim “to guard the way to the tree of life” (Genesis 3:24). From that verse to this one, nobody eats from it. The whole of Scripture happens between a tree being fenced off and a tree being handed back.

A promise kept. Ephesus was told, “To the one who conquers I will grant to eat of the tree of life, which is in the paradise of God” (2:7). Here is the tree.

Better than Eden. This isn’t simply Eden reopened. Eden was a garden; this is a garden inside a city, the river running down the middle of the street. Eden had one tree of life; here it stands “on either side of the river” — impossible to draw, easy to understand: wherever you walk, it is on both sides of you. Eden could be lost; this can’t. God doesn’t restore his people to where they started. He takes them somewhere better, and the road ran through a cross.

From the throne. “Flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb” — one throne, two names, no explanation. And what flows from it isn’t judgment but water. Ezekiel saw it: water trickling from under the temple threshold, deepening into a river no one could cross, with trees on both banks whose leaves wouldn’t wither (Ezekiel 47:1–12).

No off season. “Yielding its fruit each month.” Anyone who grows things knows fruit trees rest; there are months with nothing on them. This one doesn’t stop. The life of the city is continually supplied, not merely started.

Healing of the nations. A puzzle, rightly: there is no sickness here, and pain has just been abolished. Ezekiel is the source: “Their fruit will be for food, and their leaves for healing” (Ezekiel 47:12). The word can mean care and tending as much as cure. The most natural sense isn’t that anyone is ill but that the nations are kept well. And “nations” has been a hostile word all book — they raged, drank Babylon’s wine, served the beast. Here they are the ones tended. The long wound of human history — peoples divided at a tower and at each other’s throats ever since — has leaves growing for it. A test: whose people do you find it hardest to love? God is growing leaves for them; pray for them now.
verseByVerse.note: Eden’s river and tree of life return, now in a city.

verseByVerse.quote: No longer will there be anything accursed, but the throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it, and his servants will worship him. They will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads. And night will be no more. They will need no light of lamp or sun, for the Lord God will be their light, and they will reign forever and ever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nothing accursed will remain; God’s throne and the Lamb’s will be in the city; his servants will worship him, see his face, bear his name, live in his light without night, and reign forever. The curse of Genesis is lifted through Christ, and the heart of heaven is this: God’s people will see his face.

The curse lifted. “No longer will there be anything accursed” reaches back to the third chapter of the Bible: “cursed is the ground because of you; in pain you shall eat of it all the days of your life; thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you… till you return to the ground” (Genesis 3:17–19). Everything hard about human life — exhausting labour, resisting ground, failing body — has stood under that sentence. And it is lifted — not managed or explained but removed, because Christ redeemed us “by becoming a curse for us—for it is written, ‘Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree’” (Galatians 3:13). Two trees end this book. On one the curse was absorbed; from the other the fruit is handed out twelve times a year.

The throne in the city. The fixed point of the vision since chapter 4 has always been in heaven. Now it is “in it” — in the city, on the renewed earth, at the end of the street with the river running from it.

They will see his face. Five words, and nothing in Scripture is bigger. Moses, who spoke with God as a friend, asked for exactly this and was told, “you cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live” (Exodus 33:20); he was put in a cleft of the rock and shown God’s back. The high priest went behind the veil once a year and saw nothing. Isaiah saw the train of a robe and cried that he was lost. In chapter 6 kings begged mountains to hide them “from the face of him who is seated on the throne” (6:16). And here, without ceremony: they will see his face. Ordinary people — a slave from Laodicea, a widow from Thyatira, a man who once denied Christ in a courtyard — looking at God, and living.

What heaven is. John wrote the same promise in a letter and admitted he couldn’t fill it in: “Beloved, we are God’s children now, and what we will be has not yet appeared; but we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). Jesus: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8). That is what heaven is. Not a location with good weather; not a reunion, though there will be one; not the end of trouble, though trouble ends. It is a face. The gold, jewels, river and open gates are furniture in a room where that is happening. A test: is seeing God the thing you most long for? Ask him to make it so — and seek his face in prayer today.

His name on their foreheads. The last marked foreheads in the book, and the counterfeit is gone. The seal of 7:3, the Lamb’s name at 14:1, the beast’s mark at 13:16 all led here: everyone is labelled, and these are labelled with him.

Light and reign. No night, no need of lamp or sun, “for the Lord God will be their light” — said twice in eight verses (21:23–25), John’s underlining. And the last word is “reign”: the promise to Laodicea, the weakest church on the road, arriving in full.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 6–7: the vision is over and the book begins closing itself by matching its own opening — the Lord, the God of the spirits of the prophets, has sent his angel to show his servants what must soon take place (cf. 1:1). Then the speaker changes without warning: And behold, I am coming soon. Blessed is the one who keeps the words of the prophecy of this book — the sixth beatitude, almost word for word the first one at 1:3.

Verses 8–9: John falls down to worship the angel a second time and is stopped a second time, in almost the words of 19:10 — I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers the prophets, and with those who keep the words of this book. Worship God.

Verses 10–11: Do not seal up the words of the prophecy of this book, for the time is near — the exact reverse of what Daniel was told (Dan. 12:4, 9) — followed by the hardest verse in the chapter: Let the evildoer still do evil… and the holy still be holy.

Verses 12–13: the second I am coming soon, bringing my recompense with me, to repay each one for what he has done (cf. Isa. 40:10), and three pairs of titles: Alpha and Omega, first and last, beginning and end. Verses 14–15: the seventh and last beatitude — Blessed are those who wash their robes — and the list of those outside, ending with everyone who loves and practices falsehood. Verse 16: I, Jesus, have sent my angel… I am the root and the descendant of David, the bright morning star.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Testimony of Jesus

The book closes as it opened: blessed is the one who keeps its words. The angel refuses John’s worship again — Worship God. The book is left unsealed, for the time is near. Jesus, the Alpha and Omega, root and descendant of David, the bright morning star, is coming soon; blessed are those who wash their robes.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The whole vision was given for the churches, to be read aloud in small rooms.

Now: While the door is open, ask which way your life is already heading.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to me, "These words are trustworthy and true. And the Lord, the God of the spirits of the prophets, has sent his angel to show his servants what must soon take place." "And behold, I am coming soon. Blessed is the one who keeps the words of the prophecy of this book."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel affirms that these words are trustworthy and true, sent by the God of the prophets to show his servants what must soon take place; and Christ declares, “I am coming soon. Blessed is the one who keeps the words of the prophecy of this book.” Revelation is God’s reliable word, completing the prophets, and its blessing rests on those who obey it, not those who merely decode it.

Matching the letterhead. The vision is over; the book now closes itself by returning to its first sentence: “The revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to show to his servants the things that must soon take place” (1:1), made known by his angel to his servant John. Same chain of custody, same phrase, same servants.

The God of the prophets. “The God of the spirits of the prophets” says that the God who spoke through Isaiah, Ezekiel and Daniel — quoted on nearly every page — has spoken here. Revelation isn’t a new departure but the last chapter of a document in progress for fifteen centuries.

“I am coming soon.” The speaker changes without warning: the angel has been talking, and suddenly it is Christ. He says it three times in this chapter (vv. 7, 12, 20), the drumbeat the book ends on.

Soon, after two thousand years? The difficulty is the same as at 1:1 and deserves the same honest answer: the word concerns speed and certainty, not the calendar; the New Testament dates nearness from the cross; and much of what this book describes arrived within its first readers’ lifetimes. And Peter answered this very objection while it was fresh: “with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day. The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you” (2 Peter 3:8–9). The delay isn’t indifference. It is mercy, and someone is being brought in during it.

Keep it. The sixth of the seven blessings, almost word for word the first (1:3). The book opens and closes with a blessing on the same person — not the one who understands it, charts it or identifies the beast, but the one who keeps it. A test: what has Revelation told you to do — endure, hold fast, refuse compromise, worship, come out of Babylon? Pick one and keep it this week.

verseByVerse.quote: I, John, am the one who heard and saw these things. And when I heard and saw them, I fell down to worship at the feet of the angel who showed them to me, but he said to me, "You must not do that! I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers the prophets, and with those who keep the words of this book. Worship God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
John falls down to worship the angel who showed him these things and is stopped again: “You must not do that! I am a fellow servant… Worship God.” Even an apostle overwhelmed by glory can misdirect his worship; the whole book comes down to this command — worship God alone.

Again. He did it at 19:10 and was stopped in nearly these words; here at the very end, with the correction in his own manuscript three chapters back, he goes down a second time. Not flattering to John, and he wrote it down anyway — itself a kind of testimony. He isn’t presenting himself as a man who learned his lesson. That is a comfort to anyone who has repeated a fault he had already repented of: the last recorded act of the apostle who wrote this book is a mistake he had made before. Repent again, and get up.

Undone by beauty. Not at the dragon, beast or lake of fire, but right after the river, the tree and the face. Beauty undoes him. The instinct is right; only the direction is wrong — a man overwhelmed by glory reaches for the nearest thing holding it.

Worship God. Among the shortest complete instructions in Scripture. Twenty-two chapters of visions, and this is the summary.

Alongside the reader. The angel’s self-description is longer than at 19:10: a fellow servant with John, with the prophets, and — new — “with those who keep the words of this book.” That last group is the reader. An angel of God puts himself in the same category as an ordinary Christian who reads Revelation and does what it says.

A permanent danger. Given twice for emphasis. Those through whom God speaks — preachers, writers, movements, teachers — are always at risk of receiving what belongs to God, and most when what they bring is genuinely glorious. The remedy isn’t to think less of the messenger. It is two words. A test: is there someone whose voice you trust more than God’s word? Thank God for them — and worship him.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to me, "Do not seal up the words of the prophecy of this book, for the time is near. Let the evildoer still do evil, and the filthy still be filthy, and the righteous still do right, and the holy still be holy."
verseByVerse.commentary:
John is told not to seal the prophecy, for the time is near; and “let the evildoer still do evil… and the holy still be holy.” Revelation is an open book meant to be read and obeyed now, and there comes a point when a person’s chosen direction becomes permanent — so the time to turn is today.

Unsealed. The reverse of Daniel, who was told to “shut up the words and seal the book, until the time of the end” (Daniel 12:4). John is told to leave it open, because for Daniel the time was far off and for John it is near. And the reverse of 10:4, when John was told, “Seal up what the seven thunders have said.” There is one sealed sentence in Revelation, and we don’t have it. Everything else is open on purpose. So the book isn’t a locked document awaiting a key, and never was. Its blessing falls on the one who keeps it, not the one who cracks it.

The hardest verse. “Let the evildoer still do evil, and the filthy still be filthy, and the righteous still do right, and the holy still be holy.” Read carelessly it sounds like God shrugging — a permission slip for wickedness and a fatalistic verdict that no one changes. Three things settle it.

Its position. It sits between “the time is near” and “I am coming soon” — bracketed by urgency, the opposite of fatalism. Ezekiel was given a similar word when Israel had stopped listening (Ezekiel 3:27), and Daniel too (Daniel 12:10).

Its form. A prophetic announcement, not a divine permission: a moment comes after which character is fixed, when a person’s direction of travel becomes his destination. Everyone knows this of habits within a lifetime; the verse says it is finally true of lives.

What it does to the reader. It isn’t an instruction to the evildoer. It is set before someone holding a book that is nearly finished, and it asks: which of those four describes the direction you are already going? The door is open now, and the invitation is six verses away — “let the one who desires take the water of life without price” — but it won’t be open forever. Read so, v. 11 isn’t God abandoning anyone. It is the most serious way of saying “today.” A reader frightened by it is frightened in exactly the direction it intends, while there is still time to move. Which direction are you facing? Turn now if you must.
verseByVerse.note: Daniel was told to seal his book until the end; John is told not to, because the time is near.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, I am coming soon, bringing my recompense with me, to repay each one for what he has done. I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ says he is coming soon, bringing his reward to repay each person for what they have done, and declares himself the Alpha and Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end. Christ, who is fully God, will come with his reward in hand, and every faithful deed his grace produced will be remembered.

Reward in hand. The second of three announcements, with the reward already in his hand: “bringing my recompense with me” — not sent for afterwards or calculated on arrival. Isaiah said it of God’s coming: “behold, his reward is with him, and his recompense before him” (Isaiah 40:10; cf. 62:11).

Each one. “To repay each one for what he has done.” Raised at Thyatira (2:23) and the great white throne (20:12), and the answer hasn’t moved. A record has never admitted anyone, and never failed to identify anyone. It is the evidence of whose a person is and the measure of what is handed him afterwards. And “each one”: nothing is averaged. The visits no one recorded, the giving that hurt, the cup of cold water — each, by name.

Nothing to bring? A fear keeps quiet Christians awake. Someone converted at sixty, or a woman ill in a back bedroom for twenty years, reads “repay each one for what he has done” and thinks there is nothing of theirs to bring. Two things answer. First, what is repaid isn’t what you achieved but what Christ produced in you, and he doesn’t fail to produce — the vine bears the fruit; the branch carries it (John 15:5). Second, Christ told a parable about exactly this: the workers hired at the eleventh hour were paid the same as those who bore the heat of the day, and the owner wronged no one (Matthew 20:1–16). No one will stand there feeling short-changed, and no one thinking he earned what he holds. A test: is your service to Christ driven by fear of having too little, or by love for the One who gives the reward?

Three pairs. “Alpha and Omega” was said by God at 1:8 and 21:6. “The first and the last” was said by the risen Christ at 1:17, and it is Isaiah’s exclusive divine self-description: “I am the first and I am the last; besides me there is no god” (Isaiah 44:6). “The beginning and the end” completes it. The titles move between Father and Son without a seam, and that isn’t carelessness. Revelation never argues for Christ’s deity; it speaks as though the question couldn’t arise. The One coming soon with his reward was there before history’s first letter and will be there after its last.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are those who wash their robes, so that they may have the right to the tree of life and that they may enter the city by the gates. Outside are the dogs and sorcerers and the sexually immoral and murderers and idolaters, and everyone who loves and practices falsehood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed are those who wash their robes, for they have the right to the tree of life and may enter the city by its gates; outside are the dogs, sorcerers, sexually immoral, murderers, idolaters, and all who love and practise falsehood. Entry into God’s city comes by being washed in Christ’s blood, and those who cling to sin and love lies remain shut out.

The last blessing. The seventh and last, landing on the one act the whole book describes. Not those who understood it, nor those who suffered, though many did. “Blessed are those who wash their robes” — and 7:14 said in what: “they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.”

A manuscript detail. The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “those who do his commandments” (the King James reading). In Greek the two are startlingly close — hoi poiountes tas entolas autou against hoi plunontes tas stolas autōn — and a tired copyist could slip from one to the other. The earliest and best manuscripts read “wash their robes,” which the ESV follows and the imagery of the book requires. It matters more than most footnotes, because one makes entry depend on obedience and the other on being washed; the manuscripts favour the second, and so does every page from chapter 5 on.

What was lost, given back. “The right to the tree of life” — guarded by a flaming sword since Genesis 3:24, now theirs by right, not trespass. “That they may enter the city by the gates” — a strangely ordinary phrase after everything: not carried in or admitted by a side door, but walking through the front gates like a citizen coming home. A test: are you washed? If you are, walk in as a citizen, not a trespasser — with confidence in prayer today.

Dogs. Not a term of affection: scavengers in the street, a word the law used for what was excluded from the sanctuary (Deuteronomy 23:18), and Paul for those who added requirements to the gospel (Philippians 3:2).

Where is “outside”? Not a place beside the city where the lost live on in sight of it. It is the lake of fire, the second death (20:15; 21:8, 27), described in the language of a city wall: those who won’t enter are shut out.

Loving falsehood. The list ends as every such list in this book ends: “everyone who loves and practices falsehood.” Not merely tells lies — loves them. The dragon is the deceiver of the whole world (12:9), and of the redeemed: “in their mouth no lie was found” (14:5). At the very end, the line between the two companies runs through whether a person loved the truth.
verseByVerse.note: The last of the seven “blessed” sayings in Revelation. Some manuscripts read “do his commandments” for “wash their robes” (ESV note) — the reading of the King James Version.

verseByVerse.quote: "I, Jesus, have sent my angel to testify to you about these things for the churches. I am the root and the descendant of David, the bright morning star."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus himself declares that he has sent his angel to testify these things for the churches, and that he is the root and descendant of David, the bright morning star. The whole book is the personal word of the human and divine Jesus to ordinary churches, and he himself is the dawn that ends the night.

“I, Jesus.” The name at last — the only place he says it in the book, after twenty-one chapters of titles: the Lamb, the faithful witness, the first and the last, the Word of God, King of kings. At the end he uses the name his mother used, the human name of a carpenter’s son from a village.

For the churches. Not for scholars, a final generation, or the curious. This enormous vision — thrones, dragons, bowls, a city fourteen hundred miles high — was produced for congregations, to be read aloud in rooms. The book ends where it began (1:11), with seven small assemblies on a postal road in Asia. A test: do you read Revelation as a puzzle about others, or as Christ’s letter to your church?

Root and descendant. Both at once, deliberately impossible. To be David’s descendant is to come after him — the promised son of the royal line, born in David’s town. To be David’s root is to be what David grew from; a root isn’t produced by the tree, it produces the tree. Jesus set that riddle himself in the temple, and no one answered it: “David himself calls him Lord. So how is he his son?” (Mark 12:37). This verse is the answer, from the One who asked: David’s son by birth and David’s Lord by nature, one person.

The bright morning star. A promise made twenty chapters ago is identified. Thyatira — the church in the least important town on the road, told only to hold on until he came — was promised “the morning star” (2:28), never explained. It is himself. Behind it stands Balaam’s prophecy, of all people: “a star shall come out of Jacob, and a scepter shall rise out of Israel” (Numbers 24:17).

The last star before dawn. The morning star rises last, when the sky is darkest and the night has gone on longest. It doesn’t announce more night; it means the sun is on its way. That is what this book has said to frightened congregations from its first page. It never promises the dark will be short. It promises who is standing in it. Whatever night you are in, look for him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 17: The Spirit and the Bride say, “Come.” And let the one who hears say, “Come.” And let the one who is thirsty come; let the one who desires take the water of life without price (cf. Isa. 55:1; John 4:14; 7:37). Verses 18–19: the covenant scribe’s closing warning against adding to or taking from the words of the prophecy (cf. Deut. 4:2; 12:32; Prov. 30:5–6), with penalties that fit the offences exactly.

Verse 20: He who testifies to these things says, “Surely I am coming soon.” — the last recorded words of Jesus Christ in the Bible — and the church’s answer, Amen. Come, Lord Jesus! Verse 21: The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all. Amen.
verseByVerse.theology:
Come

The Spirit and the Bride say, “Come”; whoever hears is to say it too; whoever is thirsty may take the water of life without price. The book is not to be added to or taken from. Jesus says, “Surely I am coming soon,” and the church answers, “Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!”
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The earliest church prayed Marana tha — Our Lord, come.

Now: The most terrifying book in Scripture ends with grace, offered to all.

verseByVerse.quote: The Spirit and the Bride say, "Come." And let the one who hears say, "Come." And let the one who is thirsty come; let the one who desires take the water of life without price.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit and the Bride say “Come,” and everyone who hears is to say “Come”; let the thirsty come, and whoever desires take the water of life freely. At the end of the Bible’s most frightening book stands its widest invitation: the free gift of eternal life to anyone who wants it, proclaimed by the Spirit through the church.

The last invitation. After the dragon, the beast, the lake of fire and the great white throne, the second-to-last thing God says to the human race is: come and have a drink. The sentence is built like a chain; take it in order.

The Spirit and the Bride. The Holy Spirit and the church speaking together, one verb between them. That is the church’s whole mission in five words, and it settles the relationship: the church doesn’t invite on its own authority, and the Spirit doesn’t work around the church.

The hearer says it too. The invitation is handed on. Whoever has heard it becomes one of those saying it — no interval, no qualification, not the mature or the trained. The one who has just heard is immediately in the chorus. A test: who will you say “Come” to this week? Name them, and invite them.

The thirsty come. Now the direction reverses: the first clauses are the church calling out; this one is someone walking in. The only qualification in the whole verse is thirst — not worthiness, understanding or improvement. Wanting it is the entrance requirement.

Without price. The last clause replaces even “thirsty,” which might sound like a condition, with “the one who desires” — whoever will. And the price is the word of 21:6: as a gift, for nothing. Isaiah shouted it centuries before: “Come, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters; and he who has no money, come, buy and eat!” (Isaiah 55:1). Jesus shouted it at the feast: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37), and said it quietly to a woman at a well at noon (John 4:14).

Where it is placed. Two verses earlier the dogs and murderers are outside the gate; one verse later comes a solemn warning. In between, unfenced, is the freest offer in Scripture. That is the last word on the character of the God who has run this whole book: the One whose judgments filled sixteen chapters ends by holding out a cup and asking nothing for it.

Does “let the one who desires” mean that salvation depends on our will? The offer is free and open to all, and anyone who comes will receive. But a fallen heart doesn’t thirst for God unaided; the thirst itself is the Spirit’s work drawing people to Christ (John 6:44). The invitation is real, and so is the grace that makes people want to come.

The question of 20:15 answered. Whether a name is in the book of life isn’t settled by “Have I done enough?” — no one has. It is whether a person is thirsty and will come and take what is handed him for nothing. If you are thirsty, come today.

verseByVerse.quote: I warn everyone who hears the words of the prophecy of this book: if anyone adds to them, God will add to him the plagues described in this book, and if anyone takes away from the words of the book of this prophecy, God will take away his share in the tree of life and in the holy city, which are described in this book.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John warns that anyone who adds to this book’s words will receive its plagues, and anyone who takes away from them will lose their share in the tree of life and the holy city. God’s word must be received exactly as given — neither supplemented with our speculations nor trimmed of what we dislike.

A covenant seal. Severe, and not unprecedented. It is the standard closing formula of an ancient covenant document, used by Moses: “You shall not add to the word that I command you, nor take from it” (Deuteronomy 4:2; cf. 12:32; Proverbs 30:5–6). John does what a covenant scribe did when the text was finished: seals it against tampering.

Not a ban on scholarship. Comparing manuscripts to establish what John wrote is the opposite of tampering; it is the effort to ensure nothing has been added or lost. The ESV’s footnote at v. 14 is that work done honestly and in the open.

This book. John says “this book” four times in two verses and means the one he has just finished. The principle plainly extends to Scripture as a whole, and the church has always applied it so; but the verse isn’t a note about the canon.

Adding and taking away. It targets a live danger in every century: people who take a prophecy and improve it. Adding is supplying what God didn’t say — the date, the identity, the extra requirement, the private revelation that completes what Scripture left open. Taking away is removing what he did say — quietly setting aside the judgment, the exclusivity, or the return, because it is unpopular. And the penalties fit exactly: add to the words, and the plagues are added to you; take away from them, and the tree and the city are taken from you. Each person receives the operation he performed.

Can a true believer lose his salvation by taking away from this book? The warning describes those who falsify God’s word, and shows that such people never truly belonged to Christ (1 John 2:19). For believers it is a solemn reason to handle Scripture with reverence, and one of the means God uses to keep them faithful.

A private application. Few readers will publish an edition of Revelation. Many are tempted to do privately what the verse forbids publicly — add a chart the text doesn’t authorise, or subtract the parts that are hard to hear. The instruction of this book from start to finish has been to keep its words: neither more nor less than what is written. A test: which part of this book have you quietly subtracted because it is hard? Read it again, and receive it.

verseByVerse.quote: He who testifies to these things says, "Surely I am coming soon." Amen. Come, Lord Jesus! The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ says, “Surely I am coming soon,” the church answers, “Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!”, and the Bible ends: “The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all. Amen.” The church lives between the comings by longing and praying for Christ’s return, and the last word of the most terrifying book in Scripture is grace.

His last words. The third and last announcement, and the last recorded words of Jesus Christ in the Bible. Not a command, warning or doctrine, but a promise about arriving. Everything he is has been unfolded over twenty-two chapters — the one who walks among the lampstands, the slain and standing Lamb, the rider with the sword from his mouth, David’s root and offspring, the morning star — and the last thing he says is that he is on his way and won’t be long.

Did Jesus mean “Surely I am coming soon” after two thousand years? “Soon” means his coming is the next great event, near and sudden, not that it would come within a set time. Peter explains the delay: with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and his patience gives time for repentance (2 Peter 3:8–9). The right response is the church’s prayer.

Maranatha. “Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!” The church answers, barely a sentence: agreement and request. In Aramaic, which these congregations prayed in before Greek took over, it was one word, Marana tha, “Our Lord, come,” which Paul dropped untranslated into a letter to Corinth (1 Corinthians 16:22) — a prayer people already said without explanation. That is the church’s state between the comings, and the answer to everything the book has shown. Not a strategy or a timetable, but a prayer that Someone would come, said by people who can’t make him come and are certain he will.

A gentle test. Someone who says “Come, Lord Jesus” and means it has nothing here he would be unwilling to have interrupted. That isn’t a rebuke to anyone who finds the prayer harder than expected; it is simply what the prayer measures. Revelation was written to people who could say it because they had already lost most of what one might want to keep. Pray it today, and notice what in you resists.

The last word is grace. Consider what this book contained: four horsemen, a third of mankind dead, a dragon waiting to devour a child, a beast over every nation, bowls of undiluted wrath, a city drunk on the saints’ blood burned in an hour, a great white throne with no place for earth or sky. By a distance the most terrifying document ever written. And the last word is grace — the word Paul ended every letter with, unearned favour to people with nothing to bring, extended here “with all,” and one more Amen: it is firm, it is so.

So the Bible closes. It opened with a garden, a river and a tree, and a man and woman walking with God; it closes with a city, a river and a tree, and a countless multitude from every nation looking at his face. Between them lies all of human history, and at its centre a Lamb standing as though slain, who took the scroll no one else was worthy to open, and opened it. He is the first and the last; he died and is alive forevermore, holding the keys of Death and Hades (1:18). He is coming soon. And the last thing he leaves his church, after everything, is grace.
verseByVerse.note: “Come, Lord Jesus” matches the Aramaic prayer Maranatha that Paul quotes.

The leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations.<sup>3</sup>No longer will there be anything accursed, but the throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it, and his servants will worship him.<sup>4</sup>They will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads.<sup>5</sup>And night will be no more.
