15.title: The Song of Moses and the Lamb
15.overview:
Chapter 15 is the shortest chapter in Revelation — eight verses — but it is one of the most carefully constructed. It serves as the vestibule to the seven bowl visions of chapter 16, doing what chapters 4–5 did before the seals and what chapters 8:1–5 did before the trumpets: grounding the coming sequence in the worship and sovereignty of God before a single bowl is poured. Before heaven acts in judgment, heaven first breaks into song.

The chapter presents two contrasting scenes held in deliberate tension. The first (vv. 1–4): the victorious on the sea of glass, harps in hand, singing the Song of Moses and the Lamb. The second (vv. 5–8): seven angels emerge from the heavenly temple dressed for a solemn task, given seven golden bowls by one of the four living creatures, while the temple fills with the glory of God so completely that no one can enter until the seven bowls are finished. Praise and solemn purpose belong together. The song is not premature celebration; it is the theological foundation without which the coming acts of God would be misread.

The Song of Moses and the Lamb is one of the richest theological moments in the book. It binds together the two great saving acts of God — the Exodus and the cross — into a single song of praise. The God who opened the Red Sea is the God who opened the tomb. The Lamb who was slain is the LORD who drowned Pharaoh’s army. The song the victorious sing is drawn almost entirely from the Psalms, Jeremiah, and Deuteronomy — the whole Hebrew Scripture gathered into the church’s final praise.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — The Song of the Victorious
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 1: another sign in heaven, great and amazing — the third and last of the book’s three signs, after the woman (12:1) and the dragon (12:3). Seven angels with seven plagues, which are the last, for with them the wrath of God is finished. The verb is from teleō, the same root as the word from the cross, It is finished (John 19:30).

Verse 2: the sea of glass of 4:6 is now mingled with fire, and standing beside it are those who had conquered the beast and its image and the number of its name, holding harps — a direct contradiction of 13:7, where the beast was allowed to conquer them. The position is the far shore of the Red Sea with Egypt behind it.

Verses 3–4: they sing the song of Moses… and the song of the Lamb — one song under two names. Its words are not from Exodus 15 but are a mosaic of Scripture: Great and amazing are your deeds (Ps. 111:2), Just and true are your ways (Deut. 32:4), Who would not fear you, O King of the nations? (Jer. 10:7), All nations will come and worship you (Ps. 86:9). Four clauses, and every one is about God — not one word about the beast, the persecution, or their own endurance.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Song of Moses and the Lamb

Seven angels hold the last plagues, and with them God’s wrath is finished — it has an end, as his mercy does not. Beside the sea of glass, those who conquered the beast sing one song of Moses and the Lamb, made of Scripture and entirely about God.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Those the beast conquered in the street are standing on the far shore with harps.

Now: Faithfulness that consists in refusing to bow still counts as conquering.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw another sign in heaven, great and amazing, seven angels with seven plagues, which are the last, for with them the wrath of God is finished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John sees a great and amazing sign: seven angels with the seven last plagues, which complete God’s wrath. God’s wrath against sin is not endless or out of control; it has a fixed end — and for believers it was finished at the cross.

Getting the reader ready. The shortest chapter in Revelation does one job: preparation. Chapter 16 pours out seven bowls in twenty-one verses, faster and heavier than anything in the book; chapter 15 is the eight verses before it.

The third sign in heaven. The only other signs in heaven were in chapter 12: the woman clothed with the sun (12:1) and the red dragon (12:3). A woman, a dragon, and seven angels with the last plagues: the mother, the enemy, and the end.

Great and amazing. An odd pair for a plague, and John will use them of God’s deeds in v. 3. Not merely dreadful but astonishing, as something enormous and long-expected is when it finally begins.

Finished. “For with them the wrath of God is finished.” The verb is from the same root as Jesus’ cry from the cross: “It is finished” (John 19:30). Something is brought to its appointed completion, and the sentence says so before a single bowl is lifted.

Wrath has an end; mercy doesn’t. A reader after six chapters of dragons and beasts might fear God’s wrath is a bottomless reservoir that, once started, never stops. This verse says the opposite: it has an end, in view from the moment it begins, and a last plague after which there are no more. That isn’t true of his mercy, and the contrast is the point. Scripture says his steadfast love endures forever and never says that of his anger: “his anger is but for a moment, and his favor is for a lifetime” (Psalm 30:5); “He does not retain his anger forever, because he delights in steadfast love” (Micah 7:18). Judgment always has a stopping point written in; grace doesn’t.

Where it was finished for you. If God’s wrath against sin can be completed, the question worth asking is where it was completed for a Christian — and the answer is the cross, where the same verb was used by the same author. There are two places in this book where God’s wrath reaches its end. One is a hill outside Jerusalem, and it happened before any of this began. A test: are you living as if God’s anger still hangs over you? If you are in Christ, it was finished there.

verseByVerse.quote: And I saw what appeared to be a sea of glass mingled with fire—and also those who had conquered the beast and its image and the number of its name, standing beside the sea of glass with harps of God in their hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John sees a sea of glass mixed with fire, and beside it those who conquered the beast, its image and its number, holding harps of God. Believers whom the beast killed have actually conquered it, simply by refusing to worship it, and now stand safe like Israel beyond the Red Sea.

Fire in the glass. The sea of glass lay before the throne in chapter 4, flat, still, transparent — chaos frozen under God’s feet (4:6). Now there is fire in it: judgment, the fire taken from the altar and thrown to earth (8:5). Heaven’s floor has begun to glow.

Conquered by the conquered. At 13:7 the beast was allowed “to make war on the saints and to conquer them.” Here the same people “had conquered the beast.” Same verb, opposite direction, same encounter. Both are true, and holding them together is the most important thing this book asks of a suffering Christian. From the street, the beast won: believers were arrested, tried and killed, and nothing undoes that. From the sea of glass, they won: they are standing with instruments in their hands, and the beast isn’t in the room.

How defeat becomes victory. 12:11 explained it: “they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death.” The winning wasn’t survival but refusing to let go, and losing their lives was part of the means, not a failure of it.

A victory of refusals. What they conquered: “the beast and its image and the number of its name.” Not an army but a demand. They weren’t asked to defeat anything, only not to bow, not to worship an image, not to take a number that would let them keep trading. Their whole victory consists of things they didn’t do.

For the Christian who thinks his faithfulness too passive to count. The company on the sea of glass stormed nothing. They declined. They said no to a formality, again and again, at rising cost, and heaven files that under “conquered.” A test: what quiet “no” is faithfulness asking of you this week?

On the far shore. “Standing beside the sea” pictures Israel on the far bank of the Red Sea, with Egypt at the bottom of it — as the next verse makes plain. Those who came through stand on the shore, and the first thing they do is sing.

verseByVerse.quote: And they sing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying, "Great and amazing are your deeds, O Lord God the Almighty! Just and true are your ways, O King of the nations! Who will not fear, O Lord, and glorify your name? For you alone are holy. All nations will come and worship you, for your righteous acts have been revealed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The conquerors sing the song of Moses and the Lamb, praising God’s great deeds, his just and true ways, his unique holiness, and the coming worship of all nations. Those who suffered most praise God’s justice without complaint, sing his own words back to him, and look to the day when the nations worship him.

One song, two names. The grammar allows a single song called by two names, and the content proves it: there is one deliverance in two chapters. The song of Moses is Exodus 15, sung beyond the sea with Pharaoh’s army drowned behind them. Israel came out of Egypt through water; these came out of the beast’s empire through fire and death; and it is the same song, because the God who did the first did the second.

Sung in quotations. The words aren’t from Exodus 15 but a mosaic of Psalms and prophets: “Great are the works of the LORD” (Psalm 111:2); “all his ways are justice” (Deuteronomy 32:4); “Who would not fear you, O King of the nations?” (Jeremiah 10:7); “All the nations you have made shall come and worship before you, O Lord, and shall glorify your name” (Psalm 86:9). Heaven’s redeemed sing in quotations; their worship is built from the Scriptures they were given — a quiet argument for filling the mind with them now. A test: how much Scripture could you sing or pray from memory?

All about God. Not a word about the beast, the persecution, what they suffered, or their endurance. Four clauses, every one about God: his deeds, ways, name, righteous acts.

“Just and true are your ways.” These singers are qualified to say it. Anyone can affirm God’s justice from a comfortable chair. These were killed for refusing a number, came out the other side, and the first thing they say about how God ran history is that it was just. No complaint — not because the question was never asked (it was, loudly, in 6:10), but because it has been answered. A test: can you say “just and true are your ways” about the hardest thing in your life, trusting that it will be answered?

You alone are holy. “Who will not fear, O Lord, and glorify your name?” The expected answer: no one. And the ground is holiness, sung three times in chapter 4. “You alone”: there is one of him, and the beast that demanded worship for forty-two months isn’t in the category.

All nations will come. The widest sentence in the chapter, startling in a book so full of judgment. The nations who raged (11:18), drank Babylon’s wine (14:8), and served the beast (13:7) will come and worship — Psalm 86:9 quoted straight, and the promise to Abraham that in him all the families of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 12:3). This isn’t universalism; the same book says some are finally outside (21:8; 22:15). It is the assurance that the multitude from every nation (7:9) isn’t a consolation prize. God will have the nations, and what brings them in is “your righteous acts have been revealed” — not that God overwhelmed the world, but that he was seen clearly.
verseByVerse.note: As Israel sang beside the sea after the exodus, so God’s redeemed sing after their deliverance.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–8 — The Sanctuary Filled with Smoke
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 5: the sanctuary of the tent of witness in heaven was opened. The phrase is the Old Testament’s name for the tabernacle, the tent that housed the ark, which housed the tablets called the testimony because they are God’s witness against a people who agreed to keep them (Ex. 38:21; Num. 1:50). The bowls come out of the place where the covenant is kept.

Verse 6: out come the seven angels, clothed in pure, bright linen, with golden sashes around their chests — priestly dress (Lev. 16:4; Dan. 10:5), and precisely how the risen Christ was described at 1:13.

Verse 7: one of the four living creatures — the beings nearest the throne, who never cease to say holy, holy, holy — hands over seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God. The word is phialē, a shallow libation dish that empties in a moment, not a jug.

Verse 8: the sanctuary was filled with smoke from the glory of God and from his power, and no one could enter the sanctuary until the seven plagues of the seven angels were finished.
verseByVerse.theology:
Judgement as Liturgy

The bowls come out of the tent of witness, carried by angels in priestly linen and handed over by a worshipper. The golden bowls that once held prayers now hold wrath, and the sanctuary is closed until the plagues are finished.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The judgement rests on the covenant kept since Sinai.

Now: The sanctuary is open today, with a high priest interceding inside it — pray while it is.

verseByVerse.quote: After this I looked, and the sanctuary of the tent of witness in heaven was opened, and out of the sanctuary came the seven angels with the seven plagues, clothed in pure, bright linen, with golden sashes around their chests.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The heavenly sanctuary, the tent of witness, is opened, and the seven angels with the seven plagues come out dressed like priests in pure, bright linen with golden sashes. God’s final judgments rest on his covenant, come from his holy presence, and are carried out by pure servants as an act of holy service.

The tent of witness. An old, precise name for the tabernacle, which housed the ark, which held the two tablets — called the testimony because they are God’s witness against a people who agreed to keep them and didn’t (Exodus 38:21; Numbers 1:50).

From where the covenant is kept. The bowls come not from an armoury or a prison but from the tent holding the terms both sides signed. That is the difference between these judgments and mere destruction: what is coming has a legal basis, and the document has been in the same box since Sinai.

Opened again. At 11:19 the temple opened and the ark was seen; here the sanctuary opens again, this time not to show something but to release seven angels.

Priests, not soldiers. Linen is what the priest wore into the holy place (Leviticus 16:4); Daniel’s heavenly man was “clothed in linen, with a belt of fine gold” (Daniel 10:5); and a golden sash across the chest is exactly how the risen Christ was dressed (1:13). That refuses two easy pictures at once. These aren’t demons let loose, nor soldiers. They are ministers in priestly dress, coming from a sanctuary, carrying out a service. God’s judgment isn’t a loss of control or an outsourcing; it is worship carried out.

Clean hands. “Pure, bright linen” — “bright” is the word for the Bride’s dress (19:8). Nothing that comes through that door is dirty. Whatever one says about the severity of chapter 16, one can’t say the hands carrying it were unclean. A test: do you trust that God’s judgments, when they come, will be entirely just — or do you secretly suspect him? Look at the linen.

verseByVerse.quote: And one of the four living creatures gave to the seven angels seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God who lives forever and ever, and the sanctuary was filled with smoke from the glory of God and from his power, and no one could enter the sanctuary until the seven plagues of the seven angels were finished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of the living creatures gives the seven angels seven golden bowls full of God’s wrath, and the sanctuary fills with smoke from God’s glory, so that no one can enter until the plagues are finished. The time for warning ends and judgment is poured out — so while the door of mercy is open now, we must pray and come to God through Christ.

Handed over by worshippers. One of the living creatures — nearest the throne, crying “holy, holy, holy” without ceasing (4:8) — passes the bowls. Nothing in this chapter lets judgment be handled by anyone outside the worship of God.

A libation bowl. The word is a shallow, wide dish for pouring an offering — not a jug or jar. It empties at once. A trumpet is a warning, blown to be heard, giving time to respond. A libation bowl is tipped once and gone. The instrument itself says the era of warnings is over.

The same bowls. At 5:8 the elders held “golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints.” Same vessels, same throne room. Golden bowls went up full of prayer; golden bowls come down full of wrath. The martyrs asked “how long?”, and this is the vessel in which the answer is delivered.

Glory-smoke. When the tabernacle was finished, “the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle. And Moses was not able to enter” (Exodus 40:34–35). At Solomon’s dedication “the priests could not stand to minister because of the cloud, for the glory of the LORD filled the house of the LORD” (1 Kings 8:11). Isaiah saw the house filled with smoke and cried, “Woe is me!” (Isaiah 6:4–5). Each time, the smoke meant God had come to dwell, and the exclusion was temporary and joyful. Here it is colder: no one could enter “until the seven plagues… were finished.”

No intercession. The sanctuary is where a priest goes in to plead, bringing blood and asking mercy for someone else. For the duration of the bowls, no one goes in. There is no intercession while the plagues are poured, because its time has run out. That is the most sobering sentence in the chapter: there comes a point when the door is shut — not because God won’t hear, but because the case is closed, the warnings given, the answering begun.

“Until.” Also the mercy in the verse: even the shutting has an end date, the one in v. 1.

It is open now. For anyone reading while the door is still open, the application is simple. The sanctuary stands wide, and there is a great High Priest inside who “always lives to make intercession” for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). While that is true, pray — for yourself, and for the people whose names you wouldn’t want read out on the day the smoke fills the room. Name them to him today.

15.text: <sup>1</sup>Then I saw another sign in heaven, great and amazing, seven angels with seven plagues, which are the last, for with them the wrath of God is finished.<sup>2</sup>And I saw what appeared to be a sea of glass mingled with fire—and also those who had conquered the beast and its image and the number of its name, standing beside the sea of glass with harps of God in their hands.<sup>3</sup>And they sing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying, “Great and amazing are your deeds, O Lord God the Almighty! Just and true are your ways, O King of the nations!<sup>4</sup>Who will not fear, O Lord, and glorify your name? For you alone are holy. All nations will come and worship you, for your righteous acts have been revealed.”<sup>5</sup>After this I looked, and the sanctuary of the tent of witness in heaven was opened,<sup>6</sup>and out of the sanctuary came the seven angels with the seven plagues, clothed in pure, bright linen, with golden sashes around their chests.<sup>7</sup>And one of the four living creatures gave to the seven angels seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God who lives forever and ever,<sup>8</sup>and the sanctuary was filled with smoke from the glory of God and from his power, and no one could enter the sanctuary until the seven plagues of the seven angels were finished.

16.title: The Seven Bowls: The Completion of Divine Justice
16.overview:
Chapter 16 is the third and final series of seven judgments in Revelation, and it is the most intense. Where the seals affected a quarter of the earth and the trumpets a third, the bowls are poured on the whole earth without fraction. The escalation is deliberate: the time for partial warning has passed. These are the last plagues, and with them the response of God to the accumulated rebellion of history reaches its completion.

The bowl series follows the Exodus plague pattern more closely than either the seals or the trumpets. Bowls one through five draw on the Egyptian plagues, though not in their order: sores (bowl 1, cf. Exodus 9:8–11), water turned to blood (bowls 2–3, cf. Exodus 7:17–21), darkness (bowl 5, cf. Exodus 10:21–23). The Exodus pattern is not decorative. It carries a theological message: the God who liberated Israel from Egypt is the same God who now acts in the final Exodus. The pattern of redemptive history repeats at the cosmic scale.

The chapter reaches its climax at the seventh bowl: a loud voice from the throne declares ‘It is done!’ and the greatest earthquake in human history splits the great city into three parts. Babylon is remembered before God and given the cup of the wine of the fury of his wrath. Every island flees, every mountain disappears. The chapter ends not with despair but with the certainty that the one who declared ‘It is done’ from the cross has declared it again from the throne — all things are now moving irresistibly toward the new creation of chapters 21–22.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 1: a loud voice from the temple — almost certainly God’s own, since 15:8 has just closed the sanctuary to everyone else — orders the seven angels to pour. Verse 2: the first bowl brings harmful and painful sores on those who bore the mark of the beast and worshipped its image (cf. Ex. 9:8–11).

Verse 3: the sea becomes like the blood of a corpse and everything in it dies — against the second trumpet, which killed a third (8:8–9). Verse 4: the rivers and springs become blood, as the Nile did (Ex. 7:20–21).

Verses 5–7 stop the sequence and defend it. The angel in charge of the waters — whose department has just been ruined — declares Just are you, O Holy One… they have shed the blood of saints and prophets, and you have given them blood to drink. It is what they deserve! And then the altar itself answers: Yes, Lord God the Almighty, true and just are your judgments!

Verses 8–9: the fourth bowl turns the sun up, and they cursed the name of God who had power over these plagues. They did not repent and give him glory. Verses 10–11: the fifth falls on the throne of the beast and its kingdom goes dark (cf. Ex. 10:21–23); people gnaw their tongues in anguish and curse the God of heaven for their pain and sores, and did not repent of their deeds.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Same Ground, Undiluted

The bowls strike earth, sea, rivers, sun and the beast’s throne — the trumpets’ targets, now without limit. The angel of the waters and the altar itself declare God’s judgements true and just. Those struck curse God and do not repent.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The plagues of Egypt return in one chapter, and the mark becomes the wound.

Now: Suffering drives some to their knees and hardens others; it depends which way a person was already facing.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I heard a loud voice from the temple telling the seven angels, "Go and pour out on the earth the seven bowls of the wrath of God." So the first angel went and poured out his bowl on the earth, and harmful and painful sores came upon the people who bore the mark of the beast and worshiped its image.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God commands the seven angels to pour out the bowls of his wrath, and the first brings painful sores on those who bear the beast’s mark and worship its image. The final judgments come from God himself, fall on those who chose the beast, and often hand people over to the consequences of what they insisted on.

The voice from the closed temple. No one could enter the sanctuary (15:8), yet a voice comes out of it — almost certainly God’s own. Whoever else is involved, the order to begin comes from the throne.

The trumpets again, without limits. The targets match the trumpets in order: earth, sea, rivers and springs, sun, darkness on a kingdom, the Euphrates, and a final convulsion with hail (compare 8:7–12; 9:13–14). What has changed is the extent: the trumpets struck a third; the bowls strike everything. That parallel is one of the strongest arguments for reading the three sevens as recapitulation — the same ground covered again with greater intensity (see on 6:1–2).

Egypt, densest of all. Sores (Exodus 9:10), water to blood (7:20), darkness (10:22), frogs (8:6), hail (9:24): five of the ten plagues in one chapter. The empire is Egypt, and the God who broke Egypt hasn’t changed his methods.

The drumbeat. Three times John records that those struck cursed God and did not repent (vv. 9, 11, 21).

Sores. The sixth Egyptian plague brought boils, and the magicians “could not stand before Moses because of the boils” (Exodus 9:11). Whatever Egypt’s wisdom could imitate, it couldn’t imitate health.

The mark festers. The sores fall precisely on “the people who bore the mark of the beast and worshiped its image.” The bowls aren’t indiscriminate. In chapter 13 the mark was the ticket to a working life; here the mark itself festers. What was taken as a passport turns out to be the wound.

Handed over. That removes the sense of arbitrariness. God rarely invents a punishment unconnected to the offence. He hands people over to what they insisted on — “God gave them up,” three times in one paragraph (Romans 1:24, 26, 28). A test: what have you insisted on having that may become your wound? Let it go while you can.
verseByVerse.note: The bowls are the last and fullest judgments; unlike the trumpets, they are not limited to a third.

verseByVerse.quote: The second angel poured out his bowl into the sea, and it became like the blood of a corpse, and every living thing died that was in the sea. The third angel poured out his bowl into the rivers and the springs of water, and they became blood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second bowl turns the sea to blood like a corpse’s, killing every sea creature, and the third turns the rivers and springs to blood. What God partly struck before in warning, he now strikes completely, showing that everything the world lives on is upheld by him.

A corpse’s blood. Deliberately revolting: not bright blood but a corpse’s — dark, thickened, going bad. Anyone who has been in a room with a body knows what is meant.

No fraction. The second trumpet turned a third of the sea to blood (8:8–9). Here “every living thing died that was in the sea.” The restraint that governed every judgment since chapter 6 — a fourth, a third, a tenth, forty-two months, a fence around the winds — is gone. This is the undiluted wrath of 15:1.

The Nile returned. The first plague turned the Nile to blood; the fish died and the river stank (Exodus 7:20–21). It was the river into which Pharaoh had ordered every Hebrew boy thrown (Exodus 1:22). Egypt got the Nile back in the condition Egypt had put it in.

What the world lives on and by. The sea is where the beast came from (13:1) and where trade ran; rivers and springs are a settlement’s drinking water. Together they are commerce and survival, and both are now blood.

Warning, then verdict. At the third trumpet Wormwood made a third of the springs bitter (8:10–11). Bitter water can still be drunk by a desperate man; blood can’t. The trumpet made the water unbearable; the bowl makes it impossible. That is the distance between a warning and a verdict.

Nothing is neutral machinery. Everything the world depends on belongs to Someone. The sea a merchant sails, the spring a village was built around, the sun a farmer plants by — none of it is neutral machinery that happens to work. It is upheld moment by moment by the One who is cursed for withdrawing it. A civilisation can assume for centuries that the water will be there, be right every day, and still be wrong about why. A test: when did you last thank God for clean water, a working body, ordinary daylight?

A pause. Then John does something he does nowhere else in the bowls: he stops. Three verses of worship follow, because heaven has something to say about whether this is fair.

verseByVerse.quote: And I heard the angel in charge of the waters say, "Just are you, O Holy One, who is and who was, for you brought these judgments. For they have shed the blood of saints and prophets, and you have given them blood to drink. It is what they deserve!" And I heard the altar saying, "Yes, Lord God the Almighty, true and just are your judgments!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel over the waters declares God just, because those who shed the blood of saints and prophets are now given blood to drink, and the altar answers, “Yes, Lord God the Almighty, true and just are your judgments!” God’s judgments are perfectly fair; the punishment fits the crime, and even the martyrs who waited for justice agree.

The book’s answer to “Is this fair?” The question a reader has carried since chapter 6 is answered not by John, an apostle or an argument, but sung in the middle of the plague — by the angel whose waters have just been ruined. If anyone had grounds to object, it was him. He declares the judgment just.

The crime served back. “For they have shed the blood of saints and prophets, and you have given them blood to drink.” The oldest principle of justice. Egypt drowned Hebrew children in a river and had to drink the river. These people made the earth run with the saints’ blood, and now there is nothing else to drink. What God does to the wicked is what the wicked did, returned.

“It is what they deserve.” Not comfortable words. But notice who doesn’t say them: no human being in this book pronounces that sentence over another. The martyrs asked “how long?” and left the verdict to God (6:10). Vengeance is God’s (Romans 12:19), because only he can be trusted to get it exactly right. A test: is there someone you want to see “get what they deserve”? Hand that verdict to God, and pray for them.

Holy, not merely strong. “O Holy One, who is and who was” — the third term gone again, as at 11:17: the One who is to come has come. And the attribute picked out is holiness, not power. The angel isn’t saying God may do this because he is strong enough, but that it is consistent with what he is.

The altar answers. Under the altar are the souls of those slain for God’s word, who cried, “O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long before you will judge and avenge our blood?” (6:10). This is the altar answering its own question. The words come back — “holy and true” there, “true and just” here — and the verdict of those who actually paid for the injustice is yes. Not “at last,” not “it took long enough.” Yes.

For the reader who finds this hard. The one group whose opinion might carry most weight — the murdered, who wanted this and waited for it — declare it just when it comes. No one in heaven, seeing the whole file, thinks God has overdone it.

verseByVerse.quote: The fourth angel poured out his bowl on the sun, and it was allowed to scorch people with fire. They were scorched by the fierce heat, and they cursed the name of God who had power over these plagues. They did not repent and give him glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fourth bowl lets the sun scorch people with fire, and they curse God, who has power over the plagues, and refuse to repent and give him glory. Suffering does not automatically lead to repentance; it reveals and hardens the direction a heart is already facing.

“It was allowed.” Even at full strength, with the limits off, the divine passive holds. Nothing in this book acts on its own authority, not even the sun.

One sun, two companies. The fourth trumpet darkened a third of the sun (8:12); the fourth bowl turns it up. And the reversal is pointed, because the multitude was promised, “the sun shall not strike them, nor any scorching heat” (7:16). For the sealed, the sun is shaded by God’s tent spread over them; for these, it is a furnace. The same created thing behaves differently depending on whose you are.

They cursed. The verb used of the beast’s mouth in 13:6. Under the plague they have begun to sound like what they worshipped.

They know. They cursed “the name of God who had power over these plagues.” No ignorance, no confusion about the source, no atheism. They have correctly identified who is doing this and curse him for it. Suffering hasn’t hidden God from them; it has revealed him, and they have decided against him with the evidence in front of them.

Pain doesn’t produce repentance. “They did not repent and give him glory.” The answer, again, to a hope many quietly carry — that if things got bad enough, people would turn. Chapter 9 said it after a third of mankind died; chapter 16 says it three times more. Pain reveals what was already there, and hardens as reliably as it softens.

A warning for believers. Not chiefly about other people. Every Christian meets small versions: the illness, loss or disappointment that could go either way, and the direction isn’t decided by the size of the trouble. Two men lose the same thing in the same week; one is driven to his knees and the other never prays again. The difference isn’t the weight but which way a person was already facing when it landed. A test: which way are you facing now, before the next trouble comes?

What repentance is. “Repent and give him glory” — not merely feel sorry, but hand God back the glory given to something else. Exactly what these people won’t do: they gave it to a beast and aren’t taking it back.

verseByVerse.quote: The fifth angel poured out his bowl on the throne of the beast, and its kingdom was plunged into darkness. People gnawed their tongues in anguish and cursed the God of heaven for their pain and sores. They did not repent of their deeds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fifth bowl falls on the beast’s throne and plunges its kingdom into darkness; people gnaw their tongues in pain and curse God for their sufferings, still refusing to repent of their deeds. God exposes the emptiness of every godless regime, and those who measure God only by their comfort end in bitter cursing.

Aimed at the throne. The first four bowls fell on creation. The fifth falls on a government, precisely: not on subjects or armies but on “the throne of the beast.” The reader last heard of such a throne in Pergamum, “where Satan’s throne is” (2:13). Christians had lived under its shadow the whole book. It goes dark.

Egypt’s darkness. The ninth plague was darkness so thick no one rose from his place for three days, “but all the people of Israel had light where they lived” (Exodus 10:23). Egypt’s chief god was the sun, whose son Pharaoh claimed to be. To darken the empire is to show its god can’t keep a lamp lit.

The regime exposed. The earlier bowls damaged the world; this one exposes the regime. Every empire that demands worship rests on an appearance of permanence — the lights are on, the courts sit, the coins are minted, and it is inconceivable that any of it should stop. One bowl, and the kingdom is in the dark. It couldn’t even manage light.

Gnawing tongues. A small, credible detail: what a person does with pain he can’t escape or usefully cry out about. And the sores from the first bowl are still there; the plagues accumulate; nothing has healed.

Worship and behaviour. In v. 9, “did not repent and give him glory”; here, “did not repent of their deeds.” The first is worship, the second conduct. They won’t change what they adore or what they do.

For their pain. What they curse God for: “their pain and sores.” Not anything they have thought about him, nor any account of who he is. Their whole complaint is their own discomfort. It is possible to spend a life measuring God only by how one feels, and this is where that ends.

A test before the bowl. When you last had a grievance against God, what was it actually about? If the honest answer is that he hadn’t arranged your comfort as you would have, that is the same complaint at a survivable scale — and there is still time to bring it to him and repent.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–21 — The Sixth and Seventh Bowls
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 12: the sixth bowl dries the Euphrates to prepare the way for the kings from the east — and when Cyrus took Babylon his engineers diverted that river and his troops walked in up the empty bed, exactly as Isaiah had said (Isa. 44:27–28). Verses 13–14: three unclean spirits like frogs (Ex. 8:6) come out of the mouths of the dragon, the beast and the false prophet — the unholy trinity together for the first time — and go to the kings of the world to assemble them for battle.

Verse 15 interrupts, in brackets, in Christ’s own voice: Behold, I am coming like a thief! Blessed is the one who stays awake, keeping his garments on, that he may not go about naked and be seen exposed! — the third of the book’s seven beatitudes. Verse 16 names the muster point: Armageddon, its only occurrence in the Bible.

Verse 17: the seventh bowl is poured into the air, and a loud voice from the temple and the throne says It is done! — gegonen, a perfect tense, the completion promised at 15:1. Verse 18: the storm signs at full strength, with an earthquake such as there had never been since man was on the earth.

Verse 19: the great city splits in three, the cities of the nations fall, and God remembered Babylon the great, to make her drain the cup of the wine of the fury of his wrath. Verse 20: every island flees and no mountains are found (cf. 6:14). Verse 21: hailstones of about a hundred pounds fall (Ex. 9:24) — and they cursed God, for the third time in the chapter, which is the last thing humanity does in it.
verseByVerse.theology:
It Is Done

The Euphrates is dried, and frog-like spirits from the mouths of the dragon, beast and false prophet gather the kings to Armageddon. Christ breaks in: stay awake. The seventh bowl brings the voice from the throne, It is done!, the great earthquake, and Babylon remembered for judgement.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Babylon had fallen once before when its river was diverted.

Now: Stay awake and clothed in Christ; ask how much of what you lean on can be shaken.

verseByVerse.quote: The sixth angel poured out his bowl on the great river Euphrates, and its water was dried up, to prepare the way for the kings from the east. And I saw, coming out of the mouth of the dragon and out of the mouth of the beast and out of the mouth of the false prophet, three unclean spirits like frogs. For they are demonic spirits, performing signs, who go abroad to the kings of the whole world, to assemble them for battle on the great day of God the Almighty.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sixth bowl dries up the Euphrates for the kings of the east, and three froglike demonic spirits come from the mouths of the dragon, the beast and the false prophet to gather the world’s kings for battle on God’s great day. God opens the way to the final conflict, and evil gathers the world against him chiefly through lies.

The river goes. The Euphrates, the empire’s eastern frontier and the direction every invasion of Israel came from. At the sixth trumpet four angels bound there were released (9:14); now the river itself goes.

A road cleared. A dried river is Scripture’s picture of God clearing a road: the Red Sea for Israel (Exodus 14:21), the Jordan into the land (Joshua 3:16). And when Cyrus took Babylon, ancient historians say his engineers diverted the Euphrates and his troops walked in up the empty riverbed — as Isaiah foretold when God said to the deep, “Be dry; I will dry up your rivers,” and named Cyrus (Isaiah 44:27–28). A first-century reader knew exactly how the last great Babylon fell.

The gate opened. The water is removed to make invasion easier. God isn’t defending the beast’s kingdom; he opens the gate for what will destroy it. Even the enemies of God’s people serve his purposes without knowing it.

Who are the kings from the east? John’s readers feared the Parthian armies beyond the Euphrates. Futurist readers expect a literal eastern army. The more likely reading is that John uses that fear as a picture of the nations gathered by the dragon for the final battle (v. 14), not a prediction of a particular invasion.

Three mouths. The unholy trinity appears together for the first time, and all three do the same thing: they speak. The dragon is “the deceiver of the whole world” (12:9); the beast was given “a mouth uttering haughty and blasphemous words” (13:5); the false prophet deceives by signs. Evil’s whole arsenal in this book is rhetorical.

Frogs. The second plague of Egypt (Exodus 8:6), and unclean to a Jewish reader. Also deliberately ridiculous. Everything about the villains so far has been magnificent: seven heads, ten diadems, a healed wound, the worship of the earth. When their propaganda is finally shown, it hops.

A persuasion campaign. The frogs are a diplomatic service: they go to the kings, perform signs, and assemble a coalition. The last war begins not with mobilisation but persuasion, by demons who look absurd and are believed anyway. The decisive struggle isn’t chiefly about weapons or power but about what the world is told and whether it believes it. The dragon’s one method, from a garden conversation to the last coalition, is to say something untrue convincingly. A test: what are you being persuaded of this week that contradicts what God says? Check it against his word.

verseByVerse.quote: ("Behold, I am coming like a thief! Blessed is the one who stays awake, keeping his garments on, that he may not go about naked and be seen exposed!") And they assembled them at the place that in Hebrew is called Armageddon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ breaks in: “Behold, I am coming like a thief! Blessed is the one who stays awake, keeping his garments on” — and the kings are gathered at the place called Armageddon. At the world’s darkest hour Christ’s concern is that his people stay alert and faithful, and the famous last battle will be no contest at all.

Christ interrupts. In the middle of a sentence about demonic frogs assembling the world’s kings, another voice cuts in; the ESV rightly brackets it. Christ has scarcely spoken in his own voice since chapter 3 and won’t again until chapter 22. Here, at the darkest point, he breaks in. The armies gather — and the Lord’s concern at that moment is a Christian in Thyatira staying awake and keeping his clothes on. The cosmic scale never displaces the person reading.

Like a thief. He said it to Sardis (3:3) and on the Mount of Olives (Matthew 24:43); Paul and Peter repeat it (1 Thessalonians 5:2; 2 Peter 3:10). The point isn’t stealth but unpredictability — arriving on a night no one expected. So there is no point planning to get ready later.

Awake and dressed. The third of the book’s seven blessings. The image would have made a Christian smile before it made him think: according to the later Mishnah, a temple guard found asleep at his post had his clothes burned — caught asleep meant public shame. And garments in this book are settled: white robes for those who conquer (3:5), robes washed in the Lamb’s blood (7:14), the Bride’s fine linen, “the righteous deeds of the saints” (19:8). Laodicea was told to buy white garments so that “the shame of your nakedness may not be seen” (3:18) — the same phrase. So the instruction isn’t heroic: stay awake; keep your clothes on. Not that a Christian do something about the coalition, but that he be found alert and dressed. A test: if Christ came tonight, what would he find you doing — and wearing?

Is Armageddon a literal battle at Megiddo in Israel? The word occurs only here in the Bible, and much popular literature rests on it. The likeliest derivation is “mountain of Megiddo.” Megiddo guarded the pass into the plain of Jezreel and was the most fought-over place in the land: Deborah and Barak fought “at Taanach, by the waters of Megiddo” (Judges 5:19); Ahaziah died there (2 Kings 9:27); good King Josiah was killed there by Pharaoh Neco (2 Kings 23:29). To say Megiddo was to say the battlefield. Premillennial and dispensational Christians expect a future gathering of armies there. But Megiddo is a mound on a plain, not a mountain; some therefore read “mountain of assembly,” the phrase of the fallen day star who says, “I will sit on the mount of assembly” (Isaiah 14:13); and the battle is “on the great day of God the Almighty” (v. 14), the same final conflict as 19:19 and 20:8. In a book that calls one city Sodom, Egypt and Babylon, the more likely reading is that Armageddon is a symbolic name for the world’s last stand against God, ended at once by Christ’s coming.

The shortest battle. What isn’t uncertain is who wins, and how little of a battle it is. The kings are assembled here and nothing happens; the fighting is in 19:19–21, lasts one verse, and the weapon is a sword from a mouth. Armageddon is the most famous battle in the world’s imagination and the shortest in the book.
verseByVerse.note: Armageddon probably means “mountain of Megiddo,” a hill fortress overlooking the plain where many of Israel’s famous battles were fought.

verseByVerse.quote: The seventh angel poured out his bowl into the air, and a loud voice came out of the temple, from the throne, saying, "It is done!" And there were flashes of lightning, rumblings, peals of thunder, and a great earthquake such as there had never been since man was on the earth, so great was that earthquake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The seventh bowl is poured into the air, and God’s voice from the throne declares, “It is done!” amid the greatest earthquake in history. God’s wrath reaches its appointed end, and everything that can be shaken is shaken so that only what cannot be shaken remains.

Into the air. The one element the first six left alone, and the one no one can stand outside of. Paul calls the devil “the prince of the power of the air” (Ephesians 2:2). The last judgment falls on the atmosphere the whole world breathes.

“It is done!” From the temple and the throne — God himself. One word in Greek: it has happened, stands accomplished, with permanent result. It echoes two others that frame everything. On the cross, “It is finished” (John 19:30) — a different verb, the same force. At 21:6, of the new creation, “It is done!” — the same word. The cross, the end of wrath, the beginning of the new world. What was accomplished at the first makes the second bearable and the third certain.

The wrath finished. Chapter 15 said it in advance: “with them the wrath of God is finished” (15:1). This is that sentence arriving. There is no eighth bowl.

The storm at full strength. John’s signal that God has acted has grown through the book: three elements at 4:5; an earthquake added at 8:5; hail added at 11:19. Here the earthquake gets a clause of its own and a superlative: nothing like it “since man was on the earth.”

The great sorting. God promised through Haggai to shake heaven and earth (Haggai 2:6), and Hebrews explains why: “Yet once more I will shake not only the earth but also the heavens.” This phrase “indicates the removal of things that are shaken… in order that the things that cannot be shaken may remain. Therefore let us be grateful for receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken” (Hebrews 12:26–28). That is what the greatest earthquake in history is for. Not demolition for its own sake, but sorting: everything that can be shaken is shaken, so that what stands afterwards is only what was never going to fall.

A test. A believer’s honest question isn’t “Will I survive this?” but “How much of what I am leaning on is in the shakeable category?” Name it — and lean instead on the kingdom that can’t be shaken.

verseByVerse.quote: The great city was split into three parts, and the cities of the nations fell, and God remembered Babylon the great, to make her drain the cup of the wine of the fury of his wrath. And every island fled away, and no mountains were to be found. And great hailstones, about one hundred pounds each, fell from heaven on people; and they cursed God for the plague of the hail, because the plague was so severe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The great city splits into three, the cities of the nations fall, and God remembers Babylon to make her drain the cup of his wrath; islands and mountains vanish, and hundred-pound hailstones fall, yet people curse God. God acts at last on the long record of the godless world-system, and judgment alone still changes no one’s heart — only the gospel of the Lamb does.

The great city. The phrase used at 11:8 of the city “symbolically… called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified” — Babylon, named in the same sentence. Split in three: total collapse; Ezekiel divided his hair in three as a sign of Jerusalem’s ruin (Ezekiel 5:1–2).

“God remembered.” In Scripture God’s remembering never means something had slipped his mind. It is covenant language: he is about to act on what he has long known. “God remembered Noah,” and the waters went down (Genesis 8:1). God remembered his covenant with Abraham, and the exodus began (Exodus 2:24). The thief asked to be remembered and heard, “today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:42–43). So a long-open file has come to the top. Babylon was announced fallen at 14:8; chapters 17–18 will do nothing else. This is the hinge between announcement and account.

Drain the cup. Not sip — drain it to the bottom. The cup of 14:10, poured full strength, and the cup Babylon herself passed round (14:8). She poured; she drinks; she finishes the glass.

No fixed points. Islands and mountains — things that don’t move, what people steer by and shelter behind — are gone. The sixth seal said the same (6:14), more evidence that seals and bowls cover the same ground.

Hail. Egypt’s seventh plague was hail unlike any since the nation began (Exodus 9:24). A hundred pounds is roughly a talent, the largest standard weight. And stones falling on people had one other meaning in the law: stoning was the penalty for blasphemy (Leviticus 24:16). The chapter has said three times that these people blasphemed. The sky returns the sentence.

The last word is a curse. Not “they cried out” or “they fell down.” Humanity’s final act in this chapter, with the sky falling, is to curse.

What actually changes people. Revelation offers no picture of a world that finally comes round under pressure; it has now said four times that judgment alone changes nobody. What changes people is what was shown at 11:13, where two witnesses were killed and raised and nine-tenths of a city gave glory to God, and what was announced at 14:6, an eternal gospel flown over every nation. The bowls answer “how long?”, but they save no one. The instrument of salvation is the slain Lamb, at the centre of the throne since chapter 5, and while the sanctuary door is open, it is still working. A test: are you hoping hard times will soften someone you love? Pray, and tell them of the Lamb.
