For in a single hour she has been laid waste.<sup>20</sup>Rejoice over her, O heaven, and you saints and apostles and prophets, for God has given judgment for you against her!”<sup>21</sup>Then a mighty angel took up a stone like a great millstone and threw it into the sea, saying, “So will Babylon the great city be thrown down with violence, and will be found no more;<sup>22</sup>and the sound of harpists and musicians, of flute players and trumpeters, will be heard in you no more, and a craftsman of any craft will be found in you no more, and the sound of the mill will be heard in you no more,<sup>23</sup>and the light of a lamp will shine in you no more, and the voice of bridegroom and bride will be heard in you no more, for your merchants were the great ones of the earth, and all nations were deceived by your sorcery.<sup>24</sup>And in her was found the blood of prophets and of saints, and of all who have been slain on earth.”

19.title: Hallelujah! The Wedding and the Rider
19.overview:
Chapter 19 is the great pivot of Revelation — the hinge between Babylon’s fall and the new creation. It opens with the loudest sound in the book: the fourfold Hallelujah chorus of heaven celebrating the justice of God and the arrival of the marriage supper of the Lamb. It closes with the appearance of the Rider on the white horse, whose name is Word of God, whose robe is dipped in blood, who strikes the nations with the sword of his mouth, and who is named King of kings and Lord of lords.

The chapter falls into two movements that mirror each other. The first (vv. 1–10) is pure celebration: heaven erupts in praise, the twenty-four elders and four living creatures worship, the great multitude shouts like the roar of many waters, and the Bride has made herself ready in fine linen bright and pure — the righteous deeds of the saints. The second (vv. 11–21) is the appearing of the Rider: heaven opened, white horse, faithful and true, eyes of flame, many diadems, name unknown, Word of God, armies following, sharp sword from his mouth, King of kings. The beast and the false prophet are captured and thrown into the lake of fire.

The relationship between the two movements is crucial. The praise precedes the appearing; the wedding supper is announced before the battle is described. This is Revelation’s consistent pattern: the outcome is declared before the outworking. Heaven celebrates the marriage of the Lamb while the final confrontation with the beast is still being described. The sequence is not chronological; it is theological. The Lamb has already conquered. What the Rider on the white horse depicts is the visible manifestation of a victory already secured.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Hallelujah and the Marriage Supper
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–3: a great multitude cries Hallelujah! — Hebrew, untranslated, the great word of the psalter, and used in the New Testament only in these six verses, four times. The grounds are given: his judgments are true and just; for he has judged the great prostitute… and has avenged on her the blood of his servants — the two verbs the martyrs asked for at 6:10, now in the past tense. And the smoke from her goes up forever and ever (cf. Isa. 34:10).

Verses 4–5: the elders and living creatures, in their last appearance in the book, fall down and say two Hebrew words — Amen. Hallelujah! (cf. Ps. 106:48). Then a voice from the throne: Praise our God, all you his servants, you who fear him, small and great.

Verses 6–8: the last hallelujah, in a voice like many waters and thunder — the Lord our God the Almighty reigns (cf. Ps. 93:1; 97:1) — and the announcement the book has been travelling toward: the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his Bride has made herself ready; it was granted her to clothe herself with fine linen, bright and pure — for the fine linen is the righteous deeds of the saints.

Verses 9–10: the fourth beatitude, and one of the few sentences John is told to write down (cf. 14:13; 21:5) — Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb. John falls down to worship the angel and is stopped: You must not do that! I am a fellow servant with you… Worship God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Hallelujah and the Wedding

Heaven’s hallelujahs answer the martyrs’ prayer: God has judged and avenged. The marriage of the Lamb has come; the Bride is granted fine linen, which is the righteous deeds of the saints. Blessed are those invited — and worship God, not his messengers.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The prayer under the altar was not lost; it was answered.

Now: The hidden faithfulness of ordinary believers is being woven into the Bride’s dress.

verseByVerse.quote: After this I heard what seemed to be the loud voice of a great multitude in heaven, crying out, "Hallelujah! Salvation and glory and power belong to our God, for his judgments are true and just; for he has judged the great prostitute who corrupted the earth with her immorality, and has avenged on her the blood of his servants." Once more they cried out, "Hallelujah! The smoke from her goes up forever and ever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A great multitude in heaven cries “Hallelujah!” because salvation, glory and power belong to God, whose judgments are true and just: he has judged the great prostitute and avenged his servants’ blood, and her smoke rises forever. Heaven praises God’s just character, rejoicing that the martyrs’ prayers have been answered and the wrong put right for good.

Hallelujah. Chapter 18 ended with a millstone in the sea and a silent city. This is the reaction above. “Hallelujah” is Hebrew, left untranslated: hallelu-Yah, “praise Yah,” the short form of the divine name — the great word of the Psalter, opening and closing its final psalms. Every Jewish Christian present would hear his own liturgy. It appears four times in these six verses and nowhere else in the New Testament.

Praise for God’s character. The word most linked with Christian praise makes its only New Testament appearance at the funeral of an empire. That takes facing. But the reasons are given at once, and they aren’t what a modern reader fears: “Salvation and glory and power belong to our God, for his judgments are true and just.” The praise is for God’s character, not anyone’s suffering. Babylon had claimed all three — security, glamour, influence — for whoever would drink with her. Each turns out to have been his.

“How long” answered. “He has judged the great prostitute… and has avenged on her the blood of his servants.” Thirteen chapters ago the martyrs cried, “O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long before you will judge and avenge our blood…?” (6:10). Here are the same two verbs — judged and avenged — in the past tense, sung by a countless multitude.

Nothing forgotten. That is the whole content of the first hallelujah, and what a persecuted church most needs and most doubts. The prayer under the altar wasn’t filed and lost. It was answered, in order, at the appointed time, and the answer is being sung. A test: what prayer for justice have you been tempted to think God has filed and lost? He hasn’t.

Smoke forever. “Hallelujah! The smoke from her goes up forever and ever,” echoing Isaiah’s oracle on Edom: “its smoke shall go up forever” (Isaiah 34:10). A verdict that won’t be reversed — no rebuilding, no second edition. The city that said, “I sit as a queen… and mourning I shall never see” (18:7) got the permanence she asked for, but not the kind she wanted.
verseByVerse.note: “Hallelujah” means “praise the LORD” (Hebrew). In the New Testament it appears only here, four times in this chapter.

verseByVerse.quote: And the twenty-four elders and the four living creatures fell down and worshiped God who was seated on the throne, saying, "Amen. Hallelujah!" And from the throne came a voice saying, "Praise our God, all you his servants, you who fear him, small and great."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The elders and living creatures fall down and worship, saying, “Amen. Hallelujah!”, and a voice from the throne calls all God’s servants who fear him, small and great, to praise him. The highest beings simply agree with God’s praise, and every servant of God, however small, is equally summoned to worship.

Amen and hallelujah. The elders and creatures haven’t spoken since chapter 11, and this is their last appearance. Two Hebrew words, the oldest congregational response: “Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting! And let all the people say, ‘Amen!’ Praise the LORD!” (Psalm 106:48).

They agree. The beings closest to God add nothing original. “Amen” means it is firm, it is so; the whole contribution of the highest creatures at this moment is to say that what the multitude said is true. And they fall down — figures with thrones of their own who have spent the book throwing their crowns on the floor (4:10). The posture hasn’t changed.

“Our God.” A voice from the throne says, “Praise our God.” Not “my servants and me”: the speaker stands alongside the worshippers, so most take it as Christ’s voice or a living creature’s. Either way the summons to worship comes from inside the company, not down onto it.

Small and great. “All you his servants, you who fear him, small and great.” The phrase recurs in this book and always refuses a ranking: the servants God rewards (11:18), those who take the beast’s mark (13:16), the dead before the throne (20:12). Everyone is in one of two categories, and inside each no one is graded.

No tiers. Much Christian discouragement comes from suspecting there are tiers. The people summoned are described in exactly two ways: they serve him and they fear him. Not those who did notable things, nor those who understood this book. The choir is assembled by one qualification, and the smallest voice isn’t standing at the back. A test: do you hold back from worship because you feel second-rank? You are summoned by name. Praise him today.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I heard what seemed to be the voice of a great multitude, like the roar of many waters and like the sound of mighty peals of thunder, crying out, "Hallelujah! For the Lord our God the Almighty reigns. Let us rejoice and exult and give him the glory, for the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his Bride has made herself ready; it was granted her to clothe herself with fine linen, bright and pure"—for the fine linen is the righteous deeds of the saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A thunderous multitude cries, “Hallelujah! For the Lord our God the Almighty reigns,” and rejoices because the marriage of the Lamb has come and his Bride has made herself ready, granted fine linen that is the righteous deeds of the saints. God’s reign is visible at last, Christ and his people are united forever, and the Bride’s clothing is both his gift and her genuine godly life.

The loudest things John knows. The fourth and last hallelujah: a multitude, a waterfall, thunder — like all of them at once.

“The Lord… reigns.” The great announcement of the Psalms: “The LORD reigns” (Psalm 93:1; 97:1; 99:1). The tense means a reign has begun and stands — what the seventh trumpet announced (11:15), now sung by the whole company.

The wedding. The image isn’t new or ornamental. God is his people’s husband throughout the Old Testament: “your Maker is your husband” (Isaiah 54:5); “I will betroth you to me forever” (Hosea 2:19). Jesus called himself the bridegroom (Mark 2:19). Paul told husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church, then said it had been about Christ and the church all along (Ephesians 5:25–32). The book that opened with seven struggling congregations on a postal road ends with those congregations getting married.

“It was granted her.” One of the most carefully balanced sentences in the New Testament; hold both halves or it collapses. The dress was given. She didn’t buy, weave or earn it; the divine passive governs her wedding clothes too. Laodicea was counselled to “buy from me… white garments” (3:18); the multitude “washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (7:14). No one in this book wears anything he produced.

“The righteous deeds of the saints.” And yet the dress is made of something. John stops to say what the fabric is — not an abstraction but the actual things these people did. Both clauses are true and neither may be dropped. The righteousness that admits a sinner to the wedding is Christ’s and is given; the life that follows is truly his people’s own, and truly theirs to wear. Paul held them together easily: “work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you” (Philippians 2:12–13).

Being woven. Great comfort for a believer who suspects his life amounted to nothing. The visits no one recorded, the giving that hurt, years of patience with a difficult person, refusing to say the profitable untrue thing — they aren’t evaporating. They are being woven. When the Bride finally appears, that is what she has on. A test: what righteous deed is in front of you today? It is thread for the wedding dress.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel said to me, "Write this: Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb." And he said to me, "These are the true words of God." Then I fell down at his feet to worship him, but he said to me, "You must not do that! I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers who hold to the testimony of Jesus. Worship God." For the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John is told to write, “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb,” and when he falls to worship the angel, he is stopped: “I am a fellow servant… Worship God.” Entry to the feast is by gracious invitation, and only God may be worshipped — not even the glorious messengers through whom he speaks.

Write this. The fourth of the book’s seven blessings, and one of the few sentences John is specifically told to write (cf. 14:13; 21:5). Each time, the command comes over something a suffering church would find hard to believe.

Invited. Not those who earned a place, arranged one, or arrived early. A wedding invitation is the least meritorious document in the world; it says only that someone wanted you there. In Jesus’ parable, when the invited refused, the servants went out into the roads and gathered “all whom they found, both bad and good” (Matthew 22:10). A test: are you trying to earn your seat, or have you accepted the invitation?

Bride and guest. The church is the Bride in v. 7 and the guests in v. 9. The picture won’t resolve into one photograph and isn’t meant to. The point is relationship: the same people are married to him and welcomed by him.

“The true words of God.” The angel underwrites it, for the reader’s sake. No one needs assurance that the beast is real when the beast is at the door. It is the wedding that strains belief.

Worship God. John falls before the angel, here and again at 22:8–9, and both times is stopped. An apostle in the Spirit, who has seen the throne and the Lamb, twice goes down before a messenger. That is a comfort as well as a warning: it isn’t a stupid mistake. The angel is glorious, has brought God’s word, and has said something overwhelming. The instinct to worship is right; only the direction is wrong.

A permanent hazard. Those through whom God speaks are always in danger of receiving what belongs to God: the preacher whose congregation depends on him rather than Christ, the writer quoted more readily than Scripture, the movement that becomes the thing believed in. The angel’s answer settles it: “Worship God.” And his self-description is what every faithful minister must say: “I am a fellow servant with you” — not senior; alongside. A test: is there a teacher or leader you trust more readily than Christ himself?

The testimony of Jesus. “For the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy” — the testimony about Jesus or borne by him; both are true in this book. Everyone who holds it is in the prophetic company, so the apostle on the floor and the angel above him are colleagues. There is one rank in that room, and neither of them holds it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–21 — The Rider on the White Horse
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 11–13: heaven opens — not a door this time — and a rider comes out on a white horse, called Faithful and True (cf. 1:5; 3:14), and in righteousness he judges and makes war (cf. Isa. 11:3–4). His eyes are a flame of fire (1:14); on his head are many diadems, against the dragon’s seven and the beast’s ten; he has a name written that no one knows but himself; he is clothed in a robe dipped in blood; and he is called The Word of God — John’s own title for him (John 1:1).

Verses 14–16: the armies of heaven follow, arrayed in fine linen, white and pure — the Bride’s dress from v. 8, in the same words. From his mouth comes a sharp sword (1:16; Isa. 11:4); he will rule with a rod of iron (Ps. 2:9); he treads the winepress (Isa. 63:3). And on his robe and thigh: King of kings and Lord of lords (cf. Deut. 10:17; Rev. 17:14).

Verses 17–18: an angel standing in the sun calls the birds to the great supper of God (Ezek. 39:17–20), to eat the flesh of kings, captains, mighty men, horses and riders, both free and slave, both small and great. Verses 19–21: the beast and the kings gather to make war — and the beast was captured, with the false prophet, and both are thrown alive into the lake of fire; and the rest are slain by the sword from the rider’s mouth.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Rider on the White Horse

Faithful and True, crowned with many diadems, robed in blood, named the Word of God and King of kings and Lord of lords, the Rider strikes the nations with the sword of his mouth. The beast and false prophet are captured without a battle and thrown into the lake of fire.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The churches had no army; the armies of heaven ride out in wedding clothes and strike no blow.

Now: There are two suppers in this chapter: at one people are guests, at the other they are the meal.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw heaven opened, and behold, a white horse! The one sitting on it is called Faithful and True, and in righteousness he judges and makes war. His eyes are like a flame of fire, and on his head are many diadems, and he has a name written that no one knows but himself. He is clothed in a robe dipped in blood, and the name by which he is called is The Word of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Heaven opens and a rider on a white horse appears — called Faithful and True, judging and warring in righteousness, with eyes of fire, many crowns, a secret name, a robe dipped in blood, and the name the Word of God. This is Christ returning in glory as the righteous Judge and King, the same Lord who wrote to the churches.

Heaven opened. At 4:1 a door stood open and John was called up. This time heaven itself opens, and Someone comes out.

Not the rider of 6:2. The differences are deliberate and decisive. That rider had a bow; this one a sword from his mouth. That one was given one victor’s wreath; this one wears many royal diadems, handed to him by no one. That one was unnamed; this one has four names in six verses.

Faithful and True. Christ introduced himself to Laodicea as “the faithful and true witness” (3:14). The rider with the sword is the One who wrote the seven letters.

A war truly righteous. “In righteousness he judges and makes war” must be said in full. Every war has been declared righteous by those fighting it, and history is a graveyard of holy causes. This is the one case where the claim is true — because of who makes it, not because of the cause. Isaiah foretold a shoot from Jesse who would judge the poor with righteousness and “strike the earth with the rod of his mouth” (Isaiah 11:4).

Eyes and crowns. “Eyes… like a flame of fire” (1:14) — the eyes that saw what Sardis and Laodicea couldn’t see in themselves. “Many diadems”: the dragon wore seven (12:3), the beast ten (13:1); this rider wears uncounted crowns, and every one they claimed is on his head.

A name no one knows. Three names are given and a fourth withheld — one of the most restrained things in the book. He isn’t exhaustively knowable. After every doctrine is rightly stated, there is something in Christ no creature has been given, and Revelation says so at his moment of greatest self-disclosure. A test: does your knowledge of Christ lead you to wonder, or to think you have him figured out?

Whose blood is on his robe? He is bloodied before the battle begins (v. 19). Many take it as his own: the book turns on a Lamb “standing, as though it had been slain” (5:6), and every victory has been won by blood already shed — “they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb” (12:11). But the source is Isaiah 63, where a figure comes from Edom in crimson garments: “I have trodden the winepress alone… their lifeblood spattered on my garments” (Isaiah 63:3), and John quotes the winepress two verses later (v. 15). The more likely reading is that it is the blood of his enemies, though the Lamb who judges is the One who was slain. Either way, the outcome was settled before the battle began.

The Word of God. The one New Testament author who uses this title is the one writing: “In the beginning was the Word… and the Word was God” (John 1:1). It is his signature, identifying the rider beyond argument — and explaining the weapon. The conqueror whose name is the Word fights with his mouth.

verseByVerse.quote: And the armies of heaven, arrayed in fine linen, white and pure, were following him on white horses. From his mouth comes a sharp sword with which to strike down the nations, and he will rule them with a rod of iron. He will tread the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty. On his robe and on his thigh he has a name written, King of kings and Lord of lords.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The armies of heaven, dressed in white linen, follow him; from his mouth comes a sharp sword to strike the nations; he rules with a rod of iron and treads the winepress of God’s wrath; and on his robe and thigh is written “King of kings and Lord of lords.” Christ alone wins the final victory by his word; his people share it, dressed as his Bride, and he is the true Lord over every earthly ruler.

The army in wedding clothes. Six verses ago John told us what fine linen means: “the fine linen is the righteous deeds of the saints” (19:8). Same fabric, same words. The armies of heaven are dressed as the Bride. The church rides to the last battle in its wedding clothes — not armour, but linen. And nothing says the army does anything: no weapons, no blow struck. Its whole role in Scripture’s greatest battle is to be present, with him.

Never told to fight. That is this book’s last word on Christian militancy. The saints have been told to endure, hold fast, keep their garments on, and conquer by the Lamb’s blood and their testimony. They have never once been told to fight, and when the fighting finally comes they are spectators in white. A test: are you tempted to fight Christ’s battles with the world’s weapons — anger, force, manipulation? Your part is faithful witness.

Three images. The sword from the mouth (1:16; 2:16; cf. Isaiah 11:4); the rod of iron, Psalm 2:9 (quoted at 2:27; 12:5); the winepress, Isaiah 63:3 (trodden at 14:19–20).

Nothing in his hands. In a chapter full of horses, armies and coming slaughter, the conqueror carries nothing in his hands. What kills is what he says. That is why the church’s only armament in this book has been “the word of their testimony”: the weapon the saints have used all along is a small version of the one he finishes with.

A name on the thigh. Placed where a rider’s thigh is visible to everyone below; Greek statues sometimes bore inscriptions there. A title worn to be read. And it is God’s own: “the LORD your God is God of gods and Lord of lords” (Deuteronomy 10:17), already given the Lamb at 17:14, here with the order reversed.

Is this the second coming, and does chapter 20 follow it in time? This is Christ’s return in glory. Premillennial Christians read chapter 20 as the next stage, a thousand-year reign after his return. Amillennial Christians read chapter 20 as going back to describe the whole age leading up to it, as Revelation has done before (12:1–17). The more likely reading is the second: the battle of 19:19 and the battle of 20:8 are the same final battle, and the return in chapter 19 is the end of the thousand years, not the start.

What it meant to them. They lived where the emperor was called lord, his image on every coin they handled, their neighbours asked to say a few words about him that they couldn’t say; someone in the room had a relative in prison for it. Into that room came a sentence written on the thigh of a rider from an open heaven: “King of kings and Lord of lords.” Not a hope or a slogan, but a name already written, on Someone already riding. Who is lord in the place where you live and work? Name him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw an angel standing in the sun, and with a loud voice he called to all the birds that fly directly overhead, "Come, gather for the great supper of God, to eat the flesh of kings, the flesh of captains, the flesh of mighty men, the flesh of horses and their riders, and the flesh of all men, both free and slave, both small and great."
verseByVerse.commentary:
An angel standing in the sun calls all the birds to “the great supper of God” to eat the flesh of kings, captains, mighty men, horses and riders, and all people, free and slave, small and great. Everyone attends one of two suppers — the Lamb’s wedding feast or the feast of judgment — and no earthly rank protects those who oppose Christ.

From the highest point. The birds fly “directly overhead,” the phrase used of the eagle (8:13) and the gospel angel (14:6). Three times something is announced from the top of the sky where no one can miss it: a warning, a gospel, and this.

Ezekiel’s feast. Almost word for word Ezekiel 39, where God summons birds and beasts “to the sacrificial feast that I am preparing for you” to “eat the flesh of the mighty, and drink the blood of the princes of the earth” (Ezekiel 39:17–18).

Two suppers. The horror is the placement. Eight verses ago: “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb.” Here is the other supper, and the invitation goes to carrion birds. Two suppers, and everyone attends one. That shouldn’t be softened into a metaphor. At one, people are the guests. At the other, they are the meal. A test: to which supper are you invited — and have you accepted?

From the top down. “Flesh” five times, in a list that starts at the top: kings, commanders, strong men, cavalry — the whole apparatus of power — and then the phrase that refuses every ranking: “both small and great,” used of the beast’s mark (13:16) and of God’s worshippers (19:5), here of the dead.

The last word on human greatness. To lie unburied and eaten by birds was the ancient world’s most complete disgrace — David’s threat to Goliath (1 Samuel 17:46), what every army feared more than dying. A king in that state is indistinguishable from a slave. The chapter has just given a rider four names and an army in wedding linen; now it takes the alternative aristocracy — kings, captains, mighty men — and lists them by their meat. Whatever is built on rank, however permanent it looks, this is where it is going if it is built against him.

verseByVerse.quote: And I saw the beast and the kings of the earth with their armies gathered to make war against him who was sitting on the horse and against his army. And the beast was captured, and with it the false prophet who in its presence had done the signs by which he deceived those who had received the mark of the beast and those who worshiped its image. These two were thrown alive into the lake of fire that burns with sulfur. And the rest were slain by the sword that came from the mouth of him who was sitting on the horse, and all the birds were gorged with their flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The beast and the kings gather their armies against the rider and his army, but the beast and false prophet are simply captured and thrown alive into the lake of fire, and the rest are killed by the sword from his mouth. The final battle is no contest: Christ ends all opposition by his word, and the powers that seemed unbeatable are judged forever.

The muster arrives. This is the gathering of 16:14–16, the kings assembled by frog-spirits at Armageddon. The most famous battle in the world’s imagination is finally joined. Watch how long it lasts.

Captured. That is the battle. No engagement, no exchange, no account of fighting. The verb is passive, and the beast that the whole earth worshipped, that ruled every tribe and nation, that conquered the saints for forty-two months, is arrested in four words. John built thirteen chapters of dread and refuses the confrontation a sentence of drama. That isn’t carelessness; it is the argument. What needs no fight was never the equal of the One who ends it. Every reader frightened by the beast is told what it actually weighs when the rider arrives. A test: what fear looms largest for you? Measure it against this verse.

Charged with deception. The false prophet is named by his charge sheet: the one “who… had done the signs by which he deceived.” In a book whose enemy is “the deceiver of the whole world,” that is the indictment that matters.

The lake of fire. Its first appearance. It will receive the dragon (20:10), Death and Hades (20:14), and everyone not written in the book of life (20:15). “Alive” is deliberate: this isn’t annihilation on a battlefield.

The sword from the mouth. For the last time, this is what it does. The armies that followed the beast the whole book are ended by something spoken (cf. 2 Thessalonians 2:8). Not one member of the army in linen is recorded lifting a hand.

The book’s final answer. The seven churches had no army, legal standing, leverage, or means to resist the power arrayed against them. Revelation never tells them to acquire any of it. It tells them to endure, keep their garments on, hold the testimony, and conquer by blood already shed — and then shows them the end, in which they ride out in wedding clothes behind Someone who doesn’t need them. His eyes are fire, his crowns uncounted; he is Faithful and True, the Word of God, King of kings and Lord of lords, with a name no one knows but himself. He came out of an open heaven, and the war the whole earth assembled for was over before it began. The only weapon he used was his mouth.

20.title: The Thousand Years and the Great White Throne
20.overview:
Chapter 20 contains the most debated passage in the most debated book of the Bible: the millennium. The thousand-year reign of Christ with his saints (vv. 1–6) has divided serious, Scripture-loving Christians for two thousand years and continues to do so. The amillennial position is followed here as the Reformed mainstream, with all four major views presented with genuine respect and fairness. The stakes in this debate are high — but the non-negotiables that all four views share are higher: Christ will return, the dead will be raised, the wicked will be judged, the righteous will be glorified, and God will be all in all.

The Four Positions — Stated Fairly: Dispensational Premillennialism (MacArthur, Walvoord, Ryrie, Swindoll): After the pre-tribulation Rapture and the seven-year tribulation, Christ returns bodily to earth and establishes a literal thousand-year kingdom centred in Jerusalem, with a rebuilt temple and a restored national Israel fulfilling the Old Testament covenants. Satan is literally bound in the abyss. The martyred saints and tribulation believers are resurrected to reign with Christ. At the end of the millennium, Satan is released, defeated, and cast into the lake of fire. Then the Great White Throne judgment and the eternal state. Historic Premillennialism (Ladd, Grudem): Similar to dispensational, but without the pre-trib Rapture — the church goes through the tribulation. Christ returns, binds Satan, raises the martyrs (the first resurrection), and reigns on earth for a literal thousand years. Postmillennialism (Jonathan Edwards, Charles Hodge, Warfield in some respects): The thousand years represents the gospel era of expanding Christian influence, gradually Christianising the world through the preaching of the gospel, before Christ returns to a world largely won for the kingdom. The binding of Satan is the progressive restriction of his power through the gospel. Amillennialism (Augustine, Calvin, Vos, Berkhof, Hoekema, Beale — the position followed here): The thousand years is the entire period between the first and second comings of Christ — the church age. The binding of Satan (vv. 1–3) was accomplished at the cross (John 12:31; Colossians 2:15; Luke 10:18) and restricts his ability to deceive the nations so the gospel can go to all peoples. The first resurrection (vv. 4–6) is the spiritual resurrection of souls reigning with Christ in heaven now, or the new birth through which believers participate in Christ’s resurrection life. The thousand years is a symbolic number (10 x 10 x 10 = complete fullness) for the complete church age. Satan’s release at the end (vv. 7–9) represents the brief intensification of opposition immediately before Christ’s return. The Great White Throne (vv. 11–15) is the final universal judgment of all the dead.

The chapter divides into two sections: the millennium and Satan’s career (vv. 1–10) and the Great White Throne (vv. 11–15). Both sections are eschatologically essential and both are theologically clear on the matters that count: no one escapes the final judgment, no name not written in the book of life survives it, and the last enemies — Death and Hades themselves — are thrown into the lake of fire. Whatever one believes about the millennium, these outcomes are certain.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–3: one angel with a key and a chain seizes, binds, throws, shuts and seals the dragon — named with the four names of 12:9 — for a thousand years, and the binding is given a stated purpose: so that he might not deceive the nations any longer. After that he must be released for a little while, using the word of divine necessity.

Verse 4: thrones, with authority to judge committed to those on them; the souls of those beheaded for the testimony of Jesus and those who had not worshipped the beast or taken its mark; they came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years. Verses 5–6: the rest of the dead did not come to life until the thousand years were ended. This is the first resurrection. Then the fifth beatitude: Blessed and holy is the one who shares in the first resurrection! Over such the second death has no power, but they will be priests of God and of Christ, and they will reign with him.

Verses 7–8: Satan is released, deceives the nations at the four corners of the earth — Gog and Magog (Ezek. 38–39) — and gathers a host like the sand of the sea. Verses 9–10: they surround the camp of the saints and the beloved city, fire comes down and consumes them, and the devil is thrown into the lake of fire where the beast and false prophet already are.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Thousand Years

An angel binds the dragon so that he may no longer deceive the nations; those who refused the beast reign with Christ; and after a brief release Satan’s last host is consumed and he is thrown into the lake of fire. Premillennial, amillennial and postmillennial readers differ on the timing, and agree on all that the creeds require.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The people the world beheaded and shut out of the market are seen on thrones.

Now: Over those who share in the first resurrection the second death has no power — on that there is no dispute.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw an angel coming down from heaven, holding in his hand the key to the bottomless pit and a great chain. And he seized the dragon, that ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years, and threw him into the pit, and shut it and sealed it over him, so that he might not deceive the nations any longer, until the thousand years were ended. After that he must be released for a little while.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An angel with the key of the abyss and a great chain seizes the dragon — Satan — binds him for a thousand years, and seals him in the pit so that he can no longer deceive the nations, until he must be released for a little while. Satan is a defeated enemy whom God restrains at will; whatever view one takes of the thousand years, his power to keep the nations in darkness has been broken.

Agreed by everyone. Before the thousand years, three things all readers agree on, easily lost in the argument. First, the arrest is effortless. One angel, one chain, five verbs: seized, bound, threw, shut, sealed. The creature with seven heads and ten diadems, who gave the beast its throne and deceived the whole world, is handled by a single unnamed angel with a set of keys. No one has to fight him. Second, the four names are those of 12:9, in the same order — dragon, ancient serpent, devil, Satan — reaching back to the serpent in the garden and closing the file opened in Genesis 3. Third, the binding has a stated purpose: “so that he might not deceive the nations any longer.” John defines it himself, and it is specific.

What are the thousand years? The phrase occurs six times in six verses and nowhere else in Scripture, and godly readers understand it in three main ways. The premillennial reading takes the chapter in order: Christ returns at the end of chapter 19, Satan is bound, Christ reigns on earth for a thousand years, Satan is released, the last rebellion is crushed, and the final judgment follows. Historic premillennialism (George Eldon Ladd, Wayne Grudem) has the church go through the tribulation; dispensational premillennialism (Walvoord, Ryrie, MacArthur, the Scofield tradition) adds a pre-tribulation rapture and sees the millennium as the fulfilment of God’s promises to national Israel. What favours it is considerable: the narrative flows on from chapter 19 with “Then I saw”; the Old Testament promises of a kingdom on earth — the wolf with the lamb, a man living in the house he built (Isaiah 11:6–9; 65:20–25) — get somewhere to land; and above all, in v. 5 the verb used of the martyrs coming to life is used of “the rest of the dead,” whose resurrection everyone agrees is bodily. The amillennial reading takes the thousand years as the whole age between Christ’s comings, the age the church is in now. Satan was bound at the cross, in exactly the sense v. 3 specifies: he can no longer keep the nations in the dark. The saints’ reign is with Christ in heaven, which is why John sees “souls” (v. 4). Christ returns once; there is one resurrection and one judgment. This is the position of Augustine, the Reformers broadly, Hendriksen, Beale and Vos. What favours it: numbers in this book are symbolic throughout, and a thousand is ten cubed, completeness raised to the highest power; the chapter never places Christ on earth during these years; Jesus used this very image of his own ministry — “how can someone enter a strong man’s house and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man?” (Matthew 12:29) — and on the eve of the cross said, “now will the ruler of this world be cast out” (John 12:31), before the nations came in. Before Christ, God had one nation; since Christ the gospel has reached every continent — what a dragon prevented from deceiving the nations would look like. And “Then I saw” marks the order of John’s visions, not always of events: the seals, trumpets and bowls each reach the end, and chapter 12 goes back to Christ’s birth. The postmillennial reading holds that the gospel will succeed so widely that a long Christianised era follows, with Christ returning at its end — held by Jonathan Edwards and Charles Hodge, and today by Kenneth Gentry. It draws on the mustard seed and the leaven (Matthew 13:31–33), Psalms 2 and 72, Isaiah 2:2–4, the Great Commission, and “he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet” (1 Corinthians 15:25). Its difficulty is the New Testament’s consistent expectation of apostasy and tribulation before the end (Matthew 24:9–13; 2 Timothy 3:1–5) and the final deception in this very chapter. The more likely reading is the amillennial one: the thousand years are the present age of the gospel, which ends at Christ’s return.

What all three share. All three hold everything the creeds require and agree on far more than they dispute: Christ has decisively defeated Satan; he will return bodily, visibly, personally; the dead will be raised; there will be a final judgment; the wicked condemned and the redeemed living in a new creation; and the church’s duty now is faithfulness under pressure. The disagreement is about timing and sequence. So a Christian may hold any of the three and be entirely orthodox, and the right response to a brother who reads it differently isn’t suspicion. Some of the godliest people who ever lived have been on each side.

How can Satan be bound if he still prowls like a roaring lion? He does (1 Peter 5:8), and he blinds unbelievers (2 Corinthians 4:4). But the binding is specific: “so that he might not deceive the nations any longer.” Before Christ came, the nations were held in darkness; now the gospel goes to every nation, and Satan can’t stop it. A dog on a chain is still dangerous to anyone who comes within reach, but it can’t stop the house being plundered. A test: do you share the gospel as one who knows the strong man is bound?

Released for a little while. Even the release is on a permission with a term — “he must be released,” the divine “must” that has governed the book since 1:1. Why release him? To show the unchanged hostility of the unrepentant world toward God, and to make the justice of the final judgment plain to all. Nothing the dragon does, including his last rampage, is outside the timetable.
verseByVerse.note: The thousand years (the millennium) is read in three main ways: Christ’s present reign from heaven through the church age (amillennial); a future reign on earth after his return (premillennial); or a golden age of gospel success before his return (postmillennial).

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw thrones, and seated on them were those to whom the authority to judge was committed. Also I saw the souls of those who had been beheaded for the testimony of Jesus and for the word of God, and those who had not worshiped the beast or its image and had not received its mark on their foreheads or their hands. They came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John sees thrones given to those with authority to judge, and the souls of those beheaded for Jesus and of all who refused the beast’s mark; they come to life and reign with Christ for a thousand years. Those whom the world rejected, condemned and killed for Christ are the ones who reign with him — the world’s verdict on them is reversed.

Thrones. Plural, and John doesn’t say who sits on them. Laodicea was promised, “I will grant him to sit with me on my throne” (3:21); Jesus told the Twelve they would sit on thrones (Matthew 19:28); Paul asked, “do you not know that the saints will judge the world?” (1 Corinthians 6:2).

One company, two sides. The souls of those beheaded, “and those who had not worshiped the beast.” Two groups, or one described twice? The Greek allows either, and it may well be one company: those who died for refusing and those who lived without yielding. If so, the reign belongs to everyone who refused the mark, not to a sub-class of martyrs.

Beheaded. Execution by the axe, the Roman method for citizens, the death Paul is said to have died. John doesn’t say “killed”; he says how. And “had not received its mark” — chapter 13 said no one could buy or sell without it. These people couldn’t buy or sell, and here they are on thrones.

What does “came to life” mean here? The verb simply means “lived” or “came to life.” The premillennial reading takes it as bodily resurrection, and its argument from v. 5 is the strongest single argument in the whole debate: the identical verb is used one sentence later of “the rest of the dead,” whose coming to life is bodily, and a word ought to mean the same thing twice in two verses. The amillennial reading answers that John says what he saw, and it was souls — the word he used of the martyrs under the altar (6:9), conscious, speaking, awaiting the resurrection. On that view, coming to life is what happens to a believer at death: the soul goes to be with Christ — “My desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better” (Philippians 1:23) — and reigns with him. Some take it instead of the new birth: God “made us alive together with Christ… and seated us with him in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 2:5–6). The more likely reading is that this is the life of believers who have died, reigning now with Christ in heaven (see on vv. 5–6). The verb can bear either, and both readings are held by people who take every word of Scripture seriously.

The verdict reversed. On what the verse is for there is no dispute. Look at who reigns. None held office. They were beheaded, boycotted, shut out of the market, unable to buy bread, tried in courts that found against them, buried by people afraid to say why. The world’s verdict was recorded and is still on file. And John sees them on thrones, with authority to judge, reigning with Christ. That is what the whole book does from chapter 1: it reverses the verdict. The people the world disposed of are on the thrones, and the arrangement is already in force. A test: whose verdict on your life are you living by — the world’s, or Christ’s?

verseByVerse.quote: The rest of the dead did not come to life until the thousand years were ended. This is the first resurrection. Blessed and holy is the one who shares in the first resurrection! Over such the second death has no power, but they will be priests of God and of Christ, and they will reign with him for a thousand years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rest of the dead don’t come to life until the thousand years end; this is the first resurrection, and those who share in it are blessed and holy — the second death has no power over them, and they will be priests of God and of Christ and reign with him. Whatever the details, believers are completely safe from final condemnation and will share Christ’s priestly reign.

Two comings to life. One sentence carries the weight of the argument at v. 4. On the premillennial reading the parallel is decisive: two groups, two comings-to-life a thousand years apart, the same verb. On the amillennial reading John distinguishes them by naming only one “the first resurrection,” and saying plainly that the other happens at the end.

A clue in John’s vocabulary. He speaks of “the second death” (vv. 6, 14), which is plainly a death of a different kind from the first — the first a body in a grave, the second a lake of fire. If “second death” can name something of a different order from the first death, “first resurrection” may name something of a different order from the second. That is the amillennial answer, and a real one; a premillennial reader will reply that the parallel with v. 5 is closer. The reader should weigh both.

What is the first resurrection? Premillennial Christians take it as the bodily resurrection of believers before a literal thousand-year reign. But John sees the souls of the martyrs (v. 4), and the rest of the New Testament speaks of one resurrection of righteous and wicked at the last day: “an hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out” (John 5:28–29; cf. Acts 24:15). The more likely reading is that the first resurrection is the life of believers who have died, reigning with Christ now in heaven, matching the new birth by which they first came to life; the second resurrection is the bodily one at the end. And the thousand years is a symbolic number for the whole, complete age between Christ’s comings.

Blessed and holy. The fifth of the book’s seven blessings, the only one with a second adjective: not merely blessed but holy — set apart, belonging to God.

No jurisdiction. “Over such the second death has no power.” Not “they will probably escape it.” The word is the legal term for authority: the second death has no jurisdiction; it can’t bring a case. Smyrna was promised this: “The one who conquers will not be hurt by the second death” (2:11). That answers the deepest fear in this chapter. A Christian may reasonably be unsure of the millennium’s timing; he may not reasonably be unsure of this. Whatever is coming at the great white throne, one category of person is outside its reach, and the reason isn’t their record but that their names are in the book of the Lamb who was slain. A test: is your assurance resting on him?

Priests and kings. “They will be priests of God and of Christ” — the promise of 1:6 and 5:10 arriving. A priest has access, offers, and carries others’ names into God’s presence; they won’t be standing about being rewarded but serving in the nearest place there is. “And they will reign with him” — with him, the qualifier that keeps it from being a fantasy of vindication. No one reigns on his own account. The two offices together were promised at Sinai and never achieved — “a kingdom of priests” (Exodus 19:6) — and they meet in one person, who is King of kings and the slaughtered Lamb. His people get both because they are with him.
verseByVerse.note: The fifth of the seven “blessed” sayings in Revelation.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the thousand years are ended, Satan will be released from his prison and will come out to deceive the nations that are at the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog, to gather them for battle; their number is like the sand of the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the thousand years end, Satan is released and goes out to deceive the nations at the four corners of the earth — Gog and Magog — gathering them, countless as the sand, for battle. Evil never changes or repents; its final rebellion is still only by God’s permission and a counterfeit of his promises.

Released. The passive again; v. 3 said he “must” be. Even the last rebellion is on a licence from the throne.

Back to deceiving. He does exactly what he was bound to keep him from: he goes out “to deceive the nations,” the verb that has defined him since 12:9. Nothing learned, nothing changed; after a thousand years in a sealed pit, the first thing he does is start talking. That settles a question about the devil’s end. He doesn’t repent, negotiate or reconsider. Evil in this book has no capacity for development; it only repeats itself to a larger audience.

Gog and Magog. From Ezekiel 38–39, where Gog of the land of Magog gathers a coalition from the far north against a people living securely without walls, and is destroyed by fire from heaven (Ezekiel 38:22; 39:6). John compresses two chapters into two words. And he uses them as he has used every name in this book — as a type, not an address. Babylon wasn’t Babylon; Sodom and Egypt weren’t Sodom and Egypt; Gog and Magog isn’t a country but the last coalition of everything opposed to God. The clue: these nations are “at the four corners of the earth,” which isn’t a place either.

Like the sand of the sea. One of the most loaded phrases in the Old Testament: God’s promise to Abraham, “I will surely multiply your offspring as the stars of heaven and as the sand that is on the seashore” (Genesis 22:17). The enemy assembles a counterfeit of Abraham’s promise. That is the dragon’s last act in Scripture and what he has done at every stage: a beast parodying the Lamb’s resurrection, a false prophet with lamb’s horns, a mark answering a seal, a prostitute answering a bride, and now a countless host answering the countless family promised to a childless man outside his tent at night.

Two countless crowds. The last enemy army can’t be counted — and the multitude before the throne in chapter 7 was one “that no one could number.” Two uncountable crowds. Only one is real, and the other is about to be described in a single verse. A test: which crowd are you part of? Make sure it is the one standing before the throne.
verseByVerse.note: Gog and Magog come from Ezekiel’s vision of a last great attack on God’s people.

verseByVerse.quote: And they marched up over the broad plain of the earth and surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city, but fire came down from heaven and consumed them, and the devil who had deceived them was thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur where the beast and the false prophet were, and they will be tormented day and night forever and ever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The nations surround the camp of the saints and the beloved city, but fire from heaven consumes them, and the devil is thrown into the lake of fire with the beast and false prophet, to be tormented forever. God’s people, though surrounded and helpless, are rescued by God alone, and Satan’s defeat is final and eternal.

Camp and city. Two images for God’s people. “The camp of the saints” is Israel in the wilderness — tents, no walls, a people on the move, defended by nothing but the Presence among them. “The beloved city” is Zion, the city God loves (Psalm 78:68; 87:2). Pilgrim camp and settled city held together, which is what the church always is.

Surrounded. Not attacked at a point but encircled on every side by a host like the sand of the sea. A more hopeless military position couldn’t be described.

Then fire. “But fire came down from heaven and consumed them.” That is the battle: one clause, no engagement, the saints lifting no hand, as in chapter 19. The image is Ezekiel 39:6, with Sodom and Carmel behind it. And it is the fire James and John once asked to call down on a Samaritan village, and were rebuked (Luke 9:54–55). The fire is real, and it isn’t the church’s to call.

The posture of the whole book. The saints are surrounded and do nothing. They have no weapons, strategy or plan of breakout, and aren’t rebuked for lacking one. What is asked of them, from the first letter to the last battle, is endurance and faith — and then the sky opens over those who came to finish them. A test: when you feel hemmed in, are you scrambling for your own escape plan, or trusting God to act?

Is this the same battle as 19:19–21? The more likely reading is yes: both draw on Ezekiel 38–39, both gather the nations for battle, and both end at once with God’s judgment. Premillennial Christians see two battles a thousand years apart. And it isn’t a literal siege of Jerusalem but the world’s final assault on the camp of the saints and the beloved city — God’s people wherever they are.

The devil’s epitaph. The unholy trinity together for the last time: the beast and false prophet went in at 19:20, and here is the third — and John notes they are still there. He is described one last time by what he did: “the devil who had deceived them.” Not the great red dragon with seven diadems, nor the accuser, nor the prince of the power of the air — the one who told lies, thrown into a lake, in the passive voice, by Someone the verse doesn’t bother to name.

Is the punishment conscious and unending, and does it apply to lost people as well as the devil? “Forever and ever” is the New Testament’s strongest phrase for duration, and the lost share the same lake of fire (v. 15; 14:11; Matthew 25:41). Some evangelicals hold that the wicked will finally be destroyed and cease to exist, and that the torment is only for the devil and his agents. But Jesus sets eternal punishment beside eternal life: “these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matthew 25:46). The more likely reading is that the punishment of the lost, like the devil’s, is conscious and without end.

The heel on the head. The serpent who spoke in the garden has said his last word. Cast out at the cross, thrown down to earth, given a short time, bound, released briefly — and now finished. The head that was promised to be bruised (Genesis 3:15) is under the heel of the child the dragon stood waiting to devour.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 11: a great white throne, and one seated on it whom John does not describe — as he refused to describe the one on the throne in chapter 4. From his presence earth and sky fled away, and no place was found for them.

Verse 12: the dead, great and small, standing before the throne, and books were opened. Then another book was opened, which is the book of life. And the dead were judged by what was written in the books, according to what they had done (cf. Dan. 7:10).

Verse 13: the sea gives up its dead, and Death and Hades give up theirs, and they were judged, each one of them. Verse 14: Then Death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire. This is the second death, the lake of fire. Verse 15: And if anyone’s name was not found written in the book of life, he was thrown into the lake of fire.
verseByVerse.theology:
Judged by Works, Saved by a Name

Before the great white throne earth and sky flee, and all the dead, great and small, are judged by what is written in the books. Death and Hades are thrown into the lake of fire, and anyone whose name is not found in the book of life follows them.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Even the sea gives up its dead; nobody is missing, and each is judged by name.

Now: The question is not whether you have done enough, but whether your name is in the Lamb’s book — and the water of life is offered without price.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw a great white throne and him who was seated on it. From his presence earth and sky fled away, and no place was found for them. And I saw the dead, great and small, standing before the throne, and books were opened. Then another book was opened, which is the book of life. And the dead were judged by what was written in the books, according to what they had done.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John sees a great white throne, from whose presence earth and sky flee, and all the dead, great and small, standing before it; books are opened, and the book of life, and the dead are judged by their deeds. Every person will stand before God’s perfect justice, and while all are judged by their works, the book of life — the Lamb’s register of names — decides who is saved.

The last throne. The book has been full of thrones since chapter 4; this is the last. Great, so that its size settles who is in charge. White, the colour in this book of purity and verdicts. And John doesn’t describe who sits on it, any more than in chapter 4. He says what happens in his presence.

No scenery. “From his presence earth and sky fled away, and no place was found for them.” The most quietly terrifying sentence in the chapter. Nothing is said to be destroyed; the universe simply can’t stay in the room. The ground under your feet and the sky over your head — the definition of what is permanent — get up and leave, with nowhere to go. So the last judgment has no scenery. Every human court sits somewhere, a room in a country whose laws apply. This one has no location, because the location has gone. Nothing in the frame but a throne, its occupant, and the people standing.

Great and small. The last hierarchy flattened. Emperors and slaves, those whose statues filled the forum and those whose names were never written anywhere, standing on the same floor. No one is represented by counsel or has a better seat.

The books and the book. Books, plural, then a book, singular, and the distinction is the gospel. Daniel saw it: “the court sat in judgment, and the books were opened” (Daniel 7:10). The books hold the record — “what they had done.” Nothing is missing; Jesus said every careless word will be accounted for (Matthew 12:36).

How can anyone be judged by works if salvation is by grace through faith? The New Testament holds both: no one is justified by works of the law (Galatians 2:16), and God “will render to each one according to his works” (Romans 2:6; cf. 2 Corinthians 5:10). They aren’t in tension once it is clear what each answers. The books of deeds establish the case, and the case is unanswerable: everyone standing there is guilty on the record. The book of life isn’t a second, better record of the same kind. It is a register of names, and v. 15 says it alone decides.

Do believers stand before this throne? All the dead stand there, great and small. For believers, the book of life decides: their names are written, and they are acquitted in Christ, while their works are reviewed for reward (2 Corinthians 5:10). Premillennial Christians often distinguish a judgment of believers from this one; the more likely reading is that there is one final judgment, where the book of life separates the saved from the lost.

Not a thin file. No one is saved because his file is thin. He is saved because his name is in the book of the Lamb who was slain (13:8), written from the foundation of the world. The deeds are real, are read, and matter — and they aren’t what gets anyone through. A test: if your file were read aloud today, what would you plead? Plead only his blood.

verseByVerse.quote: And the sea gave up the dead who were in it, Death and Hades gave up the dead who were in them, and they were judged, each one of them, according to what they had done. Then Death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire. This is the second death, the lake of fire. And if anyone's name was not found written in the book of life, he was thrown into the lake of fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sea, Death and Hades give up their dead, and each is judged by what they have done; then Death and Hades are thrown into the lake of fire, the second death, along with anyone whose name is not written in the book of life. No one is forgotten, death itself will be destroyed, and the one thing that matters on that day is whether your name is in the Lamb’s book.

No one missing. Three custodians, each handing over what it held. The sea is named separately for a reason a first-century reader felt at once: lost at sea meant no grave, no body, no name on a stone — the most complete disappearance there was. The sea gives them up. The list reaches every kind of forgotten person: the sailor whose ship went down, the woman in an unmarked grave, the child in a plague pit, the person whose family died out and whose name no one has spoken for centuries. Death and Hades kept their records perfectly and hand over the whole file.

Each one. “They were judged, each one of them.” John won’t let it be a mass. In a scene including every human being who ever lived, the judgment is individual — one at a time, on the evidence, by name.

Death executed. “Death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire.” The riders of the fourth seal (6:8). The risen Christ said, “I have the keys of Death and Hades” (1:18), and this is what he does with them. Not merely disarmed — executed. “The last enemy to be destroyed is death” (1 Corinthians 15:26); “He will swallow up death forever” (Isaiah 25:8). Take that as concretely as it deserves. Death won’t be managed, explained or made bearable. It will be killed. Everything you have lost to it — the funerals, the diagnosis, the phone call at four in the morning — was inflicted by something that will itself be thrown into a lake and won’t be coming back. Grieve with that hope.

Defined. “This is the second death, the lake of fire.” John defines his term, as throughout. The promise to Smyrna — “The one who conquers will not be hurt by the second death” (2:11) — now has its definition attached.

Found. “If anyone’s name was not found written in the book of life.” Stated negatively, and with the verb “found” again: someone looked — the word used of the blood in Babylon’s foundations (18:24), here of a search through a register.

The criterion. The sentence that makes Revelation what it is, and it shouldn’t be blunted. Twenty chapters have said there are two companies, two destinations, and everyone in one of them. Here the criterion is a single sentence. Not achievement, sincerity, or how one compares with a neighbour. A name, in a book, belonging to the Lamb.

Frightening or reassuring. It is either the most frightening sentence in Scripture or the most reassuring, depending on one question, which the book answers two chapters later. It isn’t “Have I done enough?” — no one at that throne has. It is whether a person has come to the One who says, “let the one who desires take the water of life without price” (22:17). The books are opened and the record is accurate. And the other book isn’t a better record. It is a list of people the Lamb bought with his blood, written before the world was made, and nothing in the first set of books can get a name off it. A test: have you come to him? If not, come today.

After that he must be released for a little while.<sup>4</sup>Then I saw thrones, and seated on them were those to whom the authority to judge was committed. Also I saw the souls of those who had been beheaded for the testimony of Jesus and for the word of God, and those who had not worshiped the beast or its image and had not received its mark on their foreheads or their hands. They came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years.<sup>5</sup>The rest of the dead did not come to life until the thousand years were ended. This is the first resurrection.<sup>6</sup>Blessed and holy is the one who shares in the first resurrection! Over such the second death has no power, but they will be priests of God and of Christ, and they will reign with him for a thousand years.<sup>7</sup>And when the thousand years are ended, Satan will be released from his prison<sup>8</sup>and will come out to deceive the nations that are at the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog, to gather them for battle; their number is like the sand of the sea.<sup>9</sup>And they marched up over the broad plain of the earth and surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city, but fire came down from heaven and consumed them,<sup>10</sup>and the devil who had deceived them was thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur where the beast and the false prophet were, and they will be tormented day and night forever and ever.<sup>11</sup>Then I saw a great white throne and him who was seated on it. From his presence earth and sky fled away, and no place was found for them.<sup>12</sup>And I saw the dead, great and small, standing before the throne, and books were opened. Then another book was opened, which is the book of life. And the dead were judged by what was written in the books, according to what they had done.<sup>13</sup>And the sea gave up the dead who were in it, Death and Hades gave up the dead who were in them, and they were judged, each one of them, according to what they had done.<sup>14</sup>Then Death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire. This is the second death, the lake of fire.<sup>15</sup>And if anyone’s name was not found written in the book of life, he was thrown into the lake of fire.
